label: prob:ordinary
title: Problem
body_md:
\label{prob:ordinary}
Which nonabelian finite simple groups $G$ have an ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup $A$ with $1<A<G$?
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $G$ be a nonabelian finite simple group, and let $1<A<G$.
Up to isomorphism, $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable if and only if one of the following holds.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] $G=\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ with $q\geq4$ and $q\not\equiv3\pmod4$. We have $|A|=2$.
\item[(2)] $G={}^2B_2(2^{2a+1})$ with $a\geq1$. We have $|A|=2$.
\item[(3)] $G=J_1$ and $|A|=2$.
\item[(4)] $G=\operatorname{Sp}_4(4)$ and $A=\langle t\rangle$. We have $|t|=2$ and $|C_G(t)|=256$.
\item[(5)] $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(p)$, where $p$ is prime and $p\equiv1,13,17\pmod{24}$.
The subgroup $A=\langle t\rangle$ has order $2$.
There is $s\in\operatorname{Sp}_4(p)$ with $s^2=-I$ and $\pi(s)=t$,
where $\pi:\operatorname{Sp}_4(p)\to G$ is the quotient map.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: def:g-permutable
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:g-permutable}
Let $A\leq G$.
We call $A$ \emph{ordinary $G$-permutable} if every $B\leq G$ satisfies $AB^x=B^xA$ for some $x\in G$.
In addition, we call $A$ \emph{hereditarily $G$-permutable} if $A$ is ordinary $E$-permutable for every $A\leq E\leq G$.
head: environment

label: lem:max
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:max}
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable, and let $M$ be maximal in $G$.
Then, either $A\leq M^x$ or $G=AM^x$ for some $x\in G$.
If $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$, then $|A|\mid|M|$.
If $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$, then $|A|\mid\gcd\{|M|:M<G\text{ is maximal}\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We choose $x\in G$ with $AM^x=M^xA$.
Since $M^x$ is maximal and $M^x\leq AM^x\leq G$, we have $AM^x=M^x$ or $AM^x=G$.
If $AM^x=G$, then we have $G=(M^xA)^{x^{-1}}=MA^{x^{-1}}$.
If $MY\ne G$ for all $Y<G$, then we must have $A\leq M^x$.
Hence, $|A|\mid|M|$.
If $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$, then this divisibility holds for every maximal subgroup $M<G$.
Thus, $|A|\mid\gcd\{|M|:M<G\text{ is maximal}\}$.
head: environment

label: lem:involution-normalizers
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $K=\langle t\rangle B^x$ is a subgroup for some $x\in G$.
If $t\in B^x$, then $t\in N_G(B^x)$.
If $t\notin B^x$, then $[K:B^x]=2$ and hence $B^x\unlhd K$.
In both situations, we obtain that $t\in N_G(B^x)$.
Since $N_G(B^x)^{x^{-1}}=N_G(B)$, we have $t^{x^{-1}}\in N_G(B)$.

Conversely, suppose that $t^g\in N_G(B)$ for some $g\in G$.
Then, $t\in N_G(B^{g^{-1}})$, so $\langle t\rangle B^{g^{-1}}=B^{g^{-1}}\langle t\rangle$.
head: environment

label: lem:involution
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:involution}
Let $A=\langle t\rangle$ have order $2$.
Suppose that every involution of $G$ equals $t^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Then, $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable if and only if $|N_G(B)|$ is even for every $B\leq G$ with $|B|$ odd.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, every $B\leq G$ has $t^g\in N_G(B)$ for some $g\in G$.
Thus, $|N_G(B)|$ is even.
Conversely, suppose that $|N_G(B)|$ is even whenever $|B|$ is odd.
Since $B\leq N_G(B)$, we also have $|N_G(B)|$ even for $|B|$ even.
Hence, every $B\leq G$ has an involution $s\in N_G(B)$.
As every involution is conjugate to $t$, we choose $g\in G$ with $s=t^g$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, we conclude that $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

label: lem:index3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C=\operatorname{Core}_K(D)$.
Let $\rho:K\to S_{K/D}$ satisfy $\rho(k)(gD)=kgD$ for $k,g\in K$.
Since $\ker\rho=C$ and $[K:D]=3$, we have $K/C\leq S_3$.
Note that $\rho(D)$ fixes the coset $D$, so $[D:C]\leq2$.
Because $D$ is cyclic and $[D:C]\leq2$, we have $C=D$ or $C=D^2$.
As $D^2$ is characteristic in $D$, both $C=D$ and $C=D^2$ imply that $D^2\unlhd K$.
head: environment

label: lem:abelian-index
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L=K/C$ and $D=B/C$.
Next, we consider the faithful action of $L$ on the $r$ cosets of $D$.
The stabilizer $D$ is abelian. If $D=1$, then we have $[B:C]=1$.
Suppose that $D\ne1$.
Since $[L:D]=r$ is prime, $D$ is maximal in $L$.
If $N_L(D)=L$, then the subgroup $D$ lies in the kernel of the action.
Hence, $N_L(D)=D$.
For $g\in L$ with $D^g\ne D$, maximality of $D$ yields $\langle D,D^g\rangle=L$.
As $D$ and $D^g$ are abelian, both centralize $D\cap D^g$.
Hence, $D\cap D^g\leq Z(L)$.
Let $z\in Z(L)$ fix a coset $\alpha\in L/D$.
For $g\in L$, we have $z(g\alpha)=g(z\alpha)=g\alpha$.
Because $L$ is transitive and acts faithfully, we have $z=1$.
The subgroup $D\cap D^g$ fixes the coset $D$ and lies in $Z(L)$, so it is trivial.
For $g,h\in L$ with $D^g\ne D^h$, we have $(D^g\cap D^h)^{g^{-1}}=D\cap D^{hg^{-1}}=1$.
Hence, $D^g\cap D^h=1$.

Since $N_L(D)=D$, we have $r$ distinct subgroups $D^g$ with $g\in L$.
Every nonidentity element of a conjugate of $D$ fixes exactly one coset.
Therefore, we count $r|D|-1-r(|D|-1)=r-1$ elements of $L$ without a fixed point.
Every nonidentity element of a Sylow $r$-subgroup is an $r$-cycle.
Distinct Sylow $r$-subgroups of $L\leq S_r$ would contribute disjoint
sets of $r-1$ such elements. Therefore, we have a unique Sylow $r$-subgroup $R$.
As $|R|=r$ and $R\cap D=1$, we have $L=R\rtimes D$.
We consider $\theta:D\to\operatorname{Aut}(R)$ with $\theta(d)(x)=dxd^{-1}$ for $d\in D$ and $x\in R$.
Because $D$ is abelian and $R$ centralizes $\ker\theta$, we have $\ker\theta\unlhd L$ and $\ker\theta\leq D$.
As $\operatorname{Core}_L(D)=1$, we have $\ker\theta=1$.
Hence, $\theta$ is injective and $|D|\mid|\operatorname{Aut}(C_r)|=r-1$.
head: environment

label: lem:transvection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:transvection}
Let $r\geq5$ be prime and $p\ne r$.
Let $a\in\operatorname{GL}_r(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$.
Suppose that every $r$th root of unity is an eigenvalue of $a$ with multiplicity $1$.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{GL}_r(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)\to\operatorname{PGL}_r(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)$ be the quotient map.
Let $\bar a=\pi(a)$.
Then, no transvection $t$ satisfies $\pi(t)\in N_{\operatorname{PGL}_r(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p)}(\langle \bar a\rangle)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $t$ is a transvection and that $\pi(t)$ normalizes $\langle \bar a\rangle$.
We choose $\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p^*$ and $1\leq e<r$ with $tat^{-1}=\zeta a^e$.
By comparing eigenvalues, we have $\zeta^r=1$ and $e\ne0\pmod r$.
Let $\omega$ be a primitive $r$th root of unity and let $\zeta=\omega^b$ with $b\in\mathbb{F}_r$.
Let $L_j=\ker(a-\omega^jI)$ for $j\in\mathbb{F}_r$.
Since $tat^{-1}=\omega^b a^e$, we have $tL_j=L_{e^{-1}(j-b)}$.
Thus, $t$ induces $\sigma:j\mapsto e^{-1}(j-b)$ on the eigenlines.
As $t^p=I$, the order of $\sigma$ divides $p$.
If $\sigma=1$, then $t$ is diagonal on the eigenlines of $a$.
Hence, $t$ is semisimple, contrary to $t$ being a transvection.
Suppose that $\sigma\ne1$.
The nonidentity affine map $\sigma$ has order $p$.
Because $p\ne r$, it has $1$ fixed point and $(r-1)/p$ cycles of length $p$.
As $t^p=I$, the product of the scalar entries around each cycle is $1$.
Thus, $t$ has $1$ Jordan block of size $p$ on each cycle.
Consequently, we have $\operatorname{rank}(t-I)\geq(r-1)(p-1)/p\geq2$.
However, a transvection satisfies $\operatorname{rank}(t-I)=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:regular-unipotent
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:regular-unipotent}
Let $q$ have odd prime characteristic $r$, and let
$u$ be regular unipotent in $G=\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$ or $\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$.
Then, $C_G(u)$ is an $r$-group. If $r\geq5$, then
$\langle u\rangle$ is not ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=\mathbb{F}_q$ for $G=\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$ and $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ for $G=\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$.
We choose a basis of $E^r$ in which $u=I+J$, with $J$ a single nilpotent Jordan block.
Since $u=I+J$ has a single Jordan block, every $c\in C_G(u)$ has the form $c=\alpha I+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\beta_iJ^i$.
Let $\alpha\in E^*$ and $\beta_i\in E$ be the coefficients of $c$.
Since $\det c=\alpha^r=1$ in characteristic $r$, we have $\alpha=1$.
As every $c\in C_G(u)$ has order a power of $r$, we obtain from Cauchy's theorem that $C_G(u)$ is an $r$-group.

Suppose that $r\geq5$ and that $\langle u\rangle$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
In both groups, we choose an involution $t$ with eigenvalue $1$ of multiplicity $1$ and eigenvalue $-1$ of multiplicity $r-1$.
We choose $x\in G$ with $K=\langle u\rangle\langle t^x\rangle\leq G$.
Since $|u|=r$, we have $|K|=2r$ and $[K:\langle u\rangle]=2$.
Hence, $\langle u\rangle\unlhd K$.
As $C_G(u)$ has odd order, $t^x$ does not centralize $u$.
The automorphism $u\mapsto(t^x)^{-1}u(t^x)$ of $\langle u\rangle\cong C_r$ has order $2$.
Therefore, $(t^x)^{-1}u(t^x)=u^{-1}$.

Let $L=\log u=\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}(-1)^{i+1}(u-I)^i/i$.
Since $1\leq i<r$, every denominator $i$ is nonzero in $E$.
The coefficient of $J$ in $L$ is $1$.
Hence, $L$ has $1$ nilpotent Jordan block of size $r$.
As $(t^x)u(t^x)^{-1}=u^{-1}$, we have $(t^x)L(t^x)^{-1}=-L$.
Because $t^x$ is semisimple and $LE^r$ is $t^x$-invariant, we choose a $t^x$-eigenvector $v\notin LE^r$.
Since $v\notin LE^r$ and $L$ has one nilpotent Jordan block, we have $L^{r-1}v\ne0$.
Because $v$ is a $t^x$-eigenvector, $t^xv=\varepsilon v$ for some $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$.
For $0\leq j<r$, $t^x(L^jv)=\varepsilon(-1)^jL^jv$.
As $(v,Lv,\ldots,L^{r-1}v)$ is a basis, the eigenvalue multiplicities are $(r+1)/2$ and $(r-1)/2$.
Because $r\geq5$, neither multiplicity equals $r-1$.
However, $t^x$ has multiplicities $1,r-1$. We have a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:split-root-normalizer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:split-root-normalizer}
Let $q=p^f$, where $p$ is an odd prime and $f\geq1$.
Let $\mathbf G$ be a split irreducible semisimple algebraic group of rank $r\geq3$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
Let $\Phi$ be the root system of $\mathbf G$, with positive roots $\Phi^+$.
Let $G_0=\langle X_\alpha(\mathbb{F}_q)\mid\alpha\in\Phi\rangle$ and
$U=\langle X_\alpha(\mathbb{F}_q)\mid\alpha\in\Phi^+\rangle$.
There is a subgroup $H\leq U$ with
$N_{G_0}(H)\leq Z(G_0)U$.
If $f\geq2$, then $N_{G_0}(D)\leq Z(G_0)U$ for every $D\leq H$ with $[H:D]=p$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T\leq G_0$ be the split maximal torus normalizing $U$.
Next, we choose a path $A$--$B$--$C$ of $3$ simple roots.
Let $D=A+B$ and $E=B+C$.
Now, let $U_3=\langle X_\alpha(\mathbb{F}_q):\alpha\in\Phi^+,\ \operatorname{ht}(\alpha)\geq3\rangle$.
The coefficients of $ab$ and $bc$ in the $D,E$ commutator coordinates belong to $\{1,-1\}$.
We choose signs so that $[X_A(a),X_B(b)]\equiv X_D(ab)\pmod{U_3}$ for $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
Then, we also have $[X_B(b),X_C(c)]\equiv X_E(bc)\pmod{U_3}$ for $b,c\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
All root groups with $\operatorname{ht}(\alpha)=2$ are central in $U/U_3$.
Next, let $Q_2=\langle X_\alpha(\mathbb{F}_q):\alpha\in\Phi^+,\ \operatorname{ht}(\alpha)=2,\ \alpha\notin\{D,E\}\rangle$.
Let $Q=\langle U_3,Q_2,X_D(t)X_E(t):t\in\mathbb{F}_q\rangle$.
As the root groups of height $2$ are central in $U/U_3$, we have $Q\unlhd U$.
We identify $U/Q$ with $\mathbb{F}_q^r\times\mathbb{F}_q$ as a set.
For $a\in\mathbb{F}_q^r$, we use $a_1,a_2,a_3$ for the coordinates at $A,B,C$.
The multiplication is $(a,z)(a',z')=(a+a',z+z'-a'_1a_2+a'_2a_3)$.
The other simple coordinates do not enter the central term.
For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_q^r$, the commutator form is $\beta(a,b)=b_2(a_1+a_3)-a_2(b_1+b_3)$.
We have $\operatorname{rad}\beta=\{a\in\mathbb{F}_q^r:a_2=0,\ a_1+a_3=0\}$.

Let $(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{F}_q^r$.
Let $v=\sum_{i=1}^r e_i$ and $w=e_2+2e_3$.
From the multiplication formula, we obtain the abelian subgroup
$S=\{(tv+sw,t+s(t+s)):t,s\in\mathbb{F}_q\}$
with additive coordinates $t,s$.
Let $\eta:U\to U/Q$ be the quotient map and let $H=\eta^{-1}(S)$.
Let $Z_1=\{(c(v-w),c):c\in\mathbb{F}_q\}\leq U/Q$.
Then, $S\cap Z(U/Q)=Z_1$.
Let $\pi:U/Q\to\mathbb{F}_q^r$ send $(a,z)$ to $a$.
Let $P=\pi(S)=\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathbb{F}_q}$.
For $u\in U$, we consider $c_u:U/Q\to U/Q$ with $c_u(z)=\eta(u)^{-1}z\eta(u)$.
We have $c_u(s)=s$ for $s\in Z_1$ and $(\pi\circ c_u)|_S=\pi|_S$.

Now, we choose $h_0\in H$ with $\eta(h_0)=(v,1)$.
Every coordinate of $v$ equals $1$, so every simple-root coordinate of $h_0$ is nonzero.
The element $h_0$ lies in a unique algebraic Borel subgroup $\mathbf B$, with $U\leq\mathbf B$
\cite[Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3]{SteinbergRegular}.
For $g\in N_{G_0}(H)$, the element $gh_0g^{-1}\in U$ is also regular.
Hence, $g\mathbf B g^{-1}=\mathbf B$ and we have $N_{G_0}(H)\leq TU$.
For $g\in N_{G_0}(H)$, we choose $\tau\in T$ and $u\in U$ with $g=\tau u$.
For $h\in H$, we have $(\pi\circ\eta)(uhu^{-1})=(\pi\circ\eta)(h)$.
Since $gHg^{-1}=H$, we obtain that $(\pi\circ\eta)(\tau H\tau^{-1})=P$.
The coordinate columns of $P$ at $A,B,C$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(1,2)$.
As the $3$ corresponding lines are distinct, every linear map fixing them is scalar.
Every other column equals $(1,0)$.
Hence, we have $\alpha(\tau)=\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$ for every simple root $\alpha$.
We have $D(\tau)=E(\tau)=\lambda^2$, so $\tau Q\tau^{-1}=Q$.
On $U/Q$, the map $hQ\mapsto\tau h\tau^{-1}Q$ sends $(v-w,1)$ to $(\lambda(v-w),\lambda^2)$.
The map $c_u$ fixes $Z_1$ pointwise.
Because $gHg^{-1}=H$, we have $(\lambda(v-w),\lambda^2)\in Z_1$.
Thus, we have $\lambda=\lambda^2=1$.
We conclude that $\tau\in Z(G_0)$ and $N_{G_0}(H)\leq Z(G_0)U$.

Now, we suppose that $f\geq2$ and choose $D_0\leq H$ with $[H:D_0]=p$.
Let $W=\eta(D_0)\leq S$.
The restriction $\pi|_S:S\to P$ is injective.
Because $[H:D_0]=p$ and $\eta(H)=S$, we have $[S:W]\leq p$.
As $\pi|_S$ is injective, $|\pi(W)|=|W|\geq q^2/p>q$, so $\pi(W)$ spans $P$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
At most $3$ lines in $P$ have a vanishing simple coordinate.
The union of those lines has at most $3q-2$ elements, whereas
$|\pi(W)|\geq q^2/p>3q-2$.
Thus, $D_0$ contains a regular element and $N_{G_0}(D_0)\leq TU$.
Also, $|W\cap Z_1|\geq q/p>1$.
For $g\in N_{G_0}(D_0)$, we choose $\tau\in T$ and $u\in U$ with $g=\tau u$.
For $h\in D_0$, we have $(\pi\circ\eta)(uhu^{-1})=(\pi\circ\eta)(h)$.
Since $gD_0g^{-1}=D_0$, we obtain that $(\pi\circ\eta)(\tau D_0\tau^{-1})=\pi(W)$.
As $\pi(W)$ spans $P$, we obtain that $\alpha(\tau)=\lambda$ for every simple root $\alpha$.
Hence, $\tau Q\tau^{-1}=Q$.
We choose $z_1=(c(v-w),c)\in W\cap Z_1$ with $c\ne0$.
Because $z_1\in Z(U/Q)$, we have $\eta(u)z_1\eta(u)^{-1}=z_1$.
As $gD_0g^{-1}=D_0$, we have $(\lambda c(v-w),\lambda^2c)\in W\cap Z_1$.
Hence, we have $\lambda=\lambda^2=1$.
We conclude that $\tau\in Z(G_0)$ and $N_{G_0}(D_0)\leq Z(G_0)U$.

label: cor:split-odd-involutions
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:split-odd-involutions}
Let $G$ be a finite simple split group of Lie type of rank at least
$3$ in odd characteristic.
Then, no nontrivial cyclic $2$-subgroup is ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We take $G_0$ and $H$ from Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer}.
Let $\pi:G_0\to G$ be the quotient map and let $B=\pi(H)$.
Now, let $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$.
We have $|B|$ odd and $\pi^{-1}(B)=HZ(G_0)$.
Since $p\nmid|Z(G_0)|$, $H$ is the unique Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\pi^{-1}(B)$.
Therefore, $\pi^{-1}(N_G(B))\leq N_{G_0}(H)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer}, we have $\pi^{-1}(N_G(B))\leq Z(G_0)U$.
Hence, $|N_G(B)|$ is odd.
Suppose that a nontrivial cyclic subgroup $A$ of order a power of $2$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
We choose $x\in G$ with $K=AB^x\leq G$.
Since $A$ is a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup of $K$, Burnside's normal complement theorem yields $H_0\unlhd K$ with $|H_0|$ odd and $[K:H_0]=|A|$.
As $K/H_0$ is a $2$-group, we have $B^x\leq H_0$.
Because $|B^x|=|H_0|$, we have $B^x=H_0\unlhd K$.
Hence, $A\leq N_G(B^x)$, contrary to $|N_G(B^x)|$ being odd.
head: environment

label: lem:odd-normalizer-fusion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:odd-normalizer-fusion}
Let $G$ contain a $p$-subgroup $H$, with $p$ odd and $N_G(H)$ of odd order.
Then, no cyclic subgroup of order $4$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
If an ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup $A$ is isomorphic to $C_2\times C_2$, then for $s,t\in A\setminus\{1\}$ there is $g\in G$ with $s^g=t$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A\leq G$ with $|A|=4$. Suppose that $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
We choose $x\in G$ with $K=AH^x\leq G$.
Next, let $D=\operatorname{Core}_K(H^x)$.
Let $\rho:K\to S_{K/H^x}$ satisfy $\rho(k)(gH^x)=kgH^x$ for $k,g\in K$.
Then, we have $\ker\rho=D$ and $K/D\leq S_4$.
Since $D$ has odd order, $|\rho(A)|=4$.
The subgroup $\rho(H^x)$ lies in a point stabilizer $S_3$.
If $\rho(H^x)=1$, then we have $H^x\unlhd K$ and $A\leq N_G(H^x)$.
However, $|A|=4$ and $|N_G(H^x)|$ is odd. Hence, $\rho(H^x)\ne1$.
If $\rho(H^x)\ne1$, then we have $p=3$ and $|\rho(H^x)|=3$.
Hence, $|K/D|=12$ and $K/D=A_4$.
Since $\rho|_A$ is injective and $A_4$ has no cyclic subgroup of order $4$, $A$ cannot be cyclic.
If $A\cong C_2\times C_2$, then for $s,t\in A\setminus\{1\}$ we choose $k_0\in K$ with $\rho(s)^{\rho(k_0)}=\rho(t)$.

We lift the equation $\rho(s)^{\rho(k_0)}=\rho(t)$ through $D$.
Let $t_1=s^{k_0}$ and $t_2=t$.
Then, we have $\rho(t_1)=\rho(t_2)$.
Let $L_0=\rho^{-1}(\langle \rho(t_1)\rangle)$.
Since $|D|$ is odd, we have $L_0=D\rtimes\langle t_1\rangle=D\rtimes\langle t_2\rangle$.
By Schur--Zassenhaus, we choose $d\in D$ with $t_1^d=t_2$.
Consequently, $s^{k_0d}=t$ with $k_0d\in K\leq G$.
head: environment

label: thm:l3
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $1<A<G$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
For $q=2$, use $\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ and \cite{GT25}.
We now assume that $q\geq3$ and $q\ne4$.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime, and let $d=(3,q-1)$.
The split monomial subgroup $M$ is maximal and has order
$6(q-1)^2/d$, including $M\cong S_4$ for $q=3$
\cite[Table 8.3]{BHR}. By \cite[Theorem 3.3]{LiXia}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Suppose that $G=XY$ with $X,Y<G$ in a generic row.
A factor has Singer type.
Moreover, the other factor contains $\mathbb{F}_q^2\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_2(q)$.
Neither listed order divides $|M|$.
For $q=3$, the listed factors $X,Y<G$ have orders $39$ and $144$.
Neither order divides $|M|=24$.
For $q=8$, the exceptional equalities $H=XY$ in the cited list have $G<H\leq\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.
The group $H$ contains an outer field automorphism.

By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $|A|\mid|M|$.
We take a Singer torus $T$ with $|T|=(q^2+q+1)/d$.
Then, we have $(|T|,|M|)=1$ and $|G|/(|M||T|)=dq^3(q+1)/(6(q-1))>1$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AT^x$ is a subgroup.
As $|A||T|<|G|$, we have $AT^x<G$.
We choose a maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $AT^x\leq H$.
By \cite{Bereczky}, we have $H=N_G(T^x)=T^x\rtimes C_3$.
Hence, $AT^x\leq N_G(T^x)$ and $|A|\mid3$.
Let $w:\mathbb{F}_{q^3}\to\mathbb{F}_{q^3}$ be the $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear map with $w(z)=z^q$.
On a normal basis of $\mathbb{F}_{q^3}/\mathbb{F}_q$, $w$ is a $3$-cycle and lies in $\operatorname{SL}_3(q)$.
If $A\ne1$, then we choose $g\in G$ with $A^g=\langle \overline w\rangle$ by Schur--Zassenhaus.
For $p=3$, the lift $w$ is regular unipotent.
Otherwise, $w$ has eigenvalues $1,\omega,\omega^2$, where $\omega^3=1\ne\omega$.

For $p=3$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:regular-unipotent} that $C_{\operatorname{SL}_3(q)}(w)$ is a $3$-group.
The group $G$ has a cyclic subgroup $D$ of order $4$ in a torus of type $(2,1)$.
A subgroup $AD^x$ would have order $12$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:index3}, we would have $(D^x)^2\unlhd AD^x$.
Because $\operatorname{Aut}(C_2)=1$, $A$ would centralize the involution generating $(D^x)^2$.
This would place an involution in $C_G(A)$, contrary to the preceding centralizer calculation.

Suppose that $q\equiv2\pmod3$. Then, $d=1$.
We choose a Sylow $p$-subgroup $U$ of order $q^3$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AU^x$ for some $x\in G$.
If $p>3$, then $[K:U^x]=3<p$.
Hence, $U^x\lhd K$.
Therefore, $A\leq N_G(U^x)$.
But $N_G(U^x)$ is a Borel subgroup of order $q^3(q-1)^2$, which is prime to $3$.
As $|A|=3$, we have a contradiction.

For $p=2$, we have $q\geq8$.
Suppose that $K=AU^x$ is a subgroup.
Let $C=\operatorname{Core}_K(U^x)$.
Since $K$ acts on $3$ cosets, we have $[U^x:C]\leq2$.
To bound $N_G(C)$, consider an arbitrary subgroup $U_0\leq U$ with $[U:U_0]\leq2$.
The group $U$ is
$$
 U=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&a&c\\0&1&b\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}:
 a,b,c\in\mathbb{F}_q\right\}.
$$
As $[U:U_0]\leq2$, we have $[U,U]\leq U_0$.
We have $[U,U]=\{I+cE_{13}:c\in\mathbb{F}_q\}$.
The coordinate maps $\pi_a,\pi_b:U\to(\mathbb{F}_q,+)$ send the displayed matrix to $a,b$.
Since $[U:U_0]\leq2$, each coordinate image of $U_0$ has size at least $q/2>1$.
Therefore, $\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathbb{F}_q^3}(U_0)=\langle e_1\rangle$ and $\operatorname{Fix}_{(\mathbb{F}_q^3)^*}(U_0)=\langle e_3^*\rangle$.
Hence, $N_G(U_0)\leq B_0$, where $B_0$ stabilizes the flag $\langle e_1\rangle<\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$.
For $U_0=C^{x^{-1}}\leq U$, we have $N_G(U_0)\leq B_0$.
Then, $A\leq N_G(C)\leq B_0^x$, contrary to $3\nmid|B_0|$.

Finally, suppose that $q\equiv1\pmod3$.
Then, $d=3$.
We take a cyclic torus $B$ of type $(2,1)$ with $|B|=(q^2-1)/3$.
The subgroup $A$ has a noncentral lift of order $3$.
In contrast, every element of order $3$ in the inverse image of $B$ is scalar.
Thus, $A\cap B^x=1$ for every $x\in G$.
Suppose that $K=AB^x$ is a subgroup, and let $C=\operatorname{Core}_K(B^x)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:abelian-index}, we have $[B^x:C]\mid2$.
Let $\widetilde C$ be the inverse image of $C$ in $\operatorname{SL}_3(q)$.
Since $B^x$ is cyclic and $[B^x:C]\mid2$, we have $\widetilde B^2\leq\widetilde C$, where $\widetilde B$ is the inverse image of $B^x$ and $|\widetilde B|=q^2-1$.
Let $z$ generate $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$. Since $q+1\nmid2$, we have $z^2\notin\mathbb{F}_q$.
Let $\mathbb{F}_q^3=W\oplus L$ be the decomposition for $\widetilde B$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=2$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}L=1$.
Because $z^2\notin\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\widetilde B^2\leq\widetilde C$, the group $\widetilde C$ acts irreducibly on $W$ and stabilizes $L$.
Relative to $\mathbb{F}_q^3=W\oplus L$, the normalizer $N_{\operatorname{GL}_3(q)}(\widetilde C)$ lies in $(\operatorname{GL}_1(q^2)\rtimes C_2)\times\operatorname{GL}_1(q)$.
Next, a generator of $A$ lifts to a noncentral element $a$ of order $3$.
Since $C\unlhd K$, the lift $a$ normalizes $\widetilde C$.
As $3\nmid2$, the lift $a$ centralizes $\widetilde C$.
Because the $3$ eigenvalues of $a$ lie in $\mathbb{F}_q$, we have $a|_W=\lambda I_W$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
Note that $|a|=3$, so $\lambda^3=1$.
Because $\det a=1$, we have $a|_L=\lambda^{-2}I_L=\lambda I_L$.
Hence, $a$ is scalar on $\mathbb{F}_q^3$, contrary to the choice of a noncentral lift.

We now consider $q=4$.
The group $G=\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$ has order $20160$ and maximal subgroup
orders $960,360,168,72$ \cite{Atlas1985}.
Next, we claim that $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$.
In \cite[Theorem 3.3]{LiXia}, the exceptional equalities $H=XY$ with socle $G$ have $G<H\leq\operatorname{Aut}(G)$.
If $G=XY$ with $X,Y<G$ in a generic row, then the Singer normalizer of order $21$ would act regularly on the $21$ projective points.
A generator of the complement of order $3$ lifts to a matrix with $3$ distinct eigenvalues in $\mathbb{F}_4$.
Hence, the Singer normalizer has nontrivial point stabilizers and is not regular.

Therefore, $|A|\mid(960,360,168,72)=24$.
We choose $T\leq G$ of order $7$ and a subgroup $K=AT^x$ with $x\in G$.
Since $7\nmid|A|$, we have $|K|=7|A|\leq168$.
As $168$ is the only maximal subgroup order divisible by $7$, we have $K\leq L$ for some $L\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$.
By \cite{Dickson1901}, $|K|\in\{7,21,168\}$.
Hence, $|A|\in\{1,3,24\}$.
Suppose that $|A|=24$.
Since $|K|=168$, we have $K=L$.
Dickson's subgroup theorem then yields $A\cong S_4$.
Let $M_{72}\leq G$ be a maximal subgroup with $M_{72}\cong C_3^2\rtimes Q_8$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose $g\in G$ with $A^g\leq M_{72}$.
Let $\rho:M_{72}\to Q_8$ be the quotient map with kernel $C_3^2$.
Because $S_4$ has no nontrivial normal $3$-subgroup, we have $A^g\cap\ker\rho=1$.
Thus, $\rho|_{A^g}:A^g\to Q_8$ is injective.
This contradicts $24>8$.

If $|A|=3$, then we choose $B\leq G$ of order $5$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, $AB^x$ would be a cyclic subgroup of order $15$ for some $x\in G$.
But $G$ has no element of order $15$.
A semisimple lift with order divisible by $5$ acts irreducibly on $W\leq\mathbb{F}_4^3$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_4}W=2$.
As the lift is semisimple, it stabilizes a line complementary to $W$.
Thus, its projective image lies in a torus of type $(2,1)$ and order $5$.
Hence, no semisimple element has order $15$.
We conclude that $|A|\ne3$ and $A=1$.

label: thm:linear-prime
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] For $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$, $A$ stabilizes a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^r$ of dimension $2$.
\end{itemize}
Suppose that $1<A<G$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime, and let $d=(r,q-1)$.
Next, we take a Singer torus $T$ with $|T|=(q^r-1)/((q-1)d)$.
Let $N=N_G(T)=T\rtimes C_r$.
By \cite{Bereczky}, we have $H=N$ for every maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $T\leq H$.
Let $P_i=\operatorname{Stab}_G(W_i)$ for $W_i\leq\mathbb{F}_q^r$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W_i=i$.
Since $r$ is prime, we use \cite[Theorem 3.3]{LiXia} for $G=XY$ with $X,Y<G$.
In each generic row, we label the factors $X,Y$.
We then choose $u,v\in G$ with $X^u\leq N$ and $Y^v\leq P_1$ or $P_{r-1}$.
For $(r,q)=(5,2)$, the list also permits $G=NP_2$ and $G=NP_3$.
By this factorization list, $P_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$ when $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$.

Firstly, assume that $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq P_2^g$ for some $g\in G$.
If $r\mid q-1$, then $v_r(\Phi_r(q))=1$.
Otherwise, $r\nmid\Phi_r(q)$.
Since $d=(r,q-1)$, we have $r\nmid|T|$.
Every prime $\ell\mid|T|$ has $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=r$.
The factors of $|P_2|$ prime to $p$ have the form $q^i-1$ with $i<r$.
As $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=r$ for every $\ell\mid|T|$, we have $(|T|,|P_2|)=1$.
Furthermore,
$\frac{[G:P_2]}{|T|} =d\frac{q^{r-1}-1}{q^2-1}>1$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] For $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$, we have $|A|=r$ and $q\equiv1\pmod r$.
\end{itemize}
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
Since $A\leq P_2^g$, we have $|K|\leq|P_2||T|<|G|$.
As $K<G$, we choose a maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $K\leq H$.
Because $T^x\leq H$, we have $H=N^x$.
Therefore, $|A|\mid (|P_2|,|N|)\mid r$.
If $A\ne1$, then $|A|=r$.
By Schur--Zassenhaus, choose $g\in G$ with $A^g$ equal to a complement of $T$ in $N$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^r}$ as an $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space, so $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V=r$.
A generator of $A^g$ lifts to $w:V\to V$ with $w(z)=z^q$.
In a normal basis, $w$ is an $r$-cycle of determinant $1$.
For $p\ne r$, every $r$th root is an eigenvalue of $w$ with multiplicity $1$.
For $p=r$, the lift $w$ is regular unipotent.

If $p\ne r$ and $q\not\equiv1\pmod r$, then let $t$ be a transvection of order $p$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, $A\langle t^x\rangle$ would be a subgroup of order $rp$ for some $x\in G$.
For $p<r$, the Sylow $r$-subgroup $A$ would be normal.
Hence, $t^x\in N_G(A)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:transvection}, we have a contradiction.
For $p>r$, the subgroup $\langle t^x\rangle$ would be normal.
As $r\nmid p-1$, $A$ would centralize $t^x$.
Since $d=1$ in this case, $G=\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$.
A generator of $A$ is regular semisimple, with a torus centralizer containing no transvection.
This contradicts its centralization of $t^x$.
For $p=r$, we have $G=\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:regular-unipotent}, we have a contradiction.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $q\equiv1\pmod r$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Now, let $q\equiv1\pmod r$, so $d=r$.
We take the cyclic torus $B$ of type $(r-1,1)$ with $|B|=(q^{r-1}-1)/r$.
For $z\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{r-1}}^*$, let $M_z:\mathbb{F}_{q^{r-1}}\to\mathbb{F}_{q^{r-1}}$ satisfy $M_z(v)=zv$.
The inverse image of $B$ in $\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$ consists of the matrices $\operatorname{diag}(M_z,N(z)^{-1})$.
Let $N(z)=z^{(q^{r-1}-1)/(q-1)}$ be the norm from $\mathbb{F}_{q^{r-1}}$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$.
If $z^r=1$, then $z\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
Since $r\mid q-1$, we have $N(z)^{-1}=z^{-(r-1)}=z$.
Hence, every element of order $r$ in the inverse image of $B$ is scalar.
As $A$ has a noncentral lift of order $r$, we have $A\cap B^x=1$ for every $x\in G$.

Suppose that $K=AB^x$ is a subgroup.
Then, $[K:B^x]=r$.
Let $C=\operatorname{Core}_K(B^x)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:abelian-index}, we have $[B^x:C]\mid r-1$.
We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{r-1}-1$.
Since $r-1\geq4$ and $q\geq r+1$, Zsigmondy's theorem \cite{Zsigmondy1892} has no exception.
We have $\ell>r-1$ and $\ell\ne r$, so $\ell\mid|C|$.
Let $R\leq C$ have order $\ell$.
As $C$ is cyclic, $R$ is characteristic in $C$.
Because $C\unlhd K$, we have $R\unlhd K$.

The inverse image of $R$ has a unique subgroup $\widetilde R$ of order $\ell$ in $\operatorname{SL}_r(q)$.
Next, let $\mathbb{F}_q^r=W\oplus L$ be the decomposition for $\widetilde R$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=r-1$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}L=1$.
Since $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=r-1$, the group $\widetilde R$ acts irreducibly on $W$ and fixes $L$ pointwise.
Relative to $\mathbb{F}_q^r=W\oplus L$, the normalizer $N_{\operatorname{GL}_r(q)}(\widetilde R)$ lies in
$(\operatorname{GL}_1(q^{r-1})\rtimes C_{r-1})\times\operatorname{GL}_1(q)$.
Now, a generator of $A$ lifts to a noncentral element $a$ of order $r$.
Since $R\unlhd K$, the lift $a$ normalizes $\widetilde R$.
As $r\nmid r-1$, the lift $a$ centralizes $\widetilde R$.
The eigenvalues of $a$ are $r$th roots in $\mathbb{F}_q$, so $a|_W$ is multiplication by an element of $\mathbb{F}_q$.
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfy $a|_W=\lambda I_W$.
As $|a|=r$, we have $\lambda^r=1$.
Because $\det a=1$, we have $a|_L=\lambda^{-(r-1)}I_L=\lambda I_L$.
Hence, $a$ is scalar on $\mathbb{F}_q^r$, a contradiction.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] If $G=\operatorname{PSL}_5(2)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Now, we consider $G=\operatorname{PSL}_5(2)$.
Then, we have $|G|=9999360$ and $|N|=155$.
The maximal subgroups are $P_1,P_4$ of order $322560$ and $P_2,P_3$ of order $64512$.
The other maximal subgroup is
$N=C_{31}\rtimes C_5$ \cite{Atlas1985}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq N^x$ or $G=AN^x$ for some $x\in G$.

Suppose that $A\leq N^g$ for some $g\in G$ and replace $A$ by $A^{g^{-1}}$.
Then, $A\leq N$ and $|A|\in\{1,5,31,155\}$.
If $31\mid|A|$, then we choose a Sylow $2$-subgroup $U$ of order $1024$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AU^x$ for some $x\in G$.
We have $|K|\leq155\cdot1024<|G|$.
As $K<G$, we choose a maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $K\leq H$.
Because $U^x\leq H$, we obtain from the maximal subgroup list that $H$ is a parabolic subgroup of $G$.
Therefore, $A$ stabilizes a proper nonzero subspace of $\mathbb{F}_2^5$.
But a subgroup of order $31$ in $A$ acts irreducibly on $\mathbb{F}_2^5$.
Therefore, we have a contradiction.
If $|A|=5$, then a generator has eigenvalue multiplicities $1+4$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
Over the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_2$, the eigenvalues are the $5$ distinct $5$th roots.
We choose a transvection $t$ of order $2$.
If $A\langle t^x\rangle$ were a subgroup for some $x\in G$, then its Sylow $5$-subgroup $A$ would be normal.
This contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:transvection}.
Thus, no $A\langle t^x\rangle$ with $x\in G$ is a subgroup.

Suppose that $G=AN^x$ with $A,N^x<G$.
By \cite[Theorem 3.3]{LiXia}, we choose $g\in G$ with $A^g=P_i$ for some $i\in\{1,2,3,4\}$.
By duality, we need only consider $P_1$ and $P_2$.
Let $L\leq\mathbb{F}_2^5$ be the line stabilized by $P_1$.
The subspaces $W\leq\mathbb{F}_2^5$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W=2$ and $L\leq W$ form a proper $P_1$-invariant set.
Hence, $P_1$ is not transitive on the subspaces of dimension $2$.
Since $|P_1|>|P_2|$, we have $P_1\nleq P_2^h$ for every $h\in G$.
Since $P_1$ is not transitive on the subspaces of dimension $2$, we have $P_1P_2^h\ne G$ for every $h\in G$.
Together with $P_1\nleq P_2^h$, Lemma \ref{lem:max} excludes every product $P_1P_2^h$ as a subgroup.
As $P_2$ stabilizes a proper nonzero subspace, $P_2$ is not transitive on points.
Let $\mathbb{F}_2^5=W_2\oplus W_3$ be a decomposition for a Levi subgroup of $P_2$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W_i=i$ for $i=2,3$.
Because the Levi subgroup acts irreducibly on $W_2$, $P_2$ fixes no line in $W_2$.
Let $U$ be the unipotent radical of $P_2$.
Its matrices on $W_2\oplus W_3$ are $u_X=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&X\\0&I_3\end{pmatrix}$ with $X\in M_{2\times3}(\mathbb{F}_2)$.
As $\bigcap_X\ker(u_X-I)=W_2$, no line outside $W_2$ is fixed by every element of $U$.
Thus, $P_2$ has no fixed line.
Since $P_2$ is not transitive on points and fixes no line, we have $P_2P_1^h\ne G$ and $P_2\nleq P_1^h$ for every $h\in G$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, no product $P_2P_1^h$ with $h\in G$ is a subgroup.
head: environment

label: lem:linear-singer-containing-subgroups
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linear-singer-containing-subgroups}
Let $T\leq J\leq\operatorname{SL}_m(q)$, where $T$ is a Singer subgroup of order $(q^m-1)/(q-1)$.
Suppose that $m\geq2$ and $(m,q)\ne(4,3)$.
Suppose that $q\geq16$ for $m=2$, $q\geq9$ for $m=3$, and $q\geq3$ for $m\geq4$.
If $J\nleq N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$, then $J$ contains the natural subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_b(q^s)$ under an $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear identification $\mathbb{F}_q^m\cong(\mathbb{F}_{q^s})^b$ for integers $b,s\geq1$ with $bs=m$ and $b\geq2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on $m$.
For $m=2$ and $q\geq16$, we have $|T|=q+1$.
By Dickson's subgroup theorem \cite{Dickson1901}, $J\leq N_{\operatorname{SL}_2(q)}(T)$ or $J=\operatorname{SL}_2(q)$.
See also \cite[Tables 8.1--8.2]{BHR}.

Suppose that $m\geq3$.
If $J=\operatorname{SL}_m(q)$, then take $b=m$ and $s=1$.
We assume that $J$ is proper.
By Bereczky's theorem \cite{Bereczky}, we have $J\leq E$.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.1.7]{Brookfield2014}.
We take $Q=q^s$ and $V=(\mathbb{F}_Q)^b$ with $bs=m$ and $s$ prime.
Then, on the $\mathbb{F}_q$-vector space $V$, we have
$E=\bigl(\operatorname{GL}_b(Q)\rtimes\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_Q/\mathbb{F}_q)\bigr)\cap\operatorname{SL}_m(q)$.
The hypotheses imply that $(m,q)\ne(3,4)$.

We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^m-1$.
By Zsigmondy's theorem, $\ell$ exists and $\ell>m$.
Since $\ell>s$, the subgroup $T_\ell$ of order $\ell$ lies in $E\cap\operatorname{GL}_b(Q)$.
Let $E_T=C_{\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_q}(V)}(T_\ell)$.
Since $T_\ell$ acts irreducibly on $V$, we have $E_T\cong\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$.
Both $T$ and the scalar maps from $\mathbb{F}_Q$ lie in $E_T$.
As $E_T$ is commutative, every element of $T$ is $\mathbb{F}_Q$-linear.
If $b=1$, then we have $E=N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$.

Suppose that $b\geq2$.
Let $J_0=J\cap\operatorname{SL}_b(Q)$.
Then, $J_0\lhd J$ and $T_0=T\cap\operatorname{SL}_b(Q)\leq J_0$.
We have $|T_0|=(q^m-1)/(Q-1)$, so $T_0$ is a Singer subgroup of $\operatorname{SL}_b(Q)$.
The inductive hypotheses hold for $(b,Q)$.
Since $Q=q^s$ with $s$ prime, $Q=9$ would imply that $s=2$ and $q=3$.
If also $b=2$, then $m=4$.
Our hypotheses prohibit $(m,q)=(4,3)$.
Suppose that $J_0$ contains $\operatorname{SL}_a(Q^t)$ on $(\mathbb{F}_{Q^t})^a$, where $at=b$ and $a\geq2$.
As $J_0\leq J$, we have $\operatorname{SL}_a(Q^t)\leq J$.
Otherwise, $J_0\leq N_{\operatorname{SL}_b(Q)}(T_0)$.
The normalizer quotient has order dividing $b<\ell$.
Thus, the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $R_\ell$ of $J_0$ is unique.
Hence, $R_\ell$ is characteristic in $J_0$ and normal in $J$.
Since $R_\ell\unlhd J$, the group $J$ normalizes $C_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(R_\ell)=T$.
Hence, $J\leq N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$.
head: environment

label: lem:linear-singer-small-p-part
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{lem:linear-singer-small-p-part}
Under the hypotheses of \textup{Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-containing-subgroups}},
let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
If $|J|_p<q^{m/2}$, then $J\leq N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $J\nleq N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$, then Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-containing-subgroups} supplies a subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_b(q^s)\leq J$ with
$|\operatorname{SL}_b(q^s)|_p=q^{m(b-1)/2}\geq q^{m/2}$.
This contradicts $|J|_p<q^{m/2}$.
Therefore, $J\leq N_{\operatorname{SL}_m(q)}(T)$.
head: environment

label: lem:linear-singer-line
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linear-singer-line}
Let $n\geq4$ be composite and let $q$ be a prime power.
Let $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$.
Suppose that $A<G$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
Suppose that $A$ stabilizes a line in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ and that $A\leq N_G(T)$ for a Singer torus $T\leq G$.
Then, $A=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ be the projective Singer torus with $A\leq N_G(T)$.
Since a field multiplier in $T$ stabilizing a line lies in $\mathbb{F}_q$, the projective element is trivial.
Thus, $A\cap T=1$.
Let $\nu:N_G(T)\to N_G(T)/T\cong C_n$ be the quotient map.
As $\ker(\nu|_A)=A\cap T=1$, the subgroup $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid n$.

We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{n-1}-1$.
Since $n$ is composite and $n\geq4$, we have $n-1\geq3$ and $n-1\ne6$.
Therefore, there is no Zsigmondy exception.
We have $\ell\geq n$.
As $n$ is composite and $\ell$ is prime, we have $\ell>n$.
We choose $B\leq G$ of order $\ell$.
A lift of $B$ acts irreducibly on $U\leq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=n-1$ and fixes a complementary line.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AB^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $[K:B^x]\leq n<\ell$, the subgroup $B^x$ is a normal Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $K$.
The quotient $N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)$ has order dividing $n-1$.
Let $\eta:A\to N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)$ satisfy $\eta(a)=aC_G(B^x)$.
By the homomorphism $\eta$, the order $|\eta(A)|$ divides both $|A|$ and $n-1$.
Since $|A|\mid n$ and $(n,n-1)=1$, we have $\eta(A)=1$.
Therefore, $A$ centralizes $B^x$.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{SL}_n(q)\to G$ be the quotient map.
As its kernel has order prime to $\ell$, the inverse image of $B^x$ has a unique subgroup $\widetilde B_x$ of order $\ell$.
The restriction $\pi|_{\widetilde B_x}:\widetilde B_x\to B^x$ is an isomorphism.
Every lift of $A$ normalizes $\widetilde B_x$ and acts trivially on $B^x$.
Therefore, every lift of $A$ centralizes $\widetilde B_x$.

Suppose that $A\ne1$, and choose an element $a\in A$
of prime order $r$.
The image of $a$ in $N_G(T)/T$ also has order $r$.
Next, we choose a lift $\widetilde a\in\operatorname{SL}_n(q)$.
Let $\overline F$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_q$.
The inverse image of $T$ has $n$ eigenlines on $\overline F\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}\mathbb{F}_q^n$.
Because the image of $a$ in $N_G(T)/T$ has order $r$, the lift $\widetilde a$ permutes these eigenlines in $n/r$ cycles of length $r$.
Along each cycle, $\widetilde a$ sends a weight vector to a nonzero scalar multiple of the next vector.
An eigenvector is determined by one coordinate on each cycle.
Since $\widetilde a^r$ is scalar, every geometric eigenspace has dimension at most $n/r$.
This argument also applies in characteristic $r$.

We choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\operatorname{SL}_n(q)$ of $x$.
Let $U_x=\widetilde x^{-1}U$.
Since $\widetilde a$ centralizes $\widetilde B_x$, its restriction $\widetilde a|_{U_x}$ is multiplication by some $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{n-1}}^*$.
Since $\widetilde a^r=\zeta I$ for some $\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$, we have $\lambda^r=\zeta$.
The degree $e=[\mathbb{F}_q(\lambda):\mathbb{F}_q]$ divides $n-1$ and is at most $r$.
As $r\mid n$, we have $r\nmid n-1$.
Therefore, $e\leq r-1$.
Because $n$ is composite and $r\mid n$, we have $n>r$.
Since $\widetilde a|_{U_x}$ is multiplication by $\lambda$ of degree $e$, some geometric eigenspace has dimension at least $(n-1)/e\geq(n-1)/(r-1)$.
As $n>r$, we have $(n-1)/(r-1)>n/r$.
The bounds $n/r$ and $(n-1)/(r-1)$ contradict one another.
head: environment

label: thm:linear-composite-large-field
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:linear-composite-large-field}
Let $n\geq4$ be composite and let $q\geq5$ be a prime power.
Then, $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Next, let $P_2$ stabilize $W\leq\mathbb{F}_q^n$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=2$.
We have $P_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$ by \cite[Theorem C]{LPS}.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.1]{LiXia}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq P_2^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Hence, $G\ne AB$ for every proper subgroup $B<G$.
Otherwise, $G=P_2^gB$ with $P_2^g,B<G$, contrary to the cited theorem.
For every maximal subgroup $M<G$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:max} that $A\leq M^x$ for some $x\in G$.
In particular, $A$ stabilizes a line.
Let $T$ be a projective Singer torus.

Firstly, suppose that $(n,q)\ne(4,5)$.
The monomial subgroup $M$ of type $\operatorname{GL}_1(q)\wr S_n$
is maximal \cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
Hence, $A\leq M^g$ for some $g\in G$, and
$|A|_p\leq(n!)_p<q^{n/2}$.
For odd $p$, use $v_p(n!)<n/(p-1)\leq n/2$.
For $p=2$, we have $q\geq8$ and $v_2(n!)<n<fn/2$.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$, we have $K<G$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\operatorname{SL}_n(q)$ of $x$.
Next, let $\widetilde T$ be the inverse image of $T$ under $\operatorname{SL}_n(q)\to G$.
The inverse image $\widetilde K$ contains $\widetilde T^{\widetilde x}$ of order $(q^n-1)/(q-1)$.
As both $|\widetilde T|$ and the central kernel order are prime to $p$, we have $|\widetilde K|_p=|A|_p$.
By Corollary \ref{lem:linear-singer-small-p-part}, we have $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
Since $A$ stabilizes a line, Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-line} yields $A=1$.

For $(n,q)=(4,5)$, we take a maximal subgroup $M$ of type $\operatorname{GL}_2(5)\wr S_2$
\cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose $g_0\in G$ with $A\leq M^{g_0}$.
Hence, $|A|_5\leq25$.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{SL}_4(5)\to G$ be the quotient map, and let $\widetilde A=\pi^{-1}(A)$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AT^x$ a subgroup.
As $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$, we have $K<G$.
Let $\widetilde K=\pi^{-1}(K)$.
By Bereczky's theorem, we choose an $\mathbb{F}_{25}$-vector space structure on $V=\mathbb{F}_5^4$ with
$\widetilde K\leq E=\bigl(\operatorname{GL}_2(25)\rtimes C_2\bigr)\cap\operatorname{SL}_4(5)$.
Since the field automorphism part of $E$ has order $2$, every element $u\in E$ of order $5$ is $\mathbb{F}_{25}$-linear.
Hence, $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_5}(u-I)$ is even.
Suppose that $|A|_5=25$.
A Sylow $5$-subgroup of $\widetilde A$ is then a Sylow subgroup of $\pi^{-1}(M^{g_0})$.
Hence, $\widetilde A$ contains a transvection $u$ with $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_5}(u-I)=1$.
Because $u\in\widetilde A\leq\widetilde K\leq E$, we have a contradiction.
Thus, $|A|_5\leq5<25$.
By Corollary \ref{lem:linear-singer-small-p-part} and Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-line}, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:unitriangular-forms
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that a form $h:E^b\times E^b\to F$ satisfies $h(gv,gw)=h(v,w)$ for all $g\in P$ and $v,w\in E^b$.
Let $Y=Ee_1$ and $W=\ker E_{12}$.
The root group $\{I+tE_{12}:t\in E\}$ fixes $W$ pointwise.
For $t\in E$ and $w\in W$, we have $h(e_2+te_1,w)=h(e_2,w)$.
Hence, $h(te_1,w)=0$.
Thus, $Y\perp W$.
In particular, $h(Y,Y)=0$.

Firstly, suppose that $h$ is symmetric and the characteristic is odd.
For $x\ne0$ in $E$ and $t\in E$, let $g=I+tE_{12}$.
Since $g\in P$, we have $h(gxe_2,gxe_2)=h(xe_2,xe_2)$.
Hence, $2h(tx e_1,xe_2)=0$.
Varying $t$ shows that $Y\perp xe_2$.
Therefore, $Y\perp Ee_2$.
Since $Y\perp W$, the nonzero subspace $Y$ lies in the radical of $h$.
As $h$ is nondegenerate, we have a contradiction.

For a Hermitian form over $\mathbb{F}_4$, let $a\in\mathbb{F}_4$ and $v,w\in E^b$.
We use $h(av,w)=a h(v,w)$ and $h(v,aw)=a^2h(v,w)$.
Now, let $x,y\in E$ and $t\in\mathbb{F}_4$.
We take $v=xe_2$, $w=ye_2$ and $g=I+tE_{12}$.
Since $g\in P$, we have $h(gv,gw)=h(v,w)$.
As $h(Y,Y)=0$, we obtain that $t h(xe_1,ye_2)+t^2 h(xe_2,ye_1)=0$.
For $t=1$, we have $h(xe_1,ye_2)+h(xe_2,ye_1)=0$.
For $t\in\mathbb{F}_4\setminus\mathbb{F}_2$, we have $t-t^2\ne0$.
Subtracting $t^2$ times the equation for $t=1$ from the preceding identity, we obtain $(t-t^2)h(xe_1,ye_2)=0$.
Since $t-t^2\ne0$, we have $h(xe_1,ye_2)=h(xe_2,ye_1)=0$.
Because $Y\perp Ee_2$ and $Y\perp W$, the nonzero subspace $Y$ lies in the radical of $h$.
We have a contradiction.

Finally, suppose that $b\geq3$ and $h$ is alternating.
For every $t\in E$, the map $I+tE_{23}$ fixes $\ker E_{23}$ pointwise.
For $w\in\ker E_{23}$, we have $h(e_3+te_2,w)=h(e_3,w)$.
Thus, $h(te_2,w)=0$ and $Ee_2\perp\ker E_{23}$.
Since $Y\leq\ker E_{23}$, we have $Y\perp Ee_2$.
As $Y\perp W$ and $Y\perp Ee_2$, the nonzero subspace $Y$ lies in the radical of $h$.
Because $h$ is nondegenerate, we have a contradiction.
head: environment

label: thm:linear-composite-small-fields
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:linear-composite-small-fields}
Let $n\geq4$ be composite and let $q\in\{3,4\}$.
Then, $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $G=\operatorname{PSL}_4(3)$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Suppose that $(n,q)\ne(4,3)$ and that $A<G$
is ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $p$ be the characteristic.
As in Theorem \ref{thm:linear-composite-large-field}, we have $P_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Therefore, $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$.
As $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$, Lemma \ref{lem:max} yields $A\leq M^g$ for some $g\in G$ for every maximal subgroup $M<G$.
In particular, $A$ stabilizes a line.

For $q=3$, the orthogonal form stabilizer is maximal
\cite[Theorem 4.15(b)]{King2005}.
For $q=4$, the Hermitian form stabilizer is maximal
\cite[Theorem 4.15(c)]{King2005}.
We take a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of the inverse image $\widetilde A$ in $\operatorname{SL}_n(q)$.
For $q=3$, we choose a nondegenerate symmetric form $h$ on $V=\mathbb{F}_3^n$.
For $q=4$, we choose a nondegenerate Hermitian form $h$ on $V=\mathbb{F}_4^n$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for the form stabilizer, we choose $h$ so that $\widetilde A$ acts by similarities of $h$.
Let $\mu:\widetilde A\to\mathbb{F}_q^*$ satisfy $h(gv,gw)=\mu(g)h(v,w)$ for $g\in\widetilde A$ and $v,w\in V$.
Since $p\nmid|\mathbb{F}_q^*|$, we have $\mu(P)=1$.
Hence, $h(gv,gw)=h(v,w)$ for every $g\in P$ and $v,w\in V$.

Let $T$ be a projective Singer torus.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$, we have $K<G$.
The inverse image $\widetilde K$ in $\operatorname{SL}_n(q)$ contains the inverse image of $T^x$ of order $(q^n-1)/(q-1)$.
We have $|\widetilde K|_p=|A|_p$, so $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\widetilde K$.
Every $p$-subgroup $P_0\leq\widetilde K$ satisfies $P_0^g\leq P$ for some $g\in\widetilde K$.
Let $h_g:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfy $h_g(v,w)=h(g^{-1}v,g^{-1}w)$ for $V=\mathbb{F}_q^n$.
Then, $h_g(uv,uw)=h_g(v,w)$ for every $u\in P_0$.
Consider $\operatorname{SL}_b(q^s)$ acting on $V=(\mathbb{F}_{q^s})^b$ with $bs=n$ and $b\geq2$.
If this subgroup lay in $\widetilde K$, then its upper unitriangular subgroup would preserve one of the nondegenerate forms $h_g$.
This contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:unitriangular-forms}.
Thus, $\widetilde K$ contains no such subgroup.
From Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-containing-subgroups}, we obtain that $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
Then, we conclude from Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-line} that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:unitriangular-indecomposable
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X\in\operatorname{End}_F(E^b)$ commute with $P$.
Relative to $E^b=\bigoplus_{i=1}^b Ee_i$, the block matrix of $X$ is $(X_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq b}$.
Moreover, each block $X_{ij}$ belongs to $\operatorname{End}_F(E)$.
Since $X$ commutes with $P$, we have $X(I+tE_{j,j+1})=(I+tE_{j,j+1})X$ for every $t\in E$.
From the block comparison in this identity, we obtain $X_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $(i,j)\ne(1,b)$.
The diagonal blocks also coincide.
Since the common diagonal map commutes with multiplication by every $t\in E$, it is $x\mapsto ax$ for some $a\in E$.
Thus, every commuting endomorphism $X$ has $X_{ii}(x)=ax$ for $1\leq i\leq b$ and $x\in E$, with $a\in E$.
The only possible nondiagonal block is $X_{1b}=f\in\operatorname{End}_F(E)$.
An idempotent has $a^2=a$, so $a=0$ or $a=1$.
For $a=0$ or $a=1$, the $(1,b)$ block of $X^2=X$ is $2af=f$.
Thus, $f=0$.
Hence, the only idempotents are $0$ and $I$.
If $E^b=V_1\oplus V_2$ with nonzero $P$-invariant $F$-subspaces $V_1,V_2$, then the projection onto $V_1$ is an idempotent.
Because both summands are $P$-invariant, the projection lies in $\operatorname{End}_{F[P]}(E^b)$ and differs from $0,I$.
Therefore, no such decomposition exists.
head: environment

label: thm:linear-composite-two
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:linear-composite-two}
Let $n\geq4$ be composite.
Then, $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(2)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n=4$, use $\operatorname{PSL}_4(2)\cong A_8$ and Proposition
\ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Suppose that $n\geq6$ and that $A<G$ is ordinary
$G$-permutable.
We have $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(2)$.
By the argument in Theorem \ref{thm:linear-composite-large-field}, we have $P_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Therefore, $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq P_1^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Hence, $A$ stabilizes a line.

We take a Singer subgroup $T$ of order $2^n-1$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $AB\ne G$ for every $B<G$, we have $K<G$.
By Kantor's theorem \cite{Kantor1980}, we have
$\operatorname{GL}_b(2^s)\lhd K\leq\operatorname{GL}_b(2^s)\rtimes\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{2^s}/\mathbb{F}_2)$
with $bs=n$.
We use $V=(\mathbb{F}_{2^s})^b$ as an $\mathbb{F}_2$-vector space.
Because $T$ has odd order, every Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$ is a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $K$.
We prove that $b=1$.

Firstly, suppose that $n$ is odd.
We choose $n=dt$ with odd $d,t\geq3$.
The imprimitive subgroup of type $\operatorname{GL}_d(2)\wr S_t$
is maximal \cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, $A$ lies in a conjugate of this maximal subgroup.
Thus, a Sylow $2$-subgroup $P$ of $A$ permutes $t$ blocks of dimension $d$.
Since $t>1$ is odd, $P$ is intransitive on the blocks.
We sum the blocks in each $P$-orbit and obtain the decomposition $V=W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_k$ with $k>1$.
For every $u\in P$, we have $uW_i=W_i$.
If $b\geq2$, then we take $P_0=\langle I+tE_{ij}:t\in\mathbb{F}_{2^s},\ 1\leq i<j\leq b\rangle\leq\operatorname{GL}_b(2^s)$.
Then, $P_0^g\leq P$ for some $g\in K$.
As $P_0^g\leq P$, we have $u(gW_i)=gW_i$ for every $u\in P_0$ and $1\leq i\leq k$.
Thus, $V=gW_1\oplus\cdots\oplus gW_k$ contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:unitriangular-indecomposable}.

Now, suppose that $n=2m$ is even, so $m\geq3$.
The subgroup $\operatorname{Sp}_n(2)$ is maximal
\cite[Theorem 4.15(a)]{King2005}.
Let $P$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, $A$ lies in a conjugate of $\operatorname{Sp}_n(2)$.
Therefore, we choose a nondegenerate alternating form $h$ on $V$ with
$h(uv,uw)=h(v,w)$ for all $u\in P$ and $v,w\in V$.

If $b\geq3$, then a conjugate of the upper unitriangular subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_b(2^s)$ lies in $P$.
It would preserve the corresponding conjugate of $h$, contrary to Lemma \ref{lem:unitriangular-forms}.
Thus, $b<3$.
If $b=2$, then $s=m$ and $K$ contains the root group
$R=\{I+tE_{12}:t\in\mathbb{F}_{2^m}\}\cong C_2^m$.
Every nonidentity element $g\in R$ satisfies
$(g-I)^2=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}(g-I)=m$.
There is $g\in K$ such that $R^g$ lies in a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$.
Then, we replace $R$ by $R^g$.

The subgroup of type $\operatorname{GL}_m(2)\wr S_2$ is maximal
\cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, $A$ lies in a conjugate of this maximal subgroup.
Hence, $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}V_i=m$, and $R$ permutes $V_1,V_2$.
Let $R_0=\{g\in R:gV_i=V_i\text{ for }i=1,2\}$.
Since $[R:R_0]\leq2$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}R_0\geq m-1$.
For odd $m$, every involution on $1$ block has rank
at most $(m-1)/2$.
Hence, every nonidentity element of $R_0$ has total rank at most $m-1$.
But every nonidentity element of $R$ has rank $m$.
Hence, we have a contradiction.

For even $m$, each block rank is at most $m/2$.
Since the total rank is $m$, both block ranks equal $m/2$.
For $i=1,2$, let $\pi_i:R_0\to\operatorname{GL}(V_i)$ satisfy $\pi_i(g)=g|_{V_i}$.
As every nonidentity element of $R_0$ has rank $m/2$ on each block, each $\pi_i$ is injective.
Let $d=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}R_0$.
By the bound for $R_0$, we have $d\geq m-1$.
Every nonidentity element fixes exactly $2^{m/2}$ vectors
on either block.
Using Burnside's formula for the $R_0$-orbits on $V_1$, we obtain
$$
 \frac{2^m+(2^d-1)2^{m/2}}{2^d}
 =2^{m/2}+\frac{2^{m/2}(2^{m/2}-1)}{2^d}\in\mathbb{Z}.
$$
Since $2^{m/2}-1$ is odd, the integrality of the displayed expression implies $d\leq m/2$.
As $d\geq m-1$ and $m\geq4$, we have a contradiction.
Therefore, $b\ne2$.
We conclude that $b=1$ and $A\leq N_G(\operatorname{GL}_1(2^n))$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:linear-singer-line}, we have $A=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:all-linear
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:all-linear}
For every $n\geq3$ and every prime power $q$, the group
$G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Theorems \ref{thm:l3} and \ref{thm:linear-prime}, we have $A=1$ in odd prime dimensions.
By Theorem \ref{thm:linear-composite-large-field}, we have $A=1$ for composite $n$ and $q\geq5$.
For composite $n$ and $q\in\{2,3,4\}$, we obtain from Theorems \ref{thm:linear-composite-small-fields} and \ref{thm:linear-composite-two} that $A=1$.

label: lem:unitary-three-subgroups
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-three-subgroups}
Let $q\geq3$ be a prime power.
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_3(q)$ and $d=(3,q+1)$.
If $q\notin\{3,5\}$, then $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$.
For $q\notin\{3,5\}$, a Singer torus normalizer $N$ and a Borel subgroup $P$ are maximal.
Their orders are $|N|=3(q^2-q+1)/d$ and $|P|=q^3(q^2-1)/d$.
If $d=1$, then the split torus normalizer is also maximal and has
order $6(q+1)^2$.

The group $M_{10}$ is the Mathieu group of degree $10$.
In the table, $C_3\leq\operatorname{GU}_2(5)$ denotes the scalar subgroup of order $3$.
For $q=3,5$, the table lists the types and orders of maximal subgroups of $G$.
If $G=XY$ with $X,Y<G$ maximal, then one factor has the first type and the other has the second type in the row for $q$.

\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|}

$q$ & \multicolumn{4}{c|}{Maximal subgroups and orders}\\\hline
$3$ & $3^{1+2}\rtimes C_8$ & $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ & $\operatorname{GU}_2(3)$ & $(C_4\times C_4)\rtimes S_3$\\
    & $216$ & $168$ & $96$ & $96$\\\hline
$5$ & $5^{1+2}\rtimes C_8$ & $A_7$ & $M_{10}$ & $\operatorname{GU}_2(5)/C_3$\\

Every subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ of order $24$ is isomorphic to $S_4$.
Every proper subgroup of $A_7$ containing an element of order $7$ lies in a subgroup isomorphic to $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$.

body_md:

head: environment

label: prop:unitary-three-order-three
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-three-order-three}
Let $q\geq3$ be a prime power and let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_3(q)$.
Let $N$ be a Singer torus normalizer and $P$ a Borel subgroup.
Let $A\leq G$ have order $3$.
Suppose that $A^g\leq N$ and $A^h\leq P$ for some $g,h\in G$.
Then, $A$ is not ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $d=(3,q+1)$.
Choose $g\in G$ with $A^g\leq N$ and replace $A$ by $A^g$.

Let $\pi:\operatorname{SU}_3(q)\to G$ be the quotient map.
We choose a field model for the Singer torus normalized by $N$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^6}$ as an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-vector space, so $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V=3$.
We take the Hermitian form $h(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^6}/\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}(xy^{q^3})$.
For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, $h(ax,by)=ab^q h(x,y)$ and $h(y,x)=h(x,y)^q$.
We take $\widetilde T=\{M_z:z^{q^2-q+1}=1\}$, where $M_z(x)=zx$ for $x,z\in\mathbb{F}_{q^6}$.
Then, $\widetilde T$ is a Singer torus of $\operatorname{SU}_3(q)$.
Let $T=\pi(\widetilde T)$, so $N=N_G(T)$.
Let $w:V\to V$ satisfy $w(x)=x^{q^2}$.
We have $h(wx,wy)=h(x,y)$ for $x,y\in V$ and $\det w=1$.
Moreover, the map $w$ is $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear.
Furthermore, on a normal basis, the matrix of $w$ is a $3$-cycle permutation matrix.
The normal basis calculation yields $|w|=3$.
Since $wM_zw^{-1}=M_{z^{q^2}}$, we also have $w\in N_{\operatorname{SU}_3(q)}(\widetilde T)$.

We have $|T|=(q^2-q+1)/d$ and $(|T|,3)=1$.
Moreover, we have $N_G(T)=T\rtimes\langle \overline w\rangle$.
Let $C\leq N_G(T)$ have order $3$.
Since $(|T|,3)=1$, we choose $g\in N_G(T)$ with $C=\langle \overline w\rangle^{\,g}$ by Schur--Zassenhaus.
If the characteristic is $3$, then $w$ has $1$ Jordan block of size $3$.
Otherwise, $w$ has the $3$ distinct eigenvalues $1,\omega,\omega^2$, with $\omega^3=1\ne\omega$.
For every scalar $\zeta\ne0$, the eigenvalue multiplicities of $\zeta w$ equal those of $w$.


Firstly, suppose that $q\equiv1\pmod3$.
Then, $d=1$ and $q\geq4$.
We choose $s\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^{\times}$ of order $m=q+1$, so $s^{q+1}=1$.
In an orthonormal basis, we choose $b=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1},1)$.
Let $D=\langle b\rangle$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, $K=AD^x$ is a subgroup for some $x\in G$.
As $(3,m)=1$, we have $|K|=3m$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:index3}, we have $(D^x)^2\unlhd K$.
Therefore, $A\leq N_G((D^x)^2)$.

Since $q\geq4$ for even $q$ and $q\geq7$ for odd $q$, we have $|s^2|=m/(2,m)>2$.
Thus, $b^2$ has $3$ distinct eigenvalues.
Let $L_i=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}e_i$ in the chosen orthonormal basis.
For $g\in N_G(D^2)$, we have $gL_3=L_3$ and $\{gL_1,gL_2\}=\{L_1,L_2\}$.
As $|C_G(D^2)|=(q+1)^2$, we have $|N_G(D^2)|\mid2(q+1)^2$.
Because $3\nmid2(q+1)^2$, the inclusion $A\leq N_G((D^x)^2)$ is impossible.

Now, suppose that $q\equiv2\pmod3$.
Then, $d=3$, and the characteristic is not $3$.
Suppose that $v_3(q+1)=1$.
We have $|P|=q^3(q^2-1)/3$ and $3\nmid|P|$.
Hence, $A^h\nleq P$ for every $h\in G$, contrary to the hypothesis.

Suppose that $9\mid q+1$.
We take the inverse image $\widetilde P$ of $P$ under $\operatorname{SU}_3(q)\to G$.
We choose a basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $h(e_1,e_3)=h(e_3,e_1)=h(e_2,e_2)=1$.
All other values $h(e_i,e_j)$ are $0$.
In this basis, we have $C=\{z(a):a\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^{\times}\}\leq\widetilde P$.
With this basis, we use $z(a)=\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{q-1},a^{-q})$.
Let $\overline C$ be the projective image of $C$.
Since $|C\cap Z(\operatorname{SU}_3(q))|=3$, the unique subgroup $D_3\leq\overline C$ of order $3$ has inverse image of order $9$ in $C$.
For $a$ of order $9$, we have $q\equiv-1\pmod9$ and $z(a)=\operatorname{diag}(a,a^7,a)$.
Hence, $z(a)$ has a repeated eigenvalue.
Let $B\leq P$ have order $3$.
Since the unipotent radical of $P$ is normal and has order prime to $3$, we choose $u\in P$ with $B^u\leq\overline C$ by Schur--Zassenhaus.
Every subgroup of order $3$ in $N$ has a lift with $3$ distinct eigenvalues, by the calculation of $w$.
Scalar multiplication does not change eigenvalue multiplicities.
Thus, a generator of $B$ has a repeated eigenvalue in every lift.
By the preceding comparison with lifts of subgroups of order $3$ in $N$, we have $B^g\nleq N$ for every $g\in G$.
Therefore, the $2$ inclusions $A^g\leq N$ and $A^h\leq P$ cannot both hold.

Finally, suppose that $3\mid q$.
Then, $d=1$, and a generator of $A$ is regular unipotent by the computed Jordan block of $w$.
The centralizer of a generator of $A$ is a $3$-group by Lemma \ref{lem:regular-unipotent}.
We choose a cyclic subgroup $D$ of order $4$ in the Borel complement.
Suppose that $AD^x$ is a subgroup.
By Lemma \ref{lem:index3}, we have $(D^x)^2\unlhd AD^x$.
Because a normal subgroup of order $2$ is central, $A$ would centralize the involution generating $(D^x)^2$.
This contradicts the preceding conclusion that $C_G(A)$ is a $3$-group.\qedhere
