label: thm:u3
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G$ be nontrivial and ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $d=(3,q+1)$.
Next, let $N$ be a Singer torus normalizer and $P$ a Borel subgroup,
as in Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-three-subgroups}.
Firstly, suppose that $q\notin\{3,5\}$.
If $d=1$, then $q^2-q+1$ is odd and coprime to $3(q+1)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we compare $|N|$ with the split torus normalizer order.
We have $|A|\mid\gcd\bigl(3(q^2-q+1),6(q+1)^2\bigr)=3$.
If $d=3$, then let $s=(q^2-q+1)/3$.
Then,
$$
 (s,3q(q-1)(q+1))=1, |A|\mid\gcd\left(3s,\frac{q^3(q^2-1)}3\right)\mid3.
$$
Thus, $|A|=3$ for $q\notin\{3,5\}$.
Since $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$, we have $A^g\leq N$ and $A^h\leq P$ for some $g,h\in G$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-three-order-three}, we conclude that $|A|\ne3$.

For $q=3$, we have $|G|=6048$.
We choose a maximal subgroup $M<G$ of order $96$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-three-subgroups}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
It follows from Lemma \ref{lem:max} that $|A|\mid96$.
For a maximal subgroup $L\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$, $G=AL^x$ would require $36=[G:L]\mid|A|$.
Hence, $A\leq L^x$ for some $x\in G$ and $|A|\mid24$.
Since $28=[G:P]\nmid|A|$, we also have $A\leq P^y$ for some $y\in G$.
The Sylow $2$-subgroups of $P\cong3^{1+2}\rtimes C_8$ are cyclic of order $8$.

We take $T\leq G$ of order $7$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $R=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
We have $|R|=7|A|\leq168$.
Only maximal subgroups isomorphic to $L$ have order divisible by $7$.
Hence, we choose $L_0\leq G$ with $R\leq L_0$ and $L_0\cong L$.
By the subgroup list of $L_0$, we have $|R|\in\{7,21,168\}$ and $|A|\in\{1,3,24\}$.
If $|A|=24$, then $A\leq L_0$ implies that $A\cong S_4$.
As $A\leq P^y$ and every Sylow $2$-subgroup of $P^y$ is cyclic, $A\cong S_4$ is impossible.
If $|A|=3$, then $R=C_7\rtimes C_3=N_G(T^x)$.
We have $A\leq P^y$ with $y\in G$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-three-order-three}, we have a contradiction.
Therefore, $A=1$ for $q=3$.

For $q=5$, we have $|G|=126000$.
We choose a maximal subgroup $M\cong\operatorname{GU}_2(5)/C_3$ of order $240$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-three-subgroups}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Then, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:max} that $|A|\mid240$.
Since $50=[G:L]\nmid240$ for $L\cong A_7$, we have $A\leq L^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $126=[G:P]\nmid240$ for $P\cong5^{1+2}\rtimes C_8$, we have $A\leq P^y$ for some $y\in G$.
Consequently, $|A|\mid\gcd(240,2520,1000)=40$.
We choose $T\leq G$ of order $7$.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $R=AT^x$ is a subgroup.
We have $|R|=7|A|\leq280$.
As only maximal subgroups of type $A_7$ contain an element of order $7$, we choose $H\cong A_7$ with $R\leq H$.
Because $|R|<|H|$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-three-subgroups} that $R\leq L_0$ for some $L_0\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$.
Hence, $|R|\in\{7,21,168\}$ and $|A|\in\{1,3,24\}$.
As $|A|\mid40$, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: thm:unitary-prime
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-prime}
Let $r$ be an odd prime and let $q$ be a prime power.
Suppose that $G=\operatorname{PSU}_r(q)$ is simple.
Then, $G$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

For $r=3$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:u3}.
Now, assume that $r\geq5$.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime, and let $d=(r,q+1)$.
Let $A<G$ be nontrivial and ordinary $G$-permutable.
Firstly, assume that $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$.
We consider $\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$ at the end and use the following classifications.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] Since $r$ is prime, we have $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$ by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{LiXia}.
\item[(2)] We take a unitary Singer torus $T$ with $|T|=(q^r+1)/((q+1)d)$.
Let $N=N_G(T)=T\rtimes C_r$.
By \cite{Bereczky}, we have $H=N$ for every maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $T\leq H$.
The only exceptional pair with prime $r\geq5$ is $(r,q)=(5,2)$.
\end{itemize}

We take $P_1=\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$ for a singular line $L\leq\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^r$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $|A|\mid|N|$ and $|A|\mid|P_1|$.
We have $|P_1|=q^{2r-3}(q^2-1)|\operatorname{SU}_{r-2}(q)|/d$.
The integer $\Phi_{2r}(q)=(q^r+1)/(q+1)$ is odd.
If $r\nmid q+1$, then $r\nmid\Phi_{2r}(q)$.
If $r\mid q+1$, then $v_r(\Phi_{2r}(q))=1$.
Since $d=(r,q+1)$, the quotient $|T|=\Phi_{2r}(q)/d$ is odd and prime to $r$. Any prime $\ell\mid |T|$ satisfies
$\ell\nmid q+1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(-q)=r$. Such a prime
divides none of the factors $q^i-(-1)^i$ with $i<r$, nor $q^2-1$.
Therefore, $(|T|,|P_1|)=1$ and $(|N|,|P_1|)\mid r$.
As $A\ne1$, we have $|A|=r$.

Since $(|T|,r)=1$, every subgroup of $N=T\rtimes C_r$ of order $r$ equals $C_r^g$ for some $g\in N$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2r}}$ as an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-vector space, so $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V=r$.
We take $h(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^{2r}}/\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}(xy^{q^r})$.
For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, $h(ax,by)=ab^q h(x,y)$ and $h(y,x)=h(x,y)^q$.
Let $w:V\to V$ satisfy $w(x)=x^{q^2}$.
By the trace formula, we have $h(wx,wy)=h(x,y)$ for every $x,y\in V$.
On a normal basis, $w$ acts as an $r$-cycle.
Hence, $\det w=1$ and $|w|=r$.
For $p\ne r$, every $r$th root is an eigenvalue of $w$ with multiplicity $1$.
For $p=r$, the lift $w$ has $1$ Jordan block of size $r$.
For every central scalar $\zeta$, the eigenvalue multiplicities of $\zeta w$ equal those of $w$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, $A$ lies in a conjugate of $N$.
Schur--Zassenhaus then yields $g\in G$ such that $A^g=\langle \overline w\rangle$.
We replace $A$ by $A^g$.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] If $(r,q)\ne(5,2)$ and $p\ne r$ and $q\not\equiv1\pmod r$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Let $\pi:\operatorname{SU}_r(q)\to G$ be the quotient map.
Next, we choose a unitary transvection $u\in\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$.
Let $t=\pi(u)$ and $U=\langle t\rangle$.
Then, $|U|=p$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AU^x$ with $|K|=rp$ for some $x\in G$.
If $p<r$, then $A\lhd K$.
Therefore, $t^x\in N_G(A)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:transvection}, we have a contradiction.
For $p>r$, we have $U^x\lhd K$.
As $q\not\equiv1\pmod r$, we have $r\nmid p-1$.
Hence, $A$ centralizes $U^x$ in $G$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$ of $x$.
Let $u_x=u^{\widetilde x}$.
For a lift $a\in\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$ of a generator of $A$, we have $a u_x a^{-1}=\zeta u_x$ for a scalar $\zeta$.
Because $a u_x a^{-1}$ is unipotent, $\zeta=1$.
As $a$ is regular semisimple, $C_{\operatorname{GL}_r(q^2)}(a)$ is a torus.
Hence, $u_x=I$, contrary to the choice of a transvection.
The condition $r\mid q+1$ is included in $q\not\equiv1\pmod r$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] If $p\ne r$ and $q\equiv1\pmod r$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Now, suppose that $p\ne r$ and $q\equiv1\pmod r$.
Then, $d=1$, so $G=\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$.
Let $m=q+1$.
Since $q\equiv1\pmod r$ and $q\geq2$, we have $m\geq r+2$.
Let $\mu_m=\{z\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^{\times}:z^m=1\}$.
In an orthonormal basis, we take the abelian subgroup
$$
B=\{\operatorname{diag}(z,z,z_3,\ldots,z_r): z,z_i\in\mu_m,\ z^2z_3\cdots z_r=1\}.
$$
By the diagonal constraint, we have $|B|=m^{r-2}$, prime to $r$.
If $K=AB^x$ were a subgroup, then $B^x$ would have index $r$.
We replace $K,A$ by $K^{x^{-1}},A^{x^{-1}}$ with $x^{-1}\in G$.
Then, $K=AB$.
Let $C=\operatorname{Core}_K(B)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:abelian-index}, we have $[B:C]\leq r-1$.

Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^r$.
Let $V=W_1\perp\cdots\perp W_k$ be the decomposition into common eigenspaces of $C$.
Since the first $2$ coordinates have equal $C$-characters, we have $k\leq r-1$.
As $C\unlhd K$, the group $A$ permutes $W_1,\ldots,W_k$.
Because $|A|=r>k$, we have $aW_i=W_i$ for every $a\in A$ and every $i$.
As $C$ acts by scalars on each $W_i$, we have $A\leq C_G(C)$.

For a generator $a$ of $A$, the nontrivial eigenvalues pair as
$\lambda,\lambda^{-q}=\lambda^{-1}$ on each nondegenerate invariant
block. Every $r$th root is an eigenvalue of $a$ with multiplicity $1$.
Hence, the block containing the eigenvalue $1$ is the only block of odd dimension.
All other blocks have even dimension.
Therefore, $k\leq(r+1)/2$.

Let $s_i=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}W_i$ for $1\leq i\leq k$.
Let
$$
D=\{\operatorname{diag}(z_1I_{s_1},\ldots,z_kI_{s_k}):
z_i\in\mu_m,\ \prod_{i=1}^kz_i^{s_i}=1\}.
$$
By the $C$-weight space decomposition and the determinant constraint, we have $C\leq D$ and $|D|=m^{k-1}(m,s_1,\ldots,s_k)$.
Since $(m,r)=1$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k s_i=r$, we have $(m,s_1,\ldots,s_k)=1$.
Hence, $|D|=m^{k-1}$.
Consequently,
$$
[B:C]\geq m^{r-2}/m^{k-1}\geq m^{(r-3)/2}>r-1.
$$
This contradicts $[B:C]\leq r-1$ from Lemma \ref{lem:abelian-index}.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $p=r$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Now, suppose that $p=r$.
Then, $d=1$, so $G=\operatorname{SU}_r(q)$.
A generator of $A$ is regular unipotent.
By Lemma \ref{lem:regular-unipotent}, we have a contradiction.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] If $G=\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
For $G=\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$, we have $XY\ne G$ for all $X,Y<G$.
The maximal subgroups of $\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$
include $L\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$ of order $660$ and $P_1$ of order $82944$
\cite{Atlas1985}. Therefore, $|A|\mid(660,82944)=12$.
We take a Singer torus $T\leq G$ of order $11$.
By \cite{Bereczky}, we have $H\cong L$ for every maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $T\leq H$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
We have $|AT^x|=11|A|\leq132<660<|G|$.
As $AT^x<G$, we choose a maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $AT^x\leq H$.
Because $T\leq H^{x^{-1}}$, we have $H\cong L$.
Hence, $AT^x<H$.
In $\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$, every proper subgroup containing a subgroup of order
$11$ lies in $C_{11}\rtimes C_5$, by Dickson's maximal subgroup list for $\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$ \cite{Dickson1901}. Hence,
$|A|\mid5$.
As $|A|\mid12$, we conclude that $A=1$.
\qedhere
head: environment

label: lem:unitary-nondegenerate-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-nondegenerate-product}
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Let $(V,h)$ be a nondegenerate Hermitian space over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Let $B\leq\operatorname{SU}(V)$ be an abelian $p'$-subgroup such that every
$B$-invariant subspace is nondegenerate. If $P\leq\operatorname{SU}(V)$ is a
$p$-subgroup and $PB$ is a subgroup, then $B$ is normal in $PB$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $P$ and $B$ are nilpotent, $K=PB$ is soluble by the Kegel--Wielandt theorem \cite{Kegel1961}.
Let $U=O_p(K)$ and $V^U=\{v\in V:uv=v\text{ for every }u\in U\}$.
If $U\ne1$, then $V^U\ne0$ in characteristic $p$.
As $U\lhd K$, the subspace $V^U$ is $B$-invariant and nondegenerate.
The complement $(V^U)^\perp$ is $U$-invariant.
Suppose that $(V^U)^\perp\ne0$.
We have a nonzero $v\in(V^U)^\perp$ with $uv=v$ for every $u\in U$.
Then, $v\in(V^U)^\perp\cap V^U=0$, a contradiction.
Therefore, $V^U=V$.
Because $U\leq\operatorname{SU}(V)$ acts faithfully, we have $U=1$.

Since $O_p(K)=1$, the Fitting subgroup $F(K)$ is a $p'$-group.
Since $F(K)\unlhd K$ and $B$ is a Hall $p'$-subgroup, we have $F(K)\leq B$.
As $B$ is abelian, we have $B\leq C_K(F(K))$.
Because $K$ is soluble, we obtain from \cite{Isaacs2008} that $C_K(F(K))\leq F(K)$.
Consequently, $B\leq C_K(F(K))\leq F(K)\leq B$.
Therefore, $B=F(K)$ is normal in $K$.
head: environment

label: prop:unitary-p-subgroups
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-p-subgroups}
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Suppose that $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ is nonabelian simple and $n\geq3$.
Then, no nontrivial $p$-subgroup is ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the proposition into the following steps.

The case $n=3$ follows from Theorem \ref{thm:u3}.
Suppose that $n\geq4$, and let $A$ be a nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable $p$-subgroup.
Let $\widetilde G=\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$ and $Z=Z(\widetilde G)$.
Let $\pi:\widetilde G\to G$ be the quotient map.
Since $|Z|=(n,q+1)$ is prime to $p$, we have $\pi^{-1}(A)=ZP$ for a $p$-subgroup $P\leq\widetilde G$.
The restriction $\pi|_P:P\to A$ is an isomorphism.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] If $(n,p)\ne(4,3)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
We choose a maximal torus $T\leq\widetilde G$ with odd partition $(n_1,\ldots,n_t)$.
Next, let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n=V_1\perp\cdots\perp V_t$ be the decomposition for $T$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V_i=n_i$.
If $t\geq2$, then each $V_i$ is an irreducible nondegenerate $T$-module.
Let $\pi_i:T\to\operatorname{GU}(V_i)$ satisfy $\pi_i(g)=g|_{V_i}$.
For $j\ne i$, we adjust the determinant on $V_j$ to realize every torus multiplier on $V_i$.
Therefore, $\pi_i(T)$ is cyclic of order $q^{n_i}+1$.
The summands $V_i$ are mutually nonisomorphic as $T$-modules.
When $n_i=n_j=1$, the other torus factors separate the characters on $V_i$ and $V_j$.
Since $T$ has order prime to $p$ and the summands are mutually nonisomorphic, every $T$-invariant subspace is a sum of nondegenerate summands.

Suppose that $n\geq5$ is odd.
For the partition $(n)$, we have $|T|=(q^n+1)/(q+1)$.
A constituent of smaller degree would have degree $e\mid n$, with $e\leq n/3$.
The eigenvalue order on such a constituent divides $q^{2e}-1$, whereas
$\frac{q^n+1}{q+1}>q^{2n/3}-1$.
Therefore, the torus for $(n)$ acts irreducibly.
For each torus $T$ chosen below, we use Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-nondegenerate-product}.

For a partition with $m_i$ parts of size $i$, we have
$|N_{\widetilde G}(T)/T|=\prod_i i^{m_i}m_i!$
by \cite[Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.10]{Baykalov2024}.
We choose the partition in the following table.
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|}
\hline
\text{condition}&\text{partition}\\ \hline
n\text{ odd},\ p\nmid n&(n)\\
n\text{ odd},\ p\mid n&(n-2,1,1)\\
n\text{ even},\ p\nmid n-1&(n-1,1)\\
n\text{ even},\ p\mid n-1,\ p\geq5&(n-3,3)\\
n\text{ even},\ p=3,\ 3\mid n-1,\ n\geq10&(n-5,5).\\ \hline
\end{array}
$$
We next claim that each quotient order is prime to $p$.
In the fourth row, the partition for $n=6$ is $(3,3)$.
Then, we have $p=5$ and $|N_{\widetilde G}(T)/T|=18$.
In the fifth row, we have $|N_{\widetilde G}(T)/T|=50$ for $n=10$.
All other rows have distinct larger parts, so the claim
follows immediately from the displayed formula.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $A(T/Z)^x$ is a subgroup.
We choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\widetilde G$ of $x$.
As $Z\leq T$, the inverse image of $A(T/Z)^x$ is $PT^{\widetilde x}$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-nondegenerate-product}, we have $P\leq N_{\widetilde G}(T^{\widetilde x})$.
Both $|T|$ and $|N_{\widetilde G}(T)/T|$ are prime to $p$.
Because $P\ne1$, the $2$ $p'$-orders contradict $P\leq N_{\widetilde G}(T^{\widetilde x})$.

For $(n,p)\ne(4,3)$, we have proved that $A$ cannot be nontrivial.
The remaining cases are $n=4$ with $p=3$.
Now, we take $q=3^f$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] If $(n,p)=(4,3)$, then $|P|=3$ and a generator of $P$ has Jordan type $(3,1)$.
\end{itemize}
For the partition $(3,1)$, we take a torus $T$ with $|T|=q^3+1$ and $|N_{\widetilde G}(T)/T|=3$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $x\in G$ such that $A(T/Z)^x$ is a subgroup for this torus $T$.
Choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\widetilde G$ of $x$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-nondegenerate-product}, we have $P\leq N_{\widetilde G}(T^{\widetilde x})$.
Since $3\nmid|T|$, we have $|P|=3$.
Let $V=U\perp L$ be the decomposition for $T^{\widetilde x}$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}U=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}L=1$.
Now, let $u$ generate $P$.
The element $u$ cyclically permutes the $3$ eigenlines on $U$ and fixes $L$ pointwise.
As $u^3=1$ in characteristic $3$, the Jordan type of $u$ is $(3,1)$.

We choose now a cyclic torus $S$ of type $(4)$ and order
$(q-1)(q^2+1)$ in $\widetilde G$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ such that $A(S/Z)^y$ is a subgroup.
We choose a lift $\widetilde y\in\widetilde G$ of $y$.
The inverse image of $A(S/Z)^y$ is $K=PS^{\widetilde y}$.
As $|P|=3$ and $3\nmid|S|$, all Sylow subgroups of $K$ are cyclic.
By \cite[Section 2.1]{DietrichLow2020}, we have a cyclic derived subgroup $D=K'$ and a cyclic quotient $K/D$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $(n,p)=(4,3)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Firstly, suppose that $3\mid|D|$. Since $D$ is cyclic and normal in $K$, its unique subgroup of order $3$ is normal in $K$.
This subgroup equals $P$, so $P\unlhd K$.
Let $b=(q^2+1)/2$.
Because $q$ is odd, the integer $b$ is odd and greater than $1$.
Let $B_b\leq S^{\widetilde y}$ have order $b$.
As $|\operatorname{Aut}(P)|=2$ and $|B_b|$ is odd, we have $B_b\leq C_{\widetilde G}(u)$.

Every semisimple unitary element $h$ centralizing a unipotent
element of Jordan type $(3,1)$ has order dividing $q+1$.
To prove this, we decompose the module into the eigenspaces of $h$
over the algebraic closure. The unique Jordan block of size $3$
lies in an eigenspace of dimension at least $3$.
Since $h$ is unitary, the eigenvalues $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{-q}$ have equal multiplicities.
As the eigenspace containing the Jordan block of size $3$ has dimension at least $3$, we have $\lambda^{-q}=\lambda$.
Hence, $\lambda^{q+1}=1$.
Any other eigenspace has dimension $1$.
Its eigenvalue $\nu$ satisfies $\nu^{-q}=\nu$, so $\nu^{q+1}=1$.
Thus, $h^{q+1}=1$.
A generator of $B_b$ is semisimple and centralizes $u$.
Therefore, its order $b>1$ would divide $q+1$, contrary to $(b,q+1)=1$.

Suppose that $3\nmid|D|$. Since $D$ is normal and
$S^{\widetilde y}$ is a Hall $3'$-subgroup, we have
$D\leq S^{\widetilde y}$. We claim that every element of order
$3$ normalizing a cyclic subgroup $C\leq S^{\widetilde y}$ centralizes $C$.

For a generator $c$ of $C$, the eigenvalues are $\lambda,\lambda^{-q},\lambda^{q^2},\lambda^{-q^3}$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^4}^*$.
Under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-q}$, the orbit length belongs to $\{1,2,4\}$.
For lengths $1,2$, an element of order $3$ fixes each eigenspace and centralizes $c$.
For length $4$, let $\overline F$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
On $\overline V=\overline F\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$, let $\sigma(a\otimes v)=a^{q^2}\otimes v$.
The map $\sigma$ permutes the $4$ eigenlines of $c$ in $2$ transpositions.
Moreover, every $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear matrix normalizing $C$ commutes with $\sigma$ on $\overline V$.
Since the centralizer of this permutation in $S_4$ has order $8$, an element of order $3$ fixes all $4$ eigenlines.
Therefore, the element centralizes $c$.

Consequently, $P$ centralizes $D$. The abelian group
$S^{\widetilde y}$ also centralizes $D$, so $D\leq Z(K)$.
Since $K/D$ is cyclic and $D\leq Z(K)$, the group $K$ is abelian.
Since $K$ is abelian, $P$ centralizes $S^{\widetilde y}$.
A generator of $S$ has $4$ distinct eigenvalues, so $C_{\widetilde G}(S)=S$.
Hence, $P\leq S^{\widetilde y}$, a $3'$-group.
As $P\ne1$, we have a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:odd-power-two-modules
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:odd-power-two-modules}
Let $H$ be a group of odd order, and let $E$ be a finite field.
Let $V$ be an irreducible $EH$-module with $\dim_E V=2^a$ for some integer $a\geq0$.
Let $\rho:H\to\operatorname{GL}_E(V)$ be the representation.
Then, $\rho(H)$ is abelian.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The group $H$ is soluble by the Feit--Thompson theorem
\cite{FeitThompson1963}. Let $p$ be the characteristic of $E$.
By the Fong--Swan theorem \cite{Fong1961,Isaacs2006}, every irreducible Brauer character
of $H$ lifts to an ordinary irreducible character.
Every lifted character has odd degree.

Let $\overline E$ be an algebraic closure of $E$, and let $\overline V=\overline E\otimes_E V$.
For $h\in H$, the action on $\overline V$ is $h(a\otimes v)=a\otimes\rho(h)v$.
The absolutely irreducible constituents of $\overline V$ form a Galois orbit.
Each constituent has multiplicity $1$, and their common degree divides $\dim_E V$.
Since the common degree is odd and divides $2^a$, every constituent has degree $1$.
Thus, $\rho(H)$ is abelian.
head: environment

label: prop:unitary-power-two-odd
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-power-two-odd}
Let $n=2^k$ with $k\geq2$, and let $q$ be a prime power.
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$.
Then, no nontrivial subgroup of odd order is ordinary $G$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Suppose that $A$ is an ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup of odd order.
Let $\widetilde G=\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$ and let $\pi:\widetilde G\to G$ be the quotient map.
Since $n$ is a power of $2$, the central kernel $Z(\widetilde G)$ is a $2$-group.
Let $J\leq G$ have odd order.
By Schur--Zassenhaus, we choose a complement $\widehat J$ to $Z(\widetilde G)$ in $\pi^{-1}(J)$.
Any $2$ complements are conjugate by an element of $Z(\widetilde G)$.
Since $Z(\widetilde G)$ is central, $\widehat J$ is unique.
The restriction $\pi|_{\widehat J}:\widehat J\to J$ is an isomorphism.
For $B\leq G$ of odd order, every subgroup $AB^x$ with $x\in G$ also has odd order.
We identify each subgroup of odd order with its unique lift $\widehat J$.
If $AB^x$ is a subgroup, then its unique lift contains the lifts of $A$ and $B^x$.
By the product order formula, the product of those lifts equals the unique lift of $AB^x$.
For $x,y\in G$, we choose $\widetilde x,\widetilde y\in\widetilde G$ with $\pi(\widetilde x)=x$ and $\pi(\widetilde y)=y$.
For the subgroups $S,B\leq\widetilde G$ used below, we use $S^x=\widetilde x^{-1}S\widetilde x$ and $B^y=\widetilde y^{-1}B\widetilde y$.
As $\ker\pi=Z(\widetilde G)$, the choices of $\widetilde x,\widetilde y$ do not affect $S^x,B^y$.

Let $d=n/2$.
Next, we take a cyclic torus $T$ of type $(n)$ with $|T|=M=(q^n-1)/(q+1)$.
Let $S$ be the Hall subgroup of $T$ of odd order.
Let $a=|S|$.
Then, $(q^d+1)_{2'}>1$ and $(q^d+1)_{2'}\mid a$.
The notation $m_{2'}$ denotes the largest odd divisor of $m$.
Since $d$ is a power of $2$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_{(q^d+1)_{2'}}(q^2)=d$.
We also have $\operatorname{ord}_{(q^d+1)_{2'}}(-q)=n$.
Next, we choose a generator $s\in S$.
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^{\,*}$ be an eigenvalue of $s$ with $|\lambda|=a$.
Let $\mathcal O_0=\{\lambda^{q^{2j}}:0\leq j<d\}$ and $\mathcal O_1=\{\alpha^{-q}:\alpha\in\mathcal O_0\}$.
As $(q^d+1)_{2'}\mid a$ and $a\mid M$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_a(q^2)=d$ and $\operatorname{ord}_a(-q)=n$.
Hence, the sets $\mathcal O_0,\mathcal O_1$ are disjoint orbits under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{q^2}$.
In particular, $|\mathcal O_0|=|\mathcal O_1|=d$.
Thus, $S$ has $2$ nonisomorphic irreducible $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-modules of dimension $d$.
As unitary duality $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-q}$ sends $\mathcal O_i$ to $\mathcal O_{1-i}$ for $i=0,1$, both modules are totally isotropic.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K_1=AS^x$ for some $x\in G$.
We use $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n$ with the natural Hermitian form $h:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Suppose that $V$ is irreducible under $K_1$.
We obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:odd-power-two-modules} that $K_1$ is abelian.
Then, every element of $K_1$ would centralize $S^x$ and stabilize both irreducible $S^x$-submodules of $V$.
This contradicts irreducibility.
Hence, we choose a nonzero proper $K_1$-invariant subspace $W$.
As $S^x\leq K_1$, the space $W$ is one of the $2$ irreducible $S^x$-submodules.
Thus, $W$ is totally isotropic and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}W=d$.
Let $\rho_W:K_1\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ satisfy $\rho_W(k)=k|_W$.
Because $\rho_W(S^x)$ is irreducible, $\rho_W(K_1)$ is irreducible.
By Lemma \ref{lem:odd-power-two-modules}, we obtain that $\rho_W(K_1)$ is abelian.
Hence, $\rho_W(K_1)$ centralizes $\rho_W(S^x)$, whose commuting algebra is $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$.
We identify $W$ with the $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-vector space $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$.
Thus, every $g\in\rho_W(K_1)$ acts by $v\mapsto\lambda v$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^{\,*}$.
For $k\in K_1$, let $g=\rho_W(k)$.
As $h(kv,kw)=h(v,w)$ for $v,w\in V$, the diagonal blocks of $k$ are $g$ and $(g^{-1})^{q\mathsf T}$ in dual bases.
Because the $2$ diagonal blocks have combined determinant $1$, we have $(\det g)^{q-1}=1$.
We also have $\det g=\lambda^{(q^n-1)/(q^2-1)}$.
Substituting the displayed determinant in $(\det g)^{q-1}=1$, we obtain $\lambda^M=1$.
Next, in the dual bases above, every element of $\ker\rho_W$ has matrix $u_C=\begin{pmatrix}I_d&C\\0&I_d\end{pmatrix}$.
We have $C\in M_d(\mathbb{F}_{q^2})$ and $C+C^{q\mathsf T}=0$.
As $u_Cu_D=u_{C+D}$, the group $\ker\rho_W$ is a $p$-group.

Let $c\ne1$ be a $p'$-element of $A$.
Since $\ker\rho_W$ is a $p$-group, the restriction $\rho_W(c)=c|_W$ has order $|c|$.
The eigenvalues of $c$ are
$\lambda,\lambda^{-q},\ldots,\lambda^{(-q)^{n-1}}$,
where $\lambda$ has order $|c|$.
Since $|\lambda|=|c|>1$ and $c$ is a $p'$-element, no eigenvalue equals $1$.
Moreover, $\lambda^M=1$ and $|c|$ is odd, so $|c|\mid M_{2'}$.
As $M\equiv-n\pmod{q+1}$ and $n$ is a power of $2$, we have $(M_{2'},q+1)=1$.

Let $r=n-1$.
Next, we choose the Hall subgroup $B$ of odd order in a torus of type $(r,1)$.
Let $V=U\perp L$ be the torus decomposition with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}U=r$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}L=1$.
The order $b=|B|=(q^r+1)_{2'}$ satisfies $b\geq(q^r+1)/(q+1)$.
For $r\geq7$, the right side exceeds $q^{2r/3}-1$.
Since the eigenvalue degree divides $r$, any proper degree is at most $r/3$.
Hence, $B$ acts irreducibly on $U$ for $r\geq7$.
For $r=3$, we have $b>q+1$ and $(q^3+1,q^2-1)=q+1$.
Hence, $B$ also acts irreducibly on $U$ for $r=3$.
The $B$-modules $U$ and $L$ are nondegenerate and nonisomorphic.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K_2=AB^y$ for some $y\in G$.
Let $U_y=\widetilde y^{-1}U$ and $L_y=\widetilde y^{-1}L$.
Since $B^y\leq K_2$, every $K_2$-invariant subspace is $B^y$-invariant and nondegenerate.
Let $X\leq V$ be any $K_2$-invariant subspace.
As $K_2\leq\operatorname{SU}(V)$, we have $gX^\perp=X^\perp$ for every $g\in K_2$.
Hence, $V$ is completely reducible under $K_2$, even when $p\mid|A|$.
Suppose that $V$ is irreducible under $K_2$.
We obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:odd-power-two-modules} that $K_2$ is abelian.
Then, every element of $K_2$ would centralize $B^y$ and stabilize its unique line $L_y$.
This contradicts irreducibility.
Therefore, $V$ is reducible under $K_2$.
The only nonzero proper $B^y$-submodules are $U_y$ and $L_y$.
We choose a nonzero proper $K_2$-invariant subspace.
Because $U_y^\perp=L_y$, we have $gL_y=L_y$ for every $g\in K_2$.

Let $c\in A$ be a $p'$-element.
The order of the scalar $c|_{L_y}$ divides $q+1$.
From $|c|\mid M_{2'}$ and $(M_{2'},q+1)=1$, we obtain $(|c|,q+1)=1$.
Therefore, $c|_{L_y}=I$.
As every nontrivial $p'$-element of $A$ has no eigenvalue $1$, we conclude that $c=1$.
By Cauchy's theorem, $A$ is a $p$-group.
By Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-p-subgroups}, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: prop:unitary-power-two-cyclic-sylow
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-power-two-cyclic-sylow}
Let $n=2^k$ with $k\geq2$, and let $q$ be a power of $2$.
If $A\leq G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ is nontrivial and ordinary
$G$-permutable, then its Sylow $2$-subgroups are noncyclic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $(n,q+1)=1$, we have $G=\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-power-two-odd}, $A$ has
even order. Suppose that the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $A$ are cyclic.
Let $T$ be a cyclic torus of type $(n)$, with odd order $(q^n-1)/(q+1)$.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K_1=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
Because $|T|$ is odd, the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $K_1$ are cyclic.

For a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup $P$ of $K_1$, the quotient
$N_{K_1}(P)/C_{K_1}(P)$ has both odd order and $2$-power order.
Thus, $P\leq Z(N_{K_1}(P))$.
By Burnside's theorem on normal complements \cite{Isaacs2008}, we have a normal Hall subgroup $H\unlhd K_1$ of odd order.
Then, $T^x\leq H$.

The $2$ irreducible $T^x$-submodules have dimension $n/2$.
Hence, every composition factor of the natural $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}K_1$-module has dimension $n/2$ or $n$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n$ and $V_{\mathrm{alg}}=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$.
For $g\in K_1$, the action on $V_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is $g(a\otimes v)=a\otimes gv$.
Let $X$ be an irreducible constituent of the $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}K_1$-module $V_{\mathrm{alg}}$.
By the preceding $T^x$-module decomposition, the irreducible constituents over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ have dimensions $n/2$ or $n$.
Their absolutely irreducible constituents have degrees dividing those dimensions.
Hence, $\dim X$ is a power of $2$.
By Clifford's theorem \cite{Isaacs2006}, every irreducible constituent of $X\!\downarrow_H$
has degree dividing $\dim X$.
The notation $X\!\downarrow_H$ denotes the restriction of the $K_1$-representation on $X$ to $H$.
Since $H$ has odd order and the characteristic is $2$, every constituent degree is odd.
The degree also divides a power of $2$.
Hence, every constituent has degree $1$.
Since $|H|$ is odd and the characteristic is $2$, the natural $H$-module is completely reducible.
Its constituents all have degree $1$, so the faithful image of $H$ is abelian.
Consequently,
$T^x\leq H\leq C_G(T^x)=T^x$.
Therefore, $H=T^x\unlhd K_1$.
Hence, $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.

The torus normalizer quotients are
$N_G(T)/T\cong C_n, N_G(R)/R\cong C_{n-1}$,
where $R$ is a cyclic torus of type $(n-1,1)$
\cite[Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.10]{Baykalov2024}.
An involution $t\in A$ has image of order $2$ in $N_G(T^x)/T^x\cong C_n$.
Hence, $t$ permutes the $n$ eigenlines in $n/2$ transpositions.
Since $t^2=1$ in characteristic $2$, the Jordan type of $t$ is $(2^{n/2})$.
Therefore,
$\operatorname{Fix}(t)=\operatorname{im}(t-1)$.
Let $h:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ be the Hermitian form.
As $t^2=I$, we have $(t-I)^2=0$ in characteristic $2$.
Because $h(tv,tw)=h(v,w)$ and $t^{-1}=t$, we obtain $h((t-I)v,w)=h(v,(t-I)w)$.
Thus, $h((t-I)v,(t-I)w)=h(v,(t-I)^2w)=0$ for $v,w\in V$.
Therefore, $\operatorname{im}(t-I)$ is totally isotropic.
In particular, $t$ fixes no nondegenerate line pointwise.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we also have a subgroup $K_2=AR^y$ for some $y\in G$.
The torus $R^y$ has irreducible nondegenerate summands
of dimensions $n-1$ and $1$.
Every $R^y$-invariant subspace is nondegenerate, so the natural $K_2$-module is completely reducible.
Let $L_y$ be the nondegenerate summand of dimension $1$ in the $R^y$-module $V$.
If $V$ is reducible under $K_2$, then we have $gL_y=L_y$ for every $g\in K_2$.
As $q+1$ is odd, the scalar action of $t$ on $L_y$ is trivial.
This contradicts $\operatorname{Fix}(t)$ being totally isotropic.

Suppose that the natural $K_2$-module $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n$ is irreducible.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V=n=2^k$.
Since the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $K_2$ are cyclic, we have a normal Hall subgroup $H_2$ of odd order by Burnside's theorem.
We use $V_{\mathrm{alg}}=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$ with $g(a\otimes v)=a\otimes gv$ for $g\in K_2$.
The absolutely irreducible constituents of $V_{\mathrm{alg}}$ have degrees dividing the power of $2$ given by $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$.
By Clifford's theorem and the odd order of $H_2$, every irreducible constituent of $V_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\downarrow_{H_2}$ has degree $1$.
As $|H_2|$ is odd, the faithful $H_2$-module is completely reducible.
Hence, $H_2$ is abelian.
Because $R^y\leq H_2$ and $C_G(R^y)=R^y$, we have $H_2=R^y$.
Therefore, $K_2\leq N_G(R^y)$.
But $|R|=q^{n-1}+1$ and $|N_G(R)/R|=n-1$ are odd.
This contradicts the even order of $A$.
head: environment

label: thm:unitary-four-even
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The case $q=2$ follows from Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Suppose that $q\geq4$ and that $A<G$ is ordinary
$G$-permutable. Since $(4,q+1)=1$, we have $G=\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$.

Let $M$ stabilize a decomposition into $4$ orthogonal
nondegenerate lines. Then,
$M\cong C_{q+1}^3\rtimes S_4$ and $|M|=24(q+1)^3$.
The soluble subgroup $M$ is maximal \cite[Table 8.10]{BHR}.
Suppose that $G=MY$ with $Y<G$.
By \cite[Proposition 4.1]{LiXia}, $Y$ is not soluble for $G=\operatorname{PSU}_4(q)$ with $q\geq4$.
By \cite[Theorem 1.1 and Tables 1.1--1.2]{LiXia}, a generic soluble factor $X<G$ in $G=XY$ has order dividing $2q^4(q-1)(q^2+1)$.
The odd part of this bound is coprime to $q+1$.
The exceptional soluble factor $X<G$ for $q=8$ has odd order, whereas $M$ has even order.
Therefore, $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $AM^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$, we have $AM^x<G$.
Because $M^x$ is maximal, we have $AM^x=M^x$ and $A\leq M^x$.

We take a cyclic torus $R$ of type $(3,1)$ with $|R|=q^3+1$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $AR^y$ for some $y\in G$.
We have $|A||R|\leq24(q+1)^3(q^3+1)<|G|=q^6(q^4-1)(q^3+1)(q^2-1)$.
Therefore, $AR^y<G$.
We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $2^{6f}-1$.
As $f\geq2$, the prime $\ell$ exists by Zsigmondy's theorem.
Then, $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(2)=6f$ and $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=6$.
Consequently, $R$ contains an element of order $\ell$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012}, every maximal
subgroup containing this element stabilizes a nondegenerate
line. None of the exceptional pairs in the lemma has even $q\geq4$.
Therefore, $AR^y$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line $L$.
Because $A\leq AR^y$, we have $aL=L$ for every $a\in A$.

Let $P$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$.
Next, let $V=L_1\perp\cdots\perp L_4$ be the line decomposition stabilized by $M^x$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}L_i=1$ for $1\leq i\leq4$.
Let $\theta:M^x\to S_4$ satisfy $gL_i=L_{\theta(g)(i)}$.
Since $\ker\theta$ is the diagonal subgroup of odd order, $\theta|_P:P\to S_4$ is injective.
Every $2$-subgroup of $S_4$ of order at least $4$ contains a double transposition.
If a $2$-subgroup $Q\leq S_4$ contains a $4$-cycle $c$, then $c^2$ is a double transposition.
Otherwise, all nonidentity elements of $Q$ are involutions, so $Q$ is elementary abelian.
Suppose that none is a double transposition.
$2$ distinct commuting transpositions have disjoint supports.
Their product is a double transposition, a contradiction.

Suppose that $|P|\geq4$.
We choose $t\in P$ such that $\theta(t)$ is a double transposition.
Since $\theta|_P$ is injective, we have $t^2=I$ and $t\ne I$.
We number the lines so that $tL_1=L_2$ and $tL_3=L_4$.
As $t^2=I$, we have $tL_2=L_1$ and $tL_4=L_3$.
Hence, the Jordan type of $t$ in characteristic $2$ is $(2,2)$.
Therefore, $\operatorname{Fix}(t)=\operatorname{im}(t-I)$.
Let $h:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ be the Hermitian form on $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^4$.
Because $t^2=I$ and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_{q^2}=2$, we have $(t-I)^2=0$.
As $h(tv,tw)=h(v,w)$ and $t^{-1}=t$, we obtain $h((t-I)v,w)=h(v,(t-I)w)$ for $v,w\in V$.
Thus, $h((t-I)v,(t-I)w)=h(v,(t-I)^2w)=0$ for $v,w\in V$.
Because $\operatorname{Fix}(t)=\operatorname{im}(t-I)$, the subspace $\operatorname{Fix}(t)$ is totally isotropic.
But $t$ stabilizes the nondegenerate line $L$.
The scalar $t|_L$ has order dividing the odd number $q+1$.
Hence, $t|_L=I$.
This places the nondegenerate line $L$ in the totally isotropic space $\operatorname{Fix}(t)$, a contradiction.

Since $|P|\leq2$, we conclude that $A=1$ by Propositions \ref{prop:unitary-power-two-odd} and \ref{prop:unitary-power-two-cyclic-sylow}.

label: thm:unitary-four
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For even $q$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-four-even}.
For $q=3$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Let $q=p^f\geq5$ be odd, and let $d=(4,q+1)$.
Suppose that $A<G$ is nontrivial and ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-power-two-odd}, $|A|$ is even.

Let $M$ be the monomial maximal subgroup.
The group $M$ is soluble and has order $24(q+1)^3/d$
\cite[Table 8.10]{BHR}.
Suppose that $G=MY$ with $Y<G$.
By \cite[Proposition 4.1]{LiXia}, $Y$ is not soluble.
By \cite[Theorem 1.1 and Tables 1.1--1.2]{LiXia}, the generic soluble factor $M$ would have order dividing
$\frac{2q^4(q-1)(q^2+1)}{d}$.
If $q+1$ has an odd prime divisor $r$, then $r\mid|M|$ but $r\nmid2q^4(q-1)(q^2+1)/d$.
If $q+1$ is a power of $2$, then we have $(2q^4(q-1)(q^2+1)/d)_2=2$.
But $|M|_2>2$.
For odd $q\geq5$, the cited list has no exceptional equality $G=XY$ with $X,Y<G$ and $X$ soluble.
Therefore, $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq M^x$ for some $x\in G$.
In particular, $A$ is soluble.

We take a cyclic torus $R$ of type $(3,1)$ with $|R|=(q^3+1)/d$.
Let $B$ be the Hall subgroup of $R$ of odd order.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K_2=AB^y$ for some $y\in G$.
As $|A||B|\leq\frac{24(q+1)^3(q^3+1)}{d^2}<|G|$, we have $K_2<G$.
A primitive prime divisor of $p^{6f}-1$ belongs to $B$.
Because $K_2<G$, we choose a maximal subgroup $H<G$ with $K_2\leq H$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012}, we have $2$ possibilities for $H$.
Either $H$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line $L\leq V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^4$, or $q=5$ and $H\cong A_7$.
The group $A_7$ has no element of order $9$.
As $B^y$ is cyclic of order $63$ for $q=5$, we cannot have both $q=5$ and $H\cong A_7$.
Thus, $K_2\leq H\leq N_1=\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$.

Let $\rho_L:\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ be the quotient map.
For $\overline g\in\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$, choose a lift $g\in\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$.
Let $\pi_L:\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ satisfy $\pi_L(\overline g)=\rho_L(g|_{L^\perp})$.
Since $2$ lifts differ by $\lambda I$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ and $\lambda^{q+1}=1$, the value of $\pi_L(\overline g)$ is independent of the lift.
The kernel is $\ker\pi_L=\{\overline g:g|_{L^\perp}=\lambda I_{L^\perp}\text{ for some }\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*\}$.
Let $J=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(K_2))\leq\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\cong\operatorname{GU}_3(q)$.
From the kernel formula and the torus decomposition, we obtain $|\ker\pi_L|=(q+1)/d$ and $\ker\pi_L\leq R^y$.
Moreover, $\pi_L(B^y)$ is a Singer torus of $\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ with order $q^2-q+1$.
Since $B^y\leq K_2$, the group $J$ contains $F=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(B^y))$.
By the preceding Singer torus calculation, $F$ is cyclic of order $q^3+1$.
Since both quotient kernels and $B^y$ have order prime to $p$, we have $|J|_p=|A|_p\leq3_p<q^3$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-singer-small-p-part}, we have $J\leq N_{\operatorname{GU}_3(q)}(F)$.
Since $\pi_L(B^y)\leq\pi_L(R^y)$ and both groups have order $q^2-q+1$, we have $\pi_L(B^y)=\pi_L(R^y)$.
Because $J$ normalizes $F$, $\pi_L(K_2)$ normalizes $\rho_L(F)=\pi_L(R^y)$.
As $\ker\pi_L\leq R^y$, we have $\pi_L^{-1}(\pi_L(R^y))=R^y$.
Therefore, $A\leq K_2\leq N_G(R^y)$.
By \cite[Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.10]{Baykalov2024}, we have $[N_G(R):R]=3$.
As $R^y$ is cyclic of odd index in $N_G(R^y)$, every Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$ lies in $R^y$ and is cyclic.
We have $v_2(|R|)=\max\{v_2(q+1)-2,0\}$.
Because $|A|$ is even, we conclude that $q\equiv7\pmod8$.
Since no power of $3$ is $7$ modulo $8$, we have $p\ne3$.
In particular, $p\nmid|M|$.

We take a torus $T$ of type $(4)$ in $G$.
Let $S$ be the Hall subgroup of $T$ of odd order.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K_1=AS^z$ for some $z\in G$.
As the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $K_1$ are cyclic, we have a normal Hall subgroup $H$ of odd order by Burnside's theorem.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{SU}_4(q)\to G$ be the quotient map.
We take the unique lift $\widetilde H\leq\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$ of odd order.
Since $H\unlhd K_1$ and its lift of odd order is unique, $\widetilde H$ is normal in the inverse image $\widetilde K_1$ of $K_1$.
The groups $K_1,H,\widetilde K_1,\widetilde H$ have order coprime to $p$.

Let $\widetilde S\leq\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$ be the unique lift of $S$ of odd order.
Next, choose $\widetilde z\in\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$ with $\pi(\widetilde z)=z$.
We use $\widetilde S^z=\widetilde z^{-1}\widetilde S\widetilde z$.
Since $\ker\pi=Z(\operatorname{SU}_4(q))$, the choice of $\widetilde z$ does not affect $\widetilde S^z$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^4=U_1\oplus U_2$ be the decomposition into the $2$ nonisomorphic irreducible $\widetilde S^z$-modules.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}U_i=2$ for $i=1,2$.
Hence, every irreducible $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}\widetilde K_1$-constituent
has dimension $2$ or $4$.
Let $V_{\mathrm{alg}}=\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$.
For $g\in\widetilde K_1$, the action on $V_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is $g(a\otimes v)=a\otimes gv$.
Let $X$ be an irreducible constituent of the $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}\widetilde K_1$-module $V_{\mathrm{alg}}$.
By scalar extension over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, the degree $\dim X$ divides $2$ or $4$.
By Clifford's theorem, we obtain that each irreducible constituent of $X\!\downarrow_{\widetilde H}$ has degree dividing $\dim X$.
The notation $X\!\downarrow_{\widetilde H}$ denotes the restriction of the $\widetilde K_1$-representation on $X$ to $\widetilde H$.
As $\widetilde H$ has odd order, the constituent degrees are odd and hence equal $1$.
Because $p\nmid|\widetilde H|$, the faithful $\widetilde H$-module is completely reducible.
Hence, $\widetilde H$ is abelian.
As $\widetilde S^z\leq\widetilde H$, we have $\widetilde H\leq C_{\operatorname{SU}_4(q)}(\widetilde S^z)$.
The centralizer is the inverse image of $T^z$, of order $(q-1)(q^2+1)$.
Its Hall subgroup of odd order is $\widetilde S^z$.
Hence, $\widetilde H=\widetilde S^z$ and $A\leq N_G(T^z)$.

We claim that $A\cap T^z=1$.
To prove this, let $a\in A\cap T^z$, and choose a lift $\widetilde a\in\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$ with multiplier $\lambda$.
The eigenvalues of $\widetilde a$ are $\lambda^{(-q)^j}$, $0\leq j\leq3$.
Since $aL=L$ and $L$ is nondegenerate, an eigenvalue of $\widetilde a$ has order dividing $q+1$.
Thus, the order of $\lambda$ divides $((q-1)(q^2+1),q+1)=d$.
Hence, $\widetilde a$ is scalar, proving $A\cap T^z=1$.
Let $\nu_z:N_G(T^z)\to N_G(T^z)/T^z\cong C_4$ be the quotient map.
As $\ker(\nu_z|_A)=A\cap T^z=1$, the homomorphism $\nu_z|_A$ is injective.

We take an involution $t\in A$.
Then, we choose a lift $\widetilde t\in\operatorname{SU}_4(q)$ of $t$.
Let $E_1,\ldots,E_4$ be the eigenlines of the inverse image of $T^z$ on $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{q^2}^{\,4}$.
The image of $t$ in $N_G(T^z)/T^z\cong C_4$ has order $2$.
Hence, we number the lines so that $\widetilde tE_1=E_2$ and $\widetilde tE_3=E_4$.
Since $\widetilde t^{\,2}$ is scalar, we have $\widetilde tE_2=E_1$ and $\widetilde tE_4=E_3$.
Let $\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ satisfy $\widetilde t^2=\zeta I$.
On each of $E_1\oplus E_2$ and $E_3\oplus E_4$, the characteristic polynomial of $\widetilde t$ is $X^2-\zeta$.
As $q$ is odd, the eigenvalue multiplicities of $\widetilde t$ are $(2,2)$.
Because $t$ lies in the cyclic $2$-part of $R^y$, we choose a $2$-element $r_t\in\pi^{-1}(R^y)$ with $\pi(r_t)=t$.
The eigenvalues of $r_t$ are $\mu,\mu,\mu,\mu^{-3}$ with $\mu^{q+1}=1$.
As $t\ne1$ projectively, $r_t$ has eigenvalue multiplicities $(3,1)$.
Because $r_t$ and $\widetilde t$ lift $t$, we have $r_t=\eta\widetilde t$ for some $\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ with $\eta^4=\eta^{q+1}=1$.
Scalar multiplication does not change eigenvalue multiplicities.
The multiplicities $(2,2)$ and $(3,1)$ are incompatible, so we have a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:unitary-order-bound
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $q=2$, let $R_n=2^{n(n-1)/2}/(n!3^{n-1})$.
Then, we have $R_8>1$ and $R_{n+1}/R_n=2^n/(3(n+1))>1$ for $n\geq8$.
For fixed $n$, the function $q^{n/2}/(q+1)$ is increasing.
Since this function is increasing, the inequality for $q=2$ implies the inequality for every $q\geq2$.
head: environment

label: lem:unitary-singer-small-p-part
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-singer-small-p-part}
\label{lem:special-unitary-singer-small-p-part}
Let $m\geq3$ be odd and let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Let $X=\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$ or $\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$.
Let $J\leq X$ and let $F\leq J$ be a Singer subgroup.
Suppose that $|F|=q^m+1$ for $X=\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$ and $|F|=(q^m+1)/(q+1)$ for $X=\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$.
Suppose that $(m,q)\notin\{(3,2),(3,3),(5,2)\}$.
For $X=\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$, also suppose that $(m,q)\ne(3,5)$.
If $|J|_p<q^m$, then $J\leq N_X(F)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on $m$.
For $X=\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$, we have $|F|=q^m+1$.
For $X=\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$, we have $|F|=(q^m+1)/(q+1)$.
Since $|J|_p<q^m\leq|X|_p=q^{m(m-1)/2}$, we have $J<X$.
By Bereczky's theorem \cite{Bereczky}, we have $J\leq E$.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.1.7]{Brookfield2014}.
Next, let $Q=q^s$, where $s$ is an odd prime and $bs=m$.
We use $V=(\mathbb{F}_{Q^2})^b$ as an $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-vector space.
Then, $E=(\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)\rtimes\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}/\mathbb{F}_{q^2}))\cap X$.

We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{2m}-1$.
By Zsigmondy's theorem, we have $\ell>2m$.
Let $F_\ell$ be the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $F$.
Since $\ell>s$, we have $F_\ell\leq E\cap\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$.
Let $E_F=C_{\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}(V)}(F_\ell)$.
Since $F_\ell$ acts irreducibly on $V$, we have $E_F\cong\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$.
Both $F$ and the scalar maps from $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ lie in $E_F$.
As $E_F$ is commutative, we have $F\leq E\cap\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$.
If $b=1$, then $E=N_X(F)$.

Suppose that $b\geq3$.
Let $Y=\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ when $X=\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$.
Let $Y=\operatorname{SU}_b(Q)$ when $X=\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$.
Then, $J_0=J\cap Y\unlhd J$ and $F_0=F\cap Y\leq J_0$.
For $X=\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$, we have $|F_0|=q^m+1$.
For $X=\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$, we have $|F_0|=(q^m+1)/(Q+1)$.
Hence, $F_0$ is a Singer subgroup of $Y$.
Also, $\ell\nmid Q+1$, so $F_\ell\leq F_0$.
Moreover, $|J_0|_p<q^m=Q^b$.
Since $Q\geq8$, the pair $(b,Q)$ satisfies the lemma's hypotheses.
By induction, we have $J_0\leq N_Y(F_0)$.
The quotient $N_Y(F_0)/F_0$ has order $b<\ell$.
Hence, $F_\ell$ is the unique Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $J_0$.
Thus, $F_\ell$ is characteristic in $J_0$ and normal in $J$.
Since $F_\ell\unlhd J$, the group $J$ normalizes $C_X(F_\ell)=F$.
Hence, $J\leq N_X(F)$.
head: environment

label: thm:unitary-odd-dimension
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-odd-dimension}
Let $n\geq3$ be odd and let $q$ be a prime power.
Suppose that $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ is simple.
Then, $G$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For prime $n$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-prime}.
Suppose that $n\geq9$ is composite and that $A<G$
is nontrivial and ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime, and let $d=(n,q+1)$.

The monomial subgroup $M$ of type $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)\wr S_n$
is maximal \cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
By \cite[Theorem C]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.3]{LiXia}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq M^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Hence, $|A|_p\leq(n!)_p<q^n$.
The strict inequality follows from $v_p(n!)<n/(p-1)\leq n$.

Let $T$ be the projective Singer subgroup of order
$(q^n+1)/((q+1)d)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-order-bound}, we have $|A||T|<|G|$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a proper subgroup $K=AT^x$ for some $x\in G$.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{SU}_n(q)\to G$ be the quotient map and let $\widetilde K=\pi^{-1}(K)$.
Then, $\widetilde K$ contains a Singer subgroup of order $(q^n+1)/(q+1)$ and satisfies $|\widetilde K|_p=|A|_p$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:special-unitary-singer-small-p-part}, we have $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.

Let $N_1<G$ be the stabilizer of a nondegenerate line.
For odd $n\geq9$, the subgroup $N_1$ is maximal and $N_1Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$
\cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.3]{LiXia}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, $A$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line.
An element of the Singer torus stabilizing such a line
has multiplier $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ with $\lambda^{q+1}=1$.
The determinant of the corresponding lift is $\lambda^n$, so the lift is central in $\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
Thus, $A\cap T^x=1$.
Let $\nu_x:N_G(T^x)\to N_G(T^x)/T^x\cong C_n$ be the quotient map.
Since $\ker(\nu_x|_A)=A\cap T^x=1$, the restriction $\nu_x|_A$ is injective.
Therefore, $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid n$.

We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{2(n-2)}-1$.
Then, $\ell>2(n-2)>n$.
We choose a nondegenerate $U\leq V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}U=n-2$.
Then, we take $\widetilde B\leq\operatorname{GU}_n(q)$ of order $\ell$ acting irreducibly on $U$ and fixing $U^\perp$ pointwise.
Since $\ell\nmid q+1$, we have $\widetilde B\leq\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
Let $B\leq G$ be the projective image of $\widetilde B$.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AB^y$ for some $y\in G$.
We have $|K|=\ell|A|$.
The number of Sylow $\ell$-subgroups of $K$ divides $|A|<\ell$ and is congruent to $1$ modulo $\ell$.
Hence, $B^y\lhd K$ and $A\leq N_G(B^y)$.
The quotient $N_G(B^y)/C_G(B^y)$ has order dividing $n-2$.
Let $\eta:A\to N_G(B^y)/C_G(B^y)$ satisfy $\eta(a)=aC_G(B^y)$.
By the homomorphism $\eta$, the order $|\eta(A)|$ divides both $|A|$ and $n-2$.
Since $|A|\mid n$ and $(n,n-2)=1$, we have $\eta(A)=1$.
Therefore, $A$ centralizes $B^y$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde y\in\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$ of $y$.
As $\ell\nmid|Z(\operatorname{SU}_n(q))|$, the inverse image of $B^y$ has a unique subgroup $\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}$ of order $\ell$.
The restriction $\pi|_{\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}}:\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}\to B^y$ is an isomorphism.
Every lift of $A$ normalizes $\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}$ and fixes its projective image pointwise.
Since this restriction is injective, every lift of $A$ centralizes $\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}$.

We choose a prime $r\mid|A|$ and an element $a\in A$
of order $r$.
Since $\nu_x|_A$ is injective, the image of $a$ in $N_G(T^x)/T^x$ has order $r$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde a\in\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
Next, let $\overline F$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
The inverse image of $T^x$ has $n$ eigenlines on $\overline F\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$.
Because the image of $a$ has order $r$, the lift $\widetilde a$ permutes these eigenlines in $n/r$ cycles of length $r$.
Along each cycle, $\widetilde a$ sends a weight vector to a nonzero scalar multiple of the next vector.
Since $\widetilde a^r$ is scalar, every geometric eigenspace has dimension at most $n/r$.
The bound also holds in characteristic $r$.

Let $U_y=\widetilde y^{-1}U$.
The lift $\widetilde a$ centralizes $\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}$.
Because $\widetilde B^{\widetilde y}$ acts irreducibly on $U_y$, its commuting algebra is $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2(n-2)}}$.
Thus, $\widetilde a|_{U_y}$ is multiplication by some $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{2(n-2)}}^*$.
Since $\widetilde a^r=\zeta I$ for some $\zeta\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$, we have $\lambda^r=\zeta$.
The degree $e=[\mathbb{F}_{q^2}(\lambda):\mathbb{F}_{q^2}]$ divides $n-2$.
As the field conjugates of $\lambda$ are roots of $X^r-\zeta$, we have $e\leq r$.
Because $r\mid n$ and $r$ is odd, $r\nmid n-2$.
Hence, $e\leq r-1$.
Since $\widetilde a|_{U_y}$ is multiplication by $\lambda$ of degree $e$, some geometric eigenspace of $\widetilde a|_{U_y}$ has dimension $(n-2)/e\geq(n-2)/(r-1)$.
As $n$ is odd and composite, we have $n\geq3r$.
Therefore, $(n-2)/(r-1)>n/r$.
The geometric eigenspace dimension exceeds $n/r$, a contradiction.
We conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: thm:unitary-six
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $1<A<G$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
Firstly, assume that $q\geq3$.
Let $d=(6,q+1)$, $F=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ and $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^6}$.
Next, we use $V=E^2$ as an $F$-vector space, with $\dim_F V=6$.
On $V$, we use the Hermitian form $h_0(v,w)=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F}(v_1w_1^{q^3}+v_2w_2^{q^3})$.
With this form, let $M$ be the projective image of
$(\operatorname{GU}_2(q^3)\rtimes\operatorname{Gal}(E/F))\cap\operatorname{SU}(V,h_0)$.
The subgroup $M$ is maximal \cite[Table 8.26]{BHR}.
The order of $M$ is
$|M|=\frac{3q^3(q^3+1)(q^6-1)}{(q+1)d}$.
By \cite[Theorem C]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.3]{LiXia}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, choose $g\in G$ with $A^g\leq M$ and replace $A$ by $A^g$.

Let $R$ be a torus of type $(5,1)$, of order $(q^5+1)/d$.
Then,
$\frac{|G|}{|M||R|} =\frac{q^{12}(q^2-1)(q^4-1)(q+1)d}{3}>1$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a subgroup $K=AR^x$ for some $x\in G$.
As $|A||R|<|G|$, we have $K<G$.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
We choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $p^{10f}-1$.
Since $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=10$ and $\ell\nmid d$, the torus $R^x\leq K$ contains an element of order $\ell$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012}, $K$ stabilizes
a nondegenerate line $L$.

Let $\rho_L:\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ be the quotient map.
For $\overline g\in\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$, choose a lift $g\in\operatorname{SU}_6(q)$.
Let $\pi_L:\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ satisfy $\pi_L(\overline g)=\rho_L(g|_{L^\perp})$.
Since $2$ lifts differ by $\lambda I$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ and $\lambda^{q+1}=1$, the value of $\pi_L(\overline g)$ is independent of the lift.
The kernel is $\ker\pi_L=\{\overline g:g|_{L^\perp}=\lambda I_{L^\perp}\text{ for some }\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*\}$.
Let $J=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(K))\leq\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\cong\operatorname{GU}_5(q)$.
Since $R^x\leq K$, the group $J$ contains $T_J=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(R^x))$.
This is a Singer subgroup of order $q^5+1$.
The kernel $\ker\pi_L$ has order $(q+1)/d$ and lies in $R^x$.
Consequently,
$|J|_p=|A|_p\leq3_pq^3<q^5$.
As $q>2$, we have $J\leq N_{\operatorname{GU}_5(q)}(T_J)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-singer-small-p-part}.
Since $J$ normalizes $T_J$, $\pi_L(K)$ normalizes $\rho_L(T_J)=\pi_L(R^x)$.
As $\ker\pi_L\leq R^x$, we have $\pi_L^{-1}(\pi_L(R^x))=R^x$.
Therefore, $A\leq N_G(R^x)$.
For $\overline g\in A$, choose a lift $g\in\operatorname{SU}_6(q)$.
Let $\sigma_g\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$ satisfy $g(av)=\sigma_g(a)g(v)$ for all $a\in E$ and $v\in E^2$.
Because $2$ lifts differ by $\lambda I_6$ with $\lambda\in F^*$, the map $\sigma_g$ depends only on $\overline g$.
The homomorphism $\chi:A\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$ sends $\overline g$ to $\sigma_g$.
Let $A_0=\ker\chi$. Then, $A_0\lhd A$ and $[A:A_0]\mid3$.
We choose $0\ne v\in L$.
Then, $L=Fv$.
Every lift $g$ of an element of $A_0$ satisfies $g(v)=\alpha v$ for some $\alpha\in F^*$.
By $E$-linearity, $g|_{Ev}=\alpha I$.
Hence, $g$ has an eigenspace of $F$-dimension at least $3$.

Let $V_5=L^\perp$.
Since $L$ is a nondegenerate line in $V$, we have $\dim_F V_5=5$.
The inverse image of $N_G(R^x)$ has quotient $C_5$ over the inverse image of $R^x$.
Consequently, a lift of an element in $N_G(R^x)\setminus R^x$ acts on $V_5$ by a $5$-cycle on the torus weight lines.
Each weight vector maps to a nonzero scalar multiple of the next vector.
Thus, every geometric eigenspace on $V_5$ has dimension at most $1$.
The bound also holds in characteristic $5$.
Hence, every geometric eigenspace on $V$ has dimension at most $2$.
A lift of an element of $A_0$ has an eigenspace of dimension at least $3$.
Hence, no such element lies outside $R^x$, and $A_0\leq R^x$.

For a lift $g$ of an element of $A_0$, the restriction $g|_{V_5}$ is multiplication by $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{10}}$.
The degree $[F(\lambda):F]$ is $1$ or $5$.
If $[F(\lambda):F]=5$, then every geometric eigenspace of $g$ on $V$ would have dimension at most $2$.
This contradicts the eigenspace of dimension at least $3$ obtained from $E$-linearity.
Thus, $\lambda\in F$.
The eigenvalues are then $\lambda$ with multiplicity $5$
and $\lambda^{-5}$ on $L$.
Since $L\leq Ev$ and $\dim_F(Ev\cap L^\perp)\geq2$, the scalar $\alpha$ equals both $\lambda^{-5}$ and $\lambda$.
Therefore, $\lambda=\lambda^{-5}$.
Every lift of $A_0$ is scalar, so $A_0=1$.

If $A\ne1$, then $|A|=3$.
The quotient $N_G(R^x)/R^x$ has order $5$, so $A\leq R^x$.
Since $A\leq R^x$ and $R^x$ has order prime to $p$, we have $p\ne3$.
We choose a lift $g\in\operatorname{SU}_6(q)$ of a generator of $A$.
Let $\mu\in F$ be its eigenvalue on $L$.
Then, let $h=\mu^{-1}g$.
Since $g$ lifts an element of order $3$ in $G$, the matrix $g^3$ is scalar.
Its scalar value is $\mu^3$, as seen on $L$.
Therefore, $h|_L=I$ and $h^3=I$.
We identify $V_5$ with $\mathbb{F}_{q^{10}}$ as an $F$-vector space.
Then, $h|_{V_5}$ is multiplication by an element $\nu\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{10}}^*$ with $|\nu|=3$.
As $[F(\nu):F]$ divides both $5$ and $2$, we have $\nu\in F$.
Thus, $h$ has the nontrivial eigenvalue $\nu$ with multiplicity $5$.
Because $A_0=1$, we have $\chi(\overline g)\ne1$.
We choose an algebraic closure $\overline F$ containing $E$.
Next, let $I=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)$.
Let $\overline V=\overline F\otimes_F V$.
Then, the operator $\overline h$ on $\overline V$ satisfies $\overline h(a\otimes v)=a\otimes h(v)$.
Let $\Phi:\overline V\to\bigoplus_{\sigma\in I}\overline F^2$ be the $\overline F$-linear isomorphism with
$$
 \Phi\bigl(a\otimes(v_1,v_2)\bigr)
 =\bigl((a\sigma(v_1),a\sigma(v_2))\bigr)_{\sigma\in I}.
$$
As $\chi(\overline g)$ has order $3$, the operator $\Phi\overline h\Phi^{-1}$ cyclically permutes the $3$ summands.
Each summand has dimension $2$ over $\overline F$.
Because $h^3=1$, the characteristic polynomial is $(X^3-1)^2$.
Every eigenvalue has multiplicity $2$.
The eigenvalue $\nu$ cannot have both multiplicity $5$ and multiplicity $2$.
Therefore, $A=1$ for $q\geq3$.

For $q=2$, let $M_2$ be a maximal subgroup of type
$\operatorname{GU}_3(2)\wr S_2$ \cite[Table 8.26]{BHR}.
The projective order is $|M_2|=93312=2^7\cdot3^6$.
Since $\operatorname{GU}_3(2)$ is soluble, so is $M_2$.
If $G=M_2Y$ with $Y<G$, then $Y$ is not soluble by \cite[Proposition 4.1]{LiXia}.
The bound for a soluble factor $X<G$ in $G=XY$ is $|X|\mid2^9\cdot7\cdot3=10752$ by \cite[Table 1.1]{LiXia}.
As $|M_2|_3=3^6>(10752)_3=3$, we have $M_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Thus, $A\leq M_2^g$ for some $g\in G$.

We take a torus $R$ of type $(5,1)$ with $|R|=11$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AR^x$ is a subgroup.
As $|A|$ divides $93312$, we have $|AR^x|\leq11\cdot93312<|G|$.
The prime divisors of $|AR^x|$ lie in $\{2,3,11\}$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012}, we choose a maximal subgroup $M<G$ with $AR^x\leq M$.
We have $M\cong\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$ or $M\cong M_{22}$.
Because $5,7\mid|M|$ and neither prime divides $|AR^x|$, we have $AR^x<M$.
We choose a maximal subgroup $L<M$ with $AR^x\leq L$.
As $R^x\leq L$ and $|R|=11$, we have $L\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$
\cite{Bereczky,Atlas1985}.
Hence,
$|A|\mid(93312,660)=12, |AR^x|\leq132<660$.
By Dickson's subgroup classification \cite{Dickson1901}, we have $AR^x\leq C_{11}\rtimes C_5$.
Hence, $|A|\mid(93312,55)=1$.
head: environment

label: thm:unitary-even-dimension
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-even-dimension}
Let $n\geq4$ be even and let $q$ be any prime power.
Then, $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] For $n\geq8$, we have $|A|_p<q^{n-1}$.
\end{itemize}
For $n=4,6$, we use Theorems \ref{thm:unitary-four} and \ref{thm:unitary-six}.
Suppose that $n\geq8$ and that $A<G$ is nontrivial and
ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $q=p^f$ with $p$ prime.
Let $m=n-1$ and $d=(n,q+1)$.

The monomial subgroup $M$ of type $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)\wr S_n$
is maximal \cite[Proposition 2.2.9]{Uffelmann2017}.
By \cite[Theorem C]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
See also \cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.3]{LiXia}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq M^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Hence, $|A|_p\leq(n!)_p$.
For odd $p$, we have $v_p(n!)<n/(p-1)\leq n/2<m$.
For $q\geq4$ even, $v_2(n!)<n\leq fm$.
Let $s_2(n)$ count the nonzero binary digits of $n$.
For $q=2$, we have $v_2(n!)=n-s_2(n)$.
For $s_2(n)>1$, we have $v_2(n!)<m$.
We consider $q=2$, $n=2^k$ after finding an invariant line.

Let $R$ be a torus of type $(m,1)$, of order $(q^m+1)/d$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-order-bound}, we have $|A||R|<|G|$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we have a proper subgroup $K=AR^x$ for some $x\in G$.
The torus $R^x$ contains an element whose order is a primitive prime divisor of $p^{2mf}-1$.
Since $K<G$, \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012} implies that $K$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line $L\leq V=\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^n$.
The line $L$ is the unique line stabilized by $R^x$.

Suppose that $q=2$ and $n=2^k$.
Then, $G=\operatorname{SU}_n(2)$.
We choose $g_0\in G$ with $A\leq M^{g_0}$.
Then, we choose an orthonormal basis on which $M^{g_0}$ acts monomially.
Let $P$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$.
By Schur--Zassenhaus, we choose $g\in M^{g_0}$ such that $P^g$ consists of permutation matrices in the chosen basis.
Replace $(A,K,L,P)$ by $(A^g,K^g,g^{-1}L,P^g)$, and replace $x$ by $xg$.
Let $h:V\times V\to\mathbb{F}_4$ be the Hermitian form.
Since $q+1$ is odd, every $u\in P$ fixes $L$ pointwise.
We choose $v=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i e_i\in L$ with $h(v,v)\ne0$.
Since $P$ consists of permutation matrices and fixes $v$, the coordinates $v_i$ are constant on each $P$-orbit on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
As the basis is orthonormal, we have $h(v,v)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^3$.
Every nonsingleton $P$-orbit has even size and contributes zero to this sum.
Since $h(v,v)\ne0$, at least one $P$-orbit has size $1$.
Thus, $P$ fixes an index in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$.
The faithful permutation action embeds $P$ in $S_{n-1}$.
Therefore, $|A|_2=|P|\leq((n-1)!)_2<2^{n-1}=q^m$.
Consequently, $|A|_p<q^m$ for all $n\geq8$ and all $q$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] $\widetilde A$ is abelian with cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroups.
\end{itemize}
By Step~1, we have $A\leq K\leq\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$.
Let $\rho_L:\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ be the quotient map.
For $\overline g\in\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$, choose a lift $g\in\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
Let $\pi_L:\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)\to\operatorname{PGU}(L^\perp)$ satisfy $\pi_L(\overline g)=\rho_L(g|_{L^\perp})$.
Since $2$ lifts differ by $\lambda I$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ and $\lambda^{q+1}=1$, the value of $\pi_L(\overline g)$ is independent of the lift.
The kernel is $\ker\pi_L=\{\overline g:g|_{L^\perp}=\lambda I_{L^\perp}\text{ for some }\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*\}$.
From the kernel formula and the torus decomposition, the kernel $\ker\pi_L$ has order $(q+1)/d$ and lies in $R^x$.
Let $J=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(K))\leq\operatorname{GU}(L^\perp)\cong\operatorname{GU}_m(q)$.
Since $R^x\leq K$, the group $J$ contains the Singer subgroup $F=\rho_L^{-1}(\pi_L(R^x))$ of order $q^m+1$.
As both quotient kernels and $R^x$ have order prime to $p$, we have $|J|_p=|A|_p<q^m$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-singer-small-p-part}, $J$ normalizes $F$.
Hence, $\pi_L(K)$ normalizes $\pi_L(R^x)$.
Because $\ker\pi_L\leq R^x$, we have $\pi_L^{-1}(\pi_L(R^x))=R^x$.
Therefore, $A\leq N_G(R^x)$.
Since $|R|$ is prime to $p$ and $[N_G(R):R]=m$, we have $|A|_p\leq m_p$.

We take a nondegenerate $W_0\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}W_0=2$.
The subgroup $N_2=\operatorname{Stab}_G(W_0)$ is maximal \cite[Theorem 4.3]{King2005}.
By \cite[Theorem 2.15 and Table A.3]{LiXia}, we have $N_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq N_2^z$ for some $z\in G$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde z\in\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$ of $z$.
Let $W=\widetilde z^{-1}W_0$.
Then, $aW=W$ for every lift $a$ of an element of $A$.
Let $\widetilde G=\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$.
Next, let $\widetilde A$ and $\widetilde R$ be the inverse images of $A$ and $R^x$ under $\widetilde G\to G$.
Let $\widetilde C=\widetilde A\cap\widetilde R$.

The torus $\widetilde R$ is cyclic of order $q^m+1$.
Now, let $U=L^\perp$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}U=m$.
For $c\in\widetilde R$, $c|_U$ is multiplication by $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$.
The degree $e=[\mathbb{F}_{q^2}(\lambda):\mathbb{F}_{q^2}]$ divides the odd integer $m$.
For $e>1$, every $c$-invariant $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-subspace of $V$ has dimension $0$ or $1$ modulo $e$.
Since $e\geq3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}W=2$, we have $cW\ne W$.
Every element of $\widetilde C$ stabilizes $W$.
Therefore, every element of $\widetilde C$ has $e=1$.
The matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(\lambda I_m,\lambda^{-m})$ with $\lambda^{q+1}=1$.
The group $N_{\widetilde G}(\widetilde R)$ stabilizes $U$ and $L$.
Since each displayed matrix is scalar on both summands, it centralizes $N_{\widetilde G}(\widetilde R)$.
As $N_{\widetilde G}(\widetilde R)/\widetilde R\cong C_m$, the quotient $\widetilde A/\widetilde C$ is cyclic.
Because $\widetilde C$ is central in $\widetilde A$ and $\widetilde A/\widetilde C$ is cyclic, $\widetilde A$ is abelian.
Because $|N_{\widetilde G}(\widetilde R)/\widetilde R|=m$ is odd, every Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\widetilde A$ lies in $\widetilde R$.
As $\widetilde R$ is cyclic, those Sylow subgroups are cyclic.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] $\widetilde K$ is metabelian and $O_p(\widetilde K)=1$.
\end{itemize}
Next, we take a cyclic torus $T\leq\widetilde G$ of type $(n)$ with $|T|=(q^n-1)/(q+1)$.
Let $S$ be the Hall subgroup of $T$ of odd order.
Let $\pi:\widetilde G\to G$ be the quotient map.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $y\in G$ with $A\pi(S)^y$ a subgroup.
Choose $\widetilde y\in\widetilde G$ with $\pi(\widetilde y)=y$.
Then, we use $S^y=\widetilde y^{-1}S\widetilde y$ and $T^y=\widetilde y^{-1}T\widetilde y$.
Since $\ker\pi=Z(\widetilde G)$, the choice of $\widetilde y$ does not affect $S^y,T^y$.
As $Z(\widetilde G)\leq\widetilde A$, the inverse image of $A\pi(S)^y$ is $\widetilde K=\widetilde A S^y$.
Because $\widetilde A$ and $S^y$ are abelian, we obtain from It\^o's theorem \cite{Ito1955} that $\widetilde K$ is metabelian.
As $|S|$ is odd, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\widetilde A$ is also Sylow in $\widetilde K$.
Hence, the Sylow $2$-subgroups of $\widetilde K$ are cyclic.
By Burnside's theorem on normal complements, we have a normal Hall subgroup $H\unlhd\widetilde K$ of odd order with $S^y\leq H$.

Let $P_0=O_p(\widetilde K)$.
Since $S^y$ and $Z(\widetilde G)$ have order prime to $p$, we have $|\widetilde K|_p=|A|_p$.
By the bound from Step~2, we have $|A|_p\leq m_p$.
Therefore, $|P_0|\leq m_p\leq m$.
We show that $P_0=1$.
If $4\mid n$, then choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$
of $p^{fn}-1$.
If $n\equiv2\pmod4$, then choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $p^{fn/2}-1$.
For $n\geq8$, neither chosen exponent has a Zsigmondy exception.
For the first choice, we have $\ell>fn\geq n$.
For the second choice with odd $f$, the integer $fn/2$ is odd and divides $\ell-1$.
Since $\ell-1$ is even, we have $\ell-1\geq fn$.
For the second choice with even $f$, we have $\ell>fn/2\geq n$.
Thus, $\ell>n$ in both choices.
Moreover,
$\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q^2)=n/2, \operatorname{ord}_\ell(-q)=n$.
Since $\ell$ is odd and $\ell\nmid q+1$, we have $\ell\mid|S|$.
Therefore, $S^y$ contains an element $z$ of order $\ell$.
Let $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^{\,*}$ be an eigenvalue of $z$ with $|\lambda|=\ell$.
Let $\mathcal O_0=\{\lambda^{q^{2j}}:0\leq j<n/2\}$ and $\mathcal O_1=\{\alpha^{-q}:\alpha\in\mathcal O_0\}$.
As $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(-q)=n$, we have $\mathcal O_0\cap\mathcal O_1=\varnothing$.
The sets $\mathcal O_0,\mathcal O_1$ are the $2$ eigenvalue orbits under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{q^2}$.
We have $|\mathcal O_0|=|\mathcal O_1|=n/2$.
Thus, $z$ has $2$ nonisomorphic irreducible constituents of dimension $n/2$.
Unitary duality $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-q}$ sends $\mathcal O_i$ to $\mathcal O_{1-i}$ for $i=0,1$.
The two disjoint orbits contain $n$ distinct eigenvalues.
Thus, $z$ is regular semisimple and $C_{\widetilde G}(z)=T^y$, a $p'$-torus.
The permutation action on $P_0$ induces an injective homomorphism $\operatorname{Aut}(P_0)\to S_{|P_0|}$.
Since $\ell>|P_0|$, we have $\ell\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(P_0)|$.
Therefore, $z$ centralizes $P_0$ and $P_0\leq C_{\widetilde G}(z)=T^y$.
As $T^y$ is a $p'$-group, we have $P_0=1$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] $\widetilde K$ normalizes $T^y$.
\end{itemize}
Let $D=H'$, where $H\unlhd\widetilde K$ is the normal Hall subgroup of odd order from Step~3.
Since $\widetilde K''=1$, we have $D'=1$.
Since $H'$ is characteristic in $H$, we have $D\unlhd\widetilde K$.
As $D$ is abelian, its Sylow $p$-subgroup is characteristic in $D$ and hence normal in $\widetilde K$.
Because $O_p(\widetilde K)=1$, that Sylow subgroup is trivial.
Thus, $D$ is a $p'$-group.
Let $\overline F$ be an algebraic closure of $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Let $\overline V=\overline F\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}V$ with $d(a\otimes v)=a\otimes dv$ for $d\in D$.
Because $D$ is abelian of order prime to $p$, its elements are simultaneously diagonalizable on $\overline V$.
Thus, $D$ has at most $n$ distinct common eigenspaces.
Because $z$ normalizes $D$, the element $z$ permutes the $D$-weight spaces.
Since $z$ has order $\ell>n$, its permutation of the $D$-weight spaces is trivial.
Because each element of $D$ is scalar on every $D$-weight space, $z$ centralizes $D$.
Therefore, $D\leq C_{\widetilde G}(z)=T^y$.
Because $|D|$ is odd, we also have $D\leq S^y$.

As $H/H'$ is abelian and $H'\leq S^y$, the subgroup $S^y$ is normal in $H$.
Therefore, $H$ normalizes its centralizer $C_{\widetilde G}(S^y)=T^y$.
Hence, $H\leq N_{\widetilde G}(T^y)$.
The quotient $N_{\widetilde G}(T^y)/T^y$ is $C_n$.
Because $\ell>n$, every $\ell$-subgroup of $H$ lies in the cyclic torus $T^y$.
Thus, $H$ has a unique Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $S_\ell$, and $S_\ell\leq S^y$.
Hence, $S_\ell$ is characteristic in $H$ and normal in $\widetilde K$.
Since $S_\ell\unlhd\widetilde K$, the group $\widetilde K$ normalizes $C_{\widetilde G}(S_\ell)=T^y$.
Hence, $\widetilde K\leq N_{\widetilde G}(T^y)$.
Let $\overline T_y=\pi(T^y)\leq G$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(\overline T_y)$.

An element of $T^y$ stabilizing the nondegenerate line $L$ has multiplier $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ with $\lambda^{q+1}=1$.
Hence, the element is $\lambda I_V$.
Since $\lambda I_V\in Z(\widetilde G)$, we have $A\cap\overline T_y=1$.
Reducing $(q^n-1)/(q+1)$ modulo $q+1$, we also obtain that $\gcd((q^n-1)/(q+1),q+1)=d$.
Let $\nu_y:N_G(\overline T_y)\to N_G(\overline T_y)/\overline T_y\cong C_n$ be the quotient map.
As $\ker(\nu_y|_A)=1$, the subgroup $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid n$.
Let $\eta:A\to N_G(R^x)/R^x\cong C_m$ satisfy $\eta(a)=aR^x$.
The order $|\eta(A)|$ divides both $|A|$ and $m$.
Since $|A|\mid n$ and $(n,m)=1$, we have $\eta(A)=1$.
Hence, $A\leq R^x$.

We choose an element $a\in A$ of prime order $r$.
By Step~2, a lift $\widetilde a\in\widetilde C$ is scalar on $U=L^\perp$ and on $L$.
Since $a\ne1$ projectively, the two scalars are distinct.
Thus, $\widetilde a$ has $2$ distinct eigenvalues with multiplicities $(n-1,1)$.
Since $\nu_y|_A$ is injective, the element $\nu_y(a)$ has order $r$.
The lift $\widetilde a$ permutes the torus weight lines in $n/r$ cycles of length $r$.
On each cycle, an eigenvector is determined by its coordinate on one weight line.
Hence, every geometric eigenspace of $\widetilde a$ has dimension at most $n/r$.
As $n-1>n/r$, we have a contradiction.
head: environment

label: cor:all-unitary
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:all-unitary}
Let $n\geq3$ and let $q$ be a prime power.
Suppose that $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ is nonabelian simple.
Then, $G$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For odd $n\geq3$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-odd-dimension}.
For even $n\geq4$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-even-dimension}.
head: environment

label: lem:symplectic-singer-involutions
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-singer-involutions}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $m\geq1$.
Let $\pi:\operatorname{Sp}_{2m}(q)\to G=\operatorname{PSp}_{2m}(q)$ be the quotient map.
Let $T\leq G$ be a Singer torus with $|T|=(q^m+1)/(2,q-1)$.
Every involution in $N_G(T)$ has rank $m$ when $q$ is even.
When $q$ is odd, every involution $t\in N_G(T)$ has a lift
$h\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2m}(q)$ with $\pi(h)=t$ and $h^2=-I_{2m}$.
Suppose that $A\leq N_G(T)$ stabilizes a line $\Lambda\leq\mathbb{F}_q^{2m}$.
Then, $A$ is cyclic with $|A|\mid2m$.
When $q\equiv3\pmod4$, such a subgroup $A$ has odd order.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$ and $F=\mathbb{F}_{q^m}$.
We choose $\mu\ne0$ with $\mu^{q^m}=-\mu$ and use the nondegenerate alternating form
$\beta(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb{F}_q}(\mu xy^{q^m})$.
For $\lambda\in E^*$ with $\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$, let $M_\lambda(x)=\lambda x$.
Together, these multipliers form the inverse image of $T$ under $\pi$ and generate the field algebra $E$.
Because each element normalizing this multiplier group normalizes $E$, the elements of $N_G(T)$ have semilinear lifts.
For each $0\leq i<2m$, let $\sigma_i(x)=x^{q^i}$.
Since $(\mu^{q^i}/\mu)^{q^m}=\mu^{q^i}/\mu$, the ratio $\mu^{q^i}/\mu$ lies in $F^*$.
As the norm $N_{E/F}:E^*\to F^*$ is surjective, choose $c_i$ with $c_i^{q^m+1}=\mu^{q^i}/\mu$.
Then, the map $h_i(x)=c_i x^{q^i}$ satisfies
$\beta(h_ix,h_iy)=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb{F}_q}((\mu xy^{q^m})^{q^i})=\beta(x,y)$.
Consequently, $h_i$ lies in $\operatorname{Sp}_{2m}(q)$.
Conjugation on the field algebra $E$ induces $\theta:N_G(T)\to\operatorname{Gal}(E/\mathbb{F}_q)$ with $\theta(\pi(h_i))=\sigma_i$.
Because a multiplier $M_\lambda$ preserves $\beta$ exactly when $\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$, we have $\ker\theta=T$.
As every $\sigma_i$ lies in the image of $\theta$, we obtain $N_G(T)/T\cong C_{2m}$.

Let $h\in\operatorname{Sp}_{2m}(q)$ lift an involution $\pi(h)\in N_G(T)$.
As $h^2\in\ker\pi$, we have $h^2=\pm I_E$.
Consequently, the field automorphism of $h$ is trivial or $x\mapsto x^{q^m}$.
If $h$ is a multiplier and $q$ is odd, then $h^2=I_E$ would imply $h=\pm I_E$.
Because $\pi(h)\ne1$, we obtain $h^2=-I_E$ in this case.
For even $q$, the order $|T|=q^m+1$ is odd, so an involution cannot lie in $T$.
If the field automorphism of $h$ is $x\mapsto x^{q^m}$, then $h(x)=cx^{q^m}$ for some $c\in E^*$.
Substituting $h(x)=cx^{q^m}$ in $\beta(hx,hy)=\beta(x,y)$ yields $c^{q^m+1}=-1$.
Hence, $h^2=-I_E$ in this case as well.
When $q$ is even, we have $c^{q^m+1}=1$.
By Hilbert's Theorem 90, choose $d\in E^*$ with $c=d/d^{q^m}$.
Then, $h(dy)=dy$ if and only if $y\in F$, so $\ker(h-I_E)=dF$ has dimension $m$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
By rank--nullity, we obtain $\operatorname{rank}(h-I_E)=m$.

Now, suppose that $A$ stabilizes the line $\Lambda$.
For $a\in A\cap T$, choose $\lambda\in E^*$ with $a=\pi(M_\lambda)$ and $\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$.
As $a\in A$, we have $M_\lambda(\Lambda)=\Lambda$.
For $0\ne v\in\Lambda$, the equality $\lambda v=cv$ holds for some $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$.
Therefore, $\lambda=c\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$ and $\lambda^2=\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$.
It follows that $M_\lambda=\lambda I_E\in\ker\pi$ and $a=1$.
Since $a\in A\cap T$ was arbitrary, we have $A\cap T=1$.
Now, consider the homomorphism $\eta:A\to N_G(T)/T$ with $\eta(a)=aT$.
Because $\ker\eta=A\cap T=1$, the map $\eta$ is injective.
Thus, $A$ is cyclic with $|A|\mid2m$.
Finally, suppose that $q\equiv3\pmod4$ and $A$ contains an involution $t=\pi(h)$.
As $h\Lambda=\Lambda$, we have $hv=cv$ for some $0\ne v\in\Lambda$ and $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$.
But $h^2=-I_E$ would imply $c^2=-1$, which is impossible for $q\equiv3\pmod4$.
Consequently, $A$ contains no involution. By Cauchy's theorem, $|A|$ is odd.
head: environment

label: lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}
Let $F\leq E$ be finite fields of characteristic $p$.
For $b\geq1$, a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\operatorname{Sp}_{2b}(E)$ acts indecomposably on $E^{2b}$ over $F$.
For $E=\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ and $b\geq3$, a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_b(Q)$ acts indecomposably on $E^b$ over $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $d=2b$ for $\operatorname{Sp}_{2b}(E)$ and $d=b$ for $\operatorname{SU}_b(Q)$.
We use the upper-triangular Sylow subgroup $P$ on $V=E^d$ with basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$.
For this subgroup, the common fixed space is $V^P=Y=Ee_1$.
Moreover, a nonidentity highest-root element $u\in P$ satisfies
$\operatorname{im}(u-I_V)=Y$ and $\ker(u-I_V)=H=Ee_1+\cdots+Ee_{d-1}$.
For every $X\in C_{\operatorname{End}_F(V)}(P)$, we have $X(Y)\leq Y$ and $X(H)\leq H$.

Suppose that $d\geq3$.
For each $a\in E$, choose the adjacent root element $u_a\in P$ satisfying
$u_a(e_2x)=e_2x+e_1ax$ for $x\in E$.
Let $X_Y=X|_Y:Y\to Y$.
Let $D:E\to E$ take $x$ to the second coordinate of $X(e_2x)$.
Since $X(e_2x)\in H$, its last coordinate is zero. Thus, the linked root terms in $Xu_a=u_aX$ vanish.
We obtain that $X_Y(ax e_1)=aD(x)e_1$.
Taking $a=1$, we have $X_Y(xe_1)=D(x)e_1$. Thus, $X_Y(axe_1)=aX_Y(xe_1)$ for $a,x\in E$.
Since $Y=Ee_1$, we have $X_Y=\lambda I_Y$ for some $\lambda\in E$.
For $\operatorname{Sp}_2(E)$, we have $X(I+aE_{12})=(I+aE_{12})X$ for every $a\in E$.
Hence, $X_Y=\lambda I_Y$ for some $\lambda\in E$.

If $X$ is idempotent, then $X|_Y=0$ or $I_Y$.
Every nonzero module for a finite $p$-group in characteristic $p$ has a nonzero fixed vector.
Since $\operatorname{im}X$ and $\ker X$ are $P$-modules, each nonzero space contains a nonzero $P$-fixed vector.
Suppose that $X_Y=0$ and $\operatorname{im}X\ne0$.
Since $V^P=Y$, we choose $0\ne v\in\operatorname{im}X\cap Y$.
Then, $Xv=v$ by $X^2=X$, whereas $Xv=0$ by $X_Y=0$.
Suppose that $X_Y=I_Y$ and $\ker X\ne0$.
We choose $0\ne v\in\ker X\cap Y$. Then, $Xv=0$ and $Xv=v$, a contradiction.
Therefore, $X=0$ or $I_V$. We conclude that $P$ acts indecomposably over $F$.
head: environment

label: lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup}
Let $Q$ be a power of a prime $p$ and $a\geq2$.
Let $F\leq E=\mathbb{F}_Q$.
The group $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ contains a $p$-subgroup acting
indecomposably on its natural module over $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r=a-1$ and $L=\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$.
On $V=E^r\oplus L\oplus E^r$, use
$\mathcal Q(x,z,y)=x^{\mathsf T}y+z\overline z, \overline z=z^Q$.
Next, let $U_r=\{g\in\operatorname{GL}_r(E):g_{ii}=1,\ g_{ij}=0\text{ for }i>j\}$.
We use $\{\operatorname{diag}(g,I_L,g^{-\mathsf T}):g\in U_r\}$ on $V$.
For $1\leq i<j\leq r$ and $b\in E$, use the maps
$$
 x_i\mapsto x_i+b y_j,\  x_j\mapsto x_j-b y_i.
$$
For $1\leq i\leq r$ and $c\in L$, use
$$
 s_i(c):z\mapsto z+c y_i,\  x_i\mapsto x_i-\operatorname{Tr}_{L/E}(\overline c z)-c\overline c y_i.
$$
Each map fixes the coordinates not displayed.
For each displayed map $g$, we have $\mathcal Q(gv)=\mathcal Q(v)$ for $v\in V$.
The maps lie in an upper unitriangular group.
Let $P$ be generated by the displayed root maps and $\{\operatorname{diag}(g,I_L,g^{-\mathsf T}):g\in U_r\}$.
For $p=2$, each generator $g$ has even $\operatorname{rank}(g-I_V)$.
By the Dickson homomorphism \cite[Proposition 1.6.11]{BHR}, we have $P\leq\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$.
For odd $p$, the generators have determinant $1$.
