Let $\rho_U:L\to\operatorname{Sp}(U)=\operatorname{SL}_2(p)$ be the representation on $U$.
If $2\mid|\rho_U(L)|$, then $-I_U\in\rho_U(L)$ acts as $z$ on both copies. This contradicts $z\notin L$.
An odd image cannot have absolute degree $2$.
Thus, this multiplicity is impossible.
For an absolutely irreducible orthogonal constituent $U$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}U=2$ and multiplicity $2$, the multiplicity space $M$ is symplectic with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}M=2$.
Under $V\cong U\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_p}M$, the maps $I_U\otimes h$ with $h\in\operatorname{Sp}(M)$ centralize $L$.
In a symplectic basis of $M$, take $h=\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$.
Then, $(I_U\otimes h)^2=z$.
For a self-dual constituent $U$ irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_p$ but not absolutely irreducible, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}U=2$.
Let $E_U=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_pL}(U)\cong\mathbb{F}_{p^2}$.
The adjoint automorphism of $E_U$ sends $a$ to $a^p$.
Thus, on the multiplicity space $M=E_U^2$, the centralizer of $L$ is $\operatorname{GU}_2(p)$.
Consequently, an element of order $4$ in $\operatorname{SU}_2(p)\leq\operatorname{GU}_2(p)$ acts on $V$ with square $z$.
Since every completely reducible $L$-module $V$ has one of the listed decompositions, we have proved the lemma.
head: environment

label: thm:symplectic-four-odd-all
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:symplectic-four-odd-all}
Let $q$ be odd and $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$.
Then, $G$ has a proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup
if and only if $q$ is prime and $q\equiv1,13,17\pmod{24}$.
In these cases, the subgroups are precisely those of order $2$
whose generating involutions have a lift of square $-I$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{thm:symplectic-odd-reduction}, a proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup has order $2$.
Its generating involution has a lift of square $-I$.
Moreover, $q$ is prime with $q\equiv1,13,17\pmod{24}$.

Let $p\equiv1,13,17\pmod{24}$ be prime. Let $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(p)$.
For the natural representation, let $V=\mathbb{F}_p^4$ and let $\pi:\operatorname{Sp}(V)\to G$ be the quotient map.
Let $A=\langle \pi(s)\rangle$ with $s\in\operatorname{Sp}(V)$ and $s^2=-I_V$.
Next, choose $i\in\mathbb{F}_p$ with $i^2=-1$.
Let $V_+=\ker(s-iI_V)$ and $V_-=\ker(s+iI_V)$.
Since $s^2=-I_V$ and $s$ is symplectic, we have $V=V_+\oplus V_-$, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}V_+=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}V_-=2$.
Moreover, $\beta(sv,sw)=\beta(v,w)$ and $i^2=-1$ show that both eigenspaces are totally isotropic.
For $2$ such subgroups $A_1,A_2$, paired symplectic bases provide $g\in G$ with $A_1^g=A_2$.
Let $B\leq G$.
If $B$ contains such a subgroup $A_1$, then choose $x\in G$ with $A_1^x=A$.
Then, $A\leq B^x$, so $AB^x$ is a subgroup.

Suppose that $B$ contains no involution with a lift of square $-I$.
We obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-complex-complement} a complement $L\cong B$ in $\pi^{-1}(B)$.
If the natural $L$-module is completely reducible, then we use Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-prime-semisimple}.
We have an involution $t_B\in N_G(B)$ with a lift of square $-I$.
Suppose that $V=\mathbb{F}_p^4$ is not completely reducible under $L$.
For a proper degenerate $L$-submodule $W$, the radical $W\cap W^\perp$ is a nonzero totally isotropic $L$-submodule.
For a proper nondegenerate $L$-submodule $W$, we have $V=W\perp W^\perp$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}W=2$.
Because $V$ is not completely reducible, at least $1$ of $W,W^\perp$ is reducible under $L$.
Thus, $L$ stabilizes an isotropic line in that plane.
Thus, $L$ stabilizes a totally isotropic subspace $W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}W=1$ or $2$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-prime-parabolic}, we have an involution $t_B\in N_G(B)$ with a lift of square $-I$.
Choose $x\in G$ with $\langle t_B^x\rangle=A$.
Then, we have $A\leq N_G(B^x)$.
Thus, for every $B\leq G$, there is $x\in G$ with $AB^x=B^xA$.
head: environment

label: thm:orthogonal-minus-even
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:orthogonal-minus-even}
Let $q$ be even and $m\geq4$.
Then, $\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
Let $G=\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$ and let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
We use the natural $G$-module $V=\mathbb{F}_q^{2m}$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] $A$ normalizes $T^x$.
\end{itemize}
Next, let $P_2$ stabilize a totally singular subspace $U\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2$.
The subgroup $P_2$ is maximal.
For every $Y<G$, we have $P_2Y\ne G$
\cite[Theorem 4.2]{King2005}\cite[Table A.5]{LiXia}.
Thus, $A\leq P_2^x$ for some $x\in G$.
Hence, $A$ stabilizes $x^{-1}U$ and $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
The anisotropic plane stabilizer $N_2^-$ is maximal
\cite[Theorem 4.3]{King2005}.
For characteristic $2$, the exception to maximality of $N_2^-$ has $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V=6$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose $y\in G$ with $A\leq(N_2^-)^y$.
Thus, $A$ stabilizes $V=V_1\perp V_2$. We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_1=2$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_2=2m-2$.

Next, we take a Singer torus $T$ of order $q^m+1$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $K=AT^x$ is a subgroup.
As $AT^x\ne G$, we have $K<G$.
Since $|T|$ is odd, we have $|K|_2=|A|_2$.
Thus, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $A$ is Sylow in $K$.
For every $2$-subgroup $P\leq K$, Sylow's theorem permits a choice of $g\in K$ with $P^g\leq A$.
Because $A$ stabilizes $V_1\perp V_2$, the group $P$ stabilizes $gV_1\perp gV_2$.
We claim that $K\leq N_G(T^x)$.
To prove $K\leq N_G(T^x)$, we choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{2m}-1$.
There is no Zsigmondy exception in this range, and $\ell>2m$.
For this primitive prime, let $T_\ell$ be the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $T^x$. We have
$C_{\operatorname{GL}_{2m}(q)}(T_\ell)=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}^*, C_G(T_\ell)=T^x$.

By Bereczky's theorem \cite{Bereczky,Brookfield2014}, we use successive subgroups $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ or $\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ with odd $b$.
At each step, intersect with the normal subgroup consisting of maps linear over $\mathbb{F}_Q$ or $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$.
For an orthogonal subgroup, also intersect with its normal $\Omega^-$ subgroup.
The intervening quotients have order at most $2m<\ell$.
At each step, let $F_0=\mathbb{F}_Q$ for an orthogonal group $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ and $F_0=\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ for a unitary group $\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$.
Since $F_0$ commutes with $T_\ell$, we have $F_0\leq\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$.
As $T^x$ centralizes $F_0$, its elements are $F_0$-linear.
Because $|T^x|$ is odd, $T^x$ lies in the relative $\Omega^-$ subgroup.
Thus, every normal intersection contains $T^x$.

By Lemma \ref{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup}, each relative $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ with $a\geq2$ contains an indecomposable $2$-subgroup.
From Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, each relative $\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ with odd $b\geq3$ contains an indecomposable $2$-subgroup.
But every $P\leq K$ of $2$-power order stabilizes $gV_1\perp gV_2$ for some $g\in K$.
Thus, an intersection cannot equal either relative group.
We continue with decreasing relative dimension.
The groups $\Omega^-_2(Q)$ and $\operatorname{GU}_1(Q)$ are tori.
For $\Omega^-_4(Q)\cong\operatorname{SL}_2(Q^2)$, we use Dickson's classification.
Every subgroup $H$ with $T^x\leq H<\Omega^-_4(Q)$ satisfies
$H\leq N_{\Omega^-_4(Q)}(T^x)$.

The relative $\Omega^-_6(2)$ and $\operatorname{GU}_3(2)$ exceptions would require
the original $m=3$ and $q=2$.
The relative fields have characteristic $2$, so none has order $3$.
For $\operatorname{GU}_5(2)$, the original pair is $(m,q)=(5,2)$.
By the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:symplectic-even}, neither $\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$ nor $A_5$ stabilizes a totally singular $U\leq\mathbb{F}_2^{10}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}U=2$.
Let $H$ be the last normal intersection.
Since $H$ lies in the relative normalizer of $T^x$, the subgroup $T_\ell$ is characteristic in $H$.
By the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-odd-singer}, we have $T_\ell\unlhd K$ through the successive normal intersections.
As $C_G(T_\ell)=T^x$ and $A\leq K$, we have $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group.
\end{itemize}
Replace $A$ by $xAx^{-1}$, with $x\in G$ from $K=AT^x$.
Then, $A\leq N_G(T)$.
We use $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$ with quadratic form
$Q(v)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_{q^m}/\mathbb{F}_q}(v^{q^m+1})$.
Since $Q$ has $q^{2m-1}-(q-1)q^{m-1}$ zeroes, we have $Q$ of minus type.
Let $\sigma:E\to E$ satisfy $\sigma(v)=v^q$. We have $|\sigma|=2m$ and $N_{\operatorname{O}(E,Q)}(T)=T\rtimes\langle \sigma\rangle$.
As $E^{\langle \sigma\rangle}=\mathbb{F}_q$, we have $\operatorname{rank}(\sigma-I_E)=2m-1$.
Thus, the Dickson invariant of $\sigma$ is $1$.
Therefore,
$N_G(T)=T\rtimes \langle \sigma^2\rangle, N_G(T)/T\cong C_m$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for the maximal singular line stabilizer, $A$ stabilizes a line $\Lambda\leq V$.
For a Singer multiplier $M_\lambda$ stabilizing $\Lambda$, we have $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$ and $\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$.
Because $q$ is even, $\lambda=1$.
Consequently, $A\cap T=1$ and $A$ is cyclic with $|A|\mid m$.

Suppose that an odd prime $r$ divides $|A|$.
Let $q=2^f$. We choose a primitive divisor $h$ of
$2^{f(2m-2)}-1$.
For $(f,m)=(1,4)$, we have $|A|\mid4$. This contradicts $r\mid|A|$.
Otherwise, $h\geq2m-1>m$.
We choose a nondegenerate subspace $U\leq V$ of minus type with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2m-2$. Let $W=U^\perp$, so $V=U\perp W$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=2$.
The space $U$ has minus type and $W$ is hyperbolic.
We take $B=C_h$ irreducible on $U$ and trivial on $W$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x\leq G$.
As $|A|<h$, we obtain by Sylow counting that $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
Let $z\in A$ have order $r$.
Because $r\mid m$ and $|N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)|$ divides $2m-2$, we have $[z,B^x]=1$.
Let $U_x=x^{-1}U$. The restriction $z|_{U_x}$
is a multiplier in $C_{q^{m-1}+1}$.
For $r<m$, an eigenvalue of $z|_{U_x}$ has multiplicity at least
$(2m-2)/(r-1)>2m/r$.
For $r=m$, we have $z|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$ by Fermat's theorem.
Either case contradicts the image of $z$ under
$N_G(T)\to N_G(T)/T=\langle \sigma^2\rangle T/T$:
the field companion of $z$ permutes the eigenlines in cycles of length $r$.
Thus, each eigenvalue of $z$ has multiplicity $2m/r$.
Consequently, $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group.
For odd $m$, we have $|A|\mid m$.
As $A$ is a $2$-group, we have $A=1$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $m$ is even, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Let $m$ be even and let $d=m-1$.
For this even $m$, we use the odd torus $B$ of signed type $(-d,+1)$, of order
$(q^d+1)(q-1)$.
Moreover, the normalizer $N_{\operatorname{O}(V)}(B)$ has Sylow $2$-subgroup $\langle b_1\rangle\times\langle b_2\rangle\cong C_2^2$.
Let $B_1,B_2$ be the torus factors on the $2$ summands of dimensions $2d$ and $2$.
For $i=1,2$ and $s\in B_i$, we have $b_i^{-1}sb_i=s^{-1}$.
We have $\operatorname{rank}(b_1-I_V)=d$ and $\operatorname{rank}(b_2-I_V)=1$.
Let $\delta:N_{\operatorname{O}(V)}(B)\to\mathbb{F}_2$ be $\delta(g)=\operatorname{rank}(g-I_V)\pmod2$.
Since $d$ is odd, the preceding rank formulas yield that $\delta(b_1)=\delta(b_2)=1$.
Therefore, $N_G(B)=\ker\delta$ has Sylow $2$-subgroup $\langle b_1b_2\rangle\cong C_2$.
For $q=2$, the plane torus is trivial. The orthogonal group of its fixed hyperbolic plane is $\operatorname{O}_2^+(2)=C_2$.
The normalizer $N_{\operatorname{O}(V)}(B)$ still has Sylow $2$-subgroup $\langle b_1\rangle\times\langle b_2\rangle\cong C_2^2$.
Since $\delta(b_1)=\delta(b_2)=1$, its Dickson kernel $N_G(B)$ has Sylow $2$-subgroup $\langle b_1b_2\rangle\cong C_2$.
We choose $x\in G$ such that $AB^x$ is a subgroup.
By Burnside's normal-complement theorem, $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
Hence, $A\leq N_G(B^x)$ and $|A|\leq2$.

Suppose that $A\ne1$, and let $t$ generate $A$.
Since $|A|\leq2$ and $A\leq N_G(T)$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-singer-involutions} that $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)=m$.
Let $k=m-1$. Then, $k\geq3$ is odd.
We use $B_k=R_{\mathcal A}\rtimes\operatorname{GL}_k(q)$ on $E=\mathbb{F}_q^{2k}$ with a form of plus type.
For its normal matrix subgroup, let $\mathcal A=\{S\in M_k(\mathbb{F}_q):S^{\mathsf T}=S,\ S_{ii}=0\text{ for }1\leq i\leq k\}$. We take
$R_{\mathcal A}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I&S\\0&I\end{pmatrix}:S\in\mathcal A\right\}$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-even-nonsingular}, we have $N_{\operatorname{Sp}_{2k}(q)}(B_k)=B_k$.
Let $D=E^\perp$ be anisotropic with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}D=2$. We take $C=C_{q+1}$ on $D$.
Then, we have $B_k\times C\leq G$ and $Z(B_k\times C)=C$.
As $C$ is characteristic, every $g\in N_{\operatorname{Sp}(V)}(B_k\times C)$ satisfies $gE=E$ and $gD=D$.
By $N_{\operatorname{Sp}(E)}(B_k)=B_k$, we obtain that
$N_{\operatorname{Sp}(V)}(B_k\times C)=B_k\times D_{2(q+1)}$.
Every element of $B_k$ has Dickson invariant zero, while the
plane reflections have invariant $1$.
Therefore,
$N_G(B_k\times C)=B_k\times C_{q+1}$.
The involutions in $N_G(B_k\times C)$ have rank at most $k-1=m-2$.
No involution in $N_G(B_k\times C)$ has rank $m$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: thm:orthogonal-minus-odd
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}
Let $q$ be odd and $m\geq4$.
Then, $\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
Let $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$ and $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$, so $q=p^f$.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] $A$ normalizes $T^x$.
\end{itemize}
Next, let $P_2$ stabilize a totally singular $U\leq V=\mathbb{F}_q^{2m}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2$.
The subgroup $P_2$ is maximal.
For every $Y<G$, we have $P_2Y\ne G$
\cite[Table A.5]{LiXia}\cite[Theorem 4.2]{King2005}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we obtain that $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
For the maximal anisotropic-plane stabilizer $M$,
some $x\in G$ satisfies $A^x\leq M$ \cite[Theorem 4.3]{King2005}.
We replace $A$ by $A^x$.
Let $\pi:\widetilde G=\Omega^-_{2m}(q)\to G$ be the quotient map and let $\widetilde A=\pi^{-1}(A)$.
Then, $\widetilde A$ stabilizes $V=V_1\perp V_2$, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_1=2$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_2=2m-2$.
The central kernel has order at most $2$, prime to the characteristic $p$.

Let $S\leq\widetilde G$ be a Singer torus of order $(q^m+1)/2$.
For its projective image, let $T=\pi(S)$.
Moreover, $\ker\pi\leq S$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $K=AT^x$ is a subgroup.
Next, choose $\widetilde x\in\widetilde G$ with $\pi(\widetilde x)=x$.
We use $S^x=\widetilde x^{-1}S\widetilde x$.
Since $\ker\pi\leq Z(\widetilde G)$, the choice of $\widetilde x$ does not affect $S^x$.
The inverse image of $K$ is $\widetilde K=\widetilde A S^x$.
We have $\widetilde K<\widetilde G$ and $|\widetilde K|_p=|\widetilde A|_p$.
For each $p$-subgroup $P\leq\widetilde K$, some $g\in\widetilde K$ satisfies $P^g\leq\widetilde A$.
Thus, $P$ stabilizes $gV_1\perp gV_2$.

We use the normal base intersections from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-even}.
For odd $q$, we make the following changes to the relative tori and scalar fields.
At each relative $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ stage, the intersection contains the Singer torus of order $(Q^a+1)/2=(q^m+1)/2$.
Thus, this torus has index $2$ in $\{M_\lambda:\lambda^{Q^a+1}=1\}$, where $M_\lambda(v)=\lambda v$.
Next, choose a primitive divisor $\ell>2m$ of $q^{2m}-1$.
The scalar field $F_0$ at each step lies in the commutative centralizer $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$ of the subgroup of order $\ell$.
Since $S^x$ centralizes $F_0$, its elements are $F_0$-linear.
At a relative unitary stage $J\leq\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ with odd $b$, let $Z=Z(\operatorname{GU}_b(Q))$.
The centre $Z$ has order $Q+1$ and lies in the cyclic torus of order $Q^b+1$.
Since $b$ is odd, we have $v_2(Q^b+1)=v_2(Q+1)$ and $|S^x\cap Z|=(Q+1)/2$.
Thus, $|S^xZ|=Q^b+1$.
We use Bereczky's classification \cite{Bereczky} for this Singer torus \cite[Theorem 2.1.7]{Brookfield2014}.
Because $JZ/J$ is a $p'$-group, every $p$-subgroup of $JZ$ lies in $J$.
Thus, each such subgroup stabilizes $gV_1\perp gV_2$ for some $g\in\widetilde K$.

By Lemmas \ref{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup} and \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, each relative group contains an indecomposable $p$-subgroup.
Thus, no intersection equals the relative orthogonal or unitary group.
The small odd-field Singer exceptions have relative field $3$
and dimension at most $6$, requiring original $m\leq3$.
Because $m\geq4$, no relative field and dimension satisfy those exceptional pairs.
At a relative $\Omega^-_4(Q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q^2)$ stage, let $H$ denote the intersection.
The subgroup $H$ contains the nonsplit torus of order $(Q^2+1)/2$.
Since $Q\geq q^2\geq9$, the nonsplit torus has order at least $41$.
Dickson's list leaves only the nonsplit torus normalizer.
By the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-odd-singer}, the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $S_\ell$ of $S^x$ satisfies $S_\ell\unlhd\widetilde K$.
As $C_{\widetilde G}(S_\ell)=S^x$, we have $\widetilde A\leq N_{\widetilde G}(S^x)$ and $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\leq2$.
\end{itemize}
Replace $A$ by $xAx^{-1}$, with $x\in G$ from $K=AT^x$.
Then, $A\leq N_G(T)$.
Let $Q=q^m$. We identify $V$ with $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ and use the quadratic form $v\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_Q/\mathbb{F}_q}(v^{Q+1})$.
For $c\in\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}^*$, let $M_c(v)=cv$. We take $S_0=\{M_c:c^{Q+1}=1\}\leq\operatorname{SO}^-_{2m}(q)$.
Then, we have $|S_0|=Q+1$.
Choose a generator $M_\lambda$ of $S_0$.
Next, let $\sigma:V\to V$ satisfy $\sigma(v)=v^q$.
In a normal basis of $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, the matrix of $\sigma$ is a cycle of length $2m$.
Thus, $\det\sigma=-1$.
Therefore, $N_{\operatorname{SO}^-_{2m}(q)}(S_0)/S_0\cong C_m$.
Let $\chi_q$ be the quadratic character of $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$.
If $F$ is a Gram matrix, then $\chi_q(\det F)=-\chi_q((-1)^m)$.
Let $v=N_{\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}/\mathbb{F}_Q}(1-\lambda)$.
Then, $v=-\lambda^{-1}(1-\lambda)^2$ and $v^{(Q-1)/2}=(-1)^{(Q-1)/2}$.
Let $\operatorname{sn}:\operatorname{SO}(V)\to\mathbb{F}_q^*/(\mathbb{F}_q^*)^2$ be the spinor norm.
By \cite[Proposition 1.6.11(ii)]{BHR}, we have $\operatorname{sn}(M_\lambda)=N_{\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}/\mathbb{F}_q}(1-\lambda)\det F\cdot(\mathbb{F}_q^*)^2$.
From the preceding norm and discriminant formulas, we obtain that
$$
 \chi_q(N_{\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}/\mathbb{F}_q}(1-\lambda)\det F)
 =(-1)^{(Q-1)/2}\chi_q(\det F)
 =\chi_q((-1)^m)\chi_q(\det F)=-1.
$$
Thus, $S=S_0^2$ has index $2$ in $S_0$.
For each $g\in N_{\operatorname{SO}(V)}(S_0)$, choose $h\in S_0$ with $\operatorname{sn}(hg)=1$.
Then, $hg\in N_{\widetilde G}(S)$ induces the field automorphism induced by $g$.
Since $C_{\operatorname{SO}(V)}(S)=S_0$, every element normalizing $S$ also normalizes $S_0$.
Consequently,
$N_{\widetilde G}(S)/S\cong N_G(T)/T\cong C_m$.

By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for the maximal singular line stabilizer, $\widetilde A$ stabilizes a line $\Lambda\leq V$.
A Singer multiplier stabilizing $\Lambda$ is $\pm I$ and has trivial projective image.
Hence, $A\cap T=1$, and $A$ is cyclic with $|A|\mid m$.
We take a primitive divisor $h\geq2m-1>m$ of $q^{2m-2}-1$.
Next, we choose a nondegenerate subspace $U\leq V$ of minus type with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2m-2$. Let $W=U^\perp$, so $V=U\perp W$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=2$.
The space $U$ has minus type and $W$ is hyperbolic.
Take $B=C_h$ irreducible on $U$ and trivial on $W$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AB^x$ is a subgroup.
By Sylow counting, $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
Let $a\in A$ have odd prime order $r$.
Since $r\mid m$ and $|N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)|$ divides $2m-2$, we have $[a,B^x]=1$.
If $r=p$, then $C_G(B^x)$ has order prime to $p$ and cannot contain $a$. We obtain a contradiction.
For $r\ne p$, every eigenvalue of the Singer companion of order $r$ has multiplicity $2m/r$ by Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-even}.
In the centralizer torus of $B^x$, an eigenvalue has multiplicity greater than $2m/r$. We obtain a contradiction.
Thus, $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group.
For odd $m$, we have $|A|\mid m$.
As $A$ is a $2$-group, we have $A=1$.

Let $m$ be even.
Since $q^m+1\equiv2\pmod4$, we have $-I_V\notin\widetilde G$ and $Z(\widetilde G)=1$.
An involution $t\in N_{\widetilde G}(S)$ has form $v\mapsto c v^{q^m}$,
with $c^{q^m+1}=1$.
By Hilbert 90, choose $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}^*$ with $c=a^{1-q^m}$.
For the multiplier $h:v\mapsto av$ in $\operatorname{GL}_{2m}(q)$, we have $t^h:v\mapsto v^{q^m}$.
Both eigenspaces of $t$ have dimension $m$.
If $|A|\geq4$, then the involution $t\in A$ lies in $A^2$.
Since $|N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)|$ divides $2m-2$, the image of $A$ in this quotient has order at most $2$.
Thus, the image of $t\in A^2$ is trivial, and $t$ centralizes $B^x$.
For $x\in G$ with $AB^x\leq G$, choose $\widetilde x\in\widetilde G$ satisfying $\pi(\widetilde x)=x$.
Let $U_x=\widetilde x^{-1}U$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U_x=2m-2$.
Since $t$ centralizes the irreducible subgroup $B^x$ on $U_x$ and $t^2=I_V$, we have $t|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$ or $-I_{U_x}$.
Thus, an eigenspace of $t$ has dimension at least $2m-2>m$.
This contradicts the dimension $m$ of both eigenspaces. Therefore, $|A|\leq2$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $m$ is even, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Let $k=m-1$. Then, $k\geq3$ is odd.
We choose $V=E\perp D$ with $E=U\oplus U^*$ of plus type and $D$ anisotropic.
For the dimensions, we require $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=k$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}D=2$.
On $E=U\oplus U^*$, let
$$
 W=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I_k&S\\0&I_k\end{pmatrix}:
 S\in M_k(\mathbb{F}_q),\ S^{\mathsf T}=-S\right\}.
$$
Next, identify $U$ with $\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
For this field structure, let $H=\{M_{\lambda^2}:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^k}^*\}$, where $M_\lambda(u)=\lambda u$.
To act on $E=U\oplus U^*$, we use $\iota:\operatorname{GL}(U)\to\operatorname{SO}(E)$ with $\iota(g)=\operatorname{diag}(g,g^{-\mathsf T})$.
Then, we have $|H|=(q^k-1)/2$.
Since $H$ contains an element of primitive prime order for $q^k-1$, we have $H$ irreducible on $U$.
For $g\in\operatorname{GL}(U)$, the spinor norm of $\iota(g)$ is $\det(g)\cdot(\mathbb{F}_q^*)^2$.
As $\det(M_{\lambda^2})=N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^k}/\mathbb{F}_q}(\lambda)^2$, every element of $\iota(H)$ has spinor norm $1$.
Thus, $B=W\rtimes\iota(H)$ lies in $\widetilde G$ and fixes $D$ pointwise.
We have $O_p(B)=W$ and $\sum_{w\in W}\operatorname{im}(w-I_V)=U$.
Because $H$ is irreducible on $U$, we have $V^B=D$.
Thus, every $g\in N_{\widetilde G}(B)$ stabilizes $E,D$ and $U$.
Let $g\in N_{\widetilde G}(B)$ be an involution.
For the action on $U$, let $\nu:\operatorname{Stab}_{\operatorname{O}(E)}(U)\to\operatorname{GL}(U)$ send $h$ to $h|_U$. Its kernel is $W$.
Next, let $\sigma:U\to U$ satisfy $\sigma(u)=u^q$ in $U=\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$.
Since $\nu(g|_E)$ normalizes $H$, it normalizes $C_{\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_q}(U)}(H)=\mathbb{F}_{q^k}$.
Thus,
$g|_E\in W\rtimes\iota(\{M_\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^k}^*\}\rtimes\langle \sigma\rangle)$.
Because $k$ is odd and $g^2=I_V$, the image of $g$ in $\langle \sigma\rangle\cong C_k$ is trivial.
Hence, $\nu(g|_E)=M_\lambda$ with $\lambda^2=1$, so $g|_E=w\iota(\pm I_U)$ for some $w\in W$.
As both scalars act trivially on $W$, we have $I_E=(g|_E)^2=w^2$.
Since $|W|$ is odd, $w=1$, and we obtain that $g|_E=\pm I_E$.
As $\det(g)=\det(g|_E)=1$, we have $g|_D\in\operatorname{SO}(D)$.
Because $g^2=I_V$ and $\operatorname{SO}(D)$ is cyclic, we have $g|_D=I_D$ or $-I_D$.
Thus, $\dim\ker(g+I_V)\in\{0,2,2m-2,2m\}$.
No listed negative eigenspace dimension equals $m$.
For every involution $t\in N_{\widetilde G}(S)$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(t+I_V)=m$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:orthogonal-minus-all
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:orthogonal-minus-all}
Let $m\geq3$ and let $q$ be any prime power.
Then, $\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_{2m}(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $m\geq4$, we obtain the conclusion from Theorems \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-even} and \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}.
For $m=3$, we use $\mathrm{P}\Omega^-_6(q)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(q)$ and Corollary \ref{cor:all-unitary}.
head: environment

label: lem:orthogonal-plus-odd-subgroup
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonal-plus-odd-subgroup}
Let $q$ be even and let $m\geq4$ be even. Let $G=\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$.
On $V=\mathbb{F}_q^{2m}$, $G$ contains a subgroup $H$ of odd order
such that $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)\leq m-1$
for every involution $t\in N_G(H)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We take $H=\langle x,y\mid x^9=y^3=1,\ yxy^{-1}=x^4\rangle$, of order $27$.
For its representation, let $E_0=\mathbb{F}_{64}$ and $D_0=\mathbb{F}_4$, viewed as vector spaces over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
On these spaces, we use $Q_E(v)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_8/\mathbb{F}_2}(v^9)$ and $Q_D(v)=v^3$.
Next, choose $\lambda\in E_0^*$ and $\eta\in D_0^*$ of orders $9$ and $3$.
Using these elements, let $\rho_0:H\to\operatorname{O}(E_0\perp D_0)$ satisfy
$\rho_0(x)(v,w)=(\lambda v,w)$ and
$\rho_0(y)(v,w)=(v^4,\eta w)$.
Suppose that $\rho_0(x^a y^b)=I$ with $0\leq a<9$ and $0\leq b<3$.
As $\rho_0(x^a y^b)|_{D_0}=M_{\eta^b}$, we have $\eta^b=1$.
Because $|\eta|=3$ and $0\leq b<3$, we obtain that $b=0$.
Since $|\rho_0(x)|=9$, we then have $a=0$.
Thus, $\rho_0$ is faithful.
Moreover, $E_0,D_0$ have minus type, so $E_0\perp D_0$ has plus type.
Next, let $E=E_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_2}\mathbb{F}_q$ and $D=D_0\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_2}\mathbb{F}_q$.
For $X=E_0,D_0$, we choose a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
Let $B_X(v,w)=Q_X(v+w)-Q_X(v)-Q_X(w)$, where $Q_{E_0}=Q_E$ and $Q_{D_0}=Q_D$.
For $a_1,\ldots,a_d\in\mathbb{F}_q$, we use the quadratic form on $X\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_2}\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfying
$$
 Q_{X,q}\left(\sum_{i=1}^d a_i(v_i\otimes1)\right)
 =\sum_{i=1}^d a_i^2Q_X(v_i)+\sum_{i<j}a_i a_jB_X(v_i,v_j).
$$
We choose $V=E\perp D\perp C$ with these forms on $E,D$.
Moreover, the space $C$ has plus type and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}C=2m-8$.
Let $\rho:H\to\operatorname{O}(V)$ satisfy $\rho(h)=(\rho_0(h)\otimes I_{\mathbb{F}_q})\oplus I_C$.
Then, we identify $H$ with $\rho(H)$. Since $|H|$ is odd, $H\leq\Omega(V)=G$.

Let $W\leq V$ satisfy $\rho(h)W=W$ for $h\in H$, and let $J\leq H$.
Let $[W,J]=\sum_{j\in J}(\rho(j)-I)W$ and $W^J=\{w\in W:\rho(j)w=w\text{ for all }j\in J\}$.
From the characteristic centre $Z(H)=\langle x^3\rangle$, we have $[V,Z(H)]=E$ and $[V^{Z(H)},H]=D$.
We also have $V^H=C$.
Thus, every $g\in N_G(H)$ satisfies $gE=E,\ gD=D,\ gC=C$.
Let $\rho_D:H\to\operatorname{O}(D)$ send $h$ to $\rho(h)|_D$.
Since $\ker\rho_D=\langle x\rangle$, we have $g^{-1}\langle x\rangle g=\langle x\rangle$ for $g\in N_G(H)$.
Suppose that $g^{-1}yg\langle x\rangle=y^{-1}\langle x\rangle$.
Then, $g^{-1}xg=x^a$ and $g^{-1}yg=x^by^{-1}$, with $(a,9)=1$.
From $g^{-1}(yxy^{-1})g=g^{-1}x^4g$, we have $x^{7a}=x^{4a}$. This contradicts $(a,9)=1$.

Let $t\in N_G(H)$ be an involution.
Because the preceding computation forbids $t^{-1}yt\langle x\rangle=y^{-1}\langle x\rangle$, we have $t^{-1}yt\langle x\rangle=y\langle x\rangle$.
As $\ker\rho_D=\langle x\rangle$, the restriction $t|_D$ centralizes $\rho_D(H)=C_3$.
Since $C_{\operatorname{O}(D)}(\rho_D(H))$ is a torus of odd order,
$t|_D=I_D$.
Also, $\operatorname{rank}(t|_E-I_E)\leq3$ and
$\operatorname{rank}(t|_C-I_C)\leq m-4$.
Therefore, $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)\leq m-1$.
head: environment

label: thm:orthogonal-plus
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:orthogonal-plus}
Let $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ with $m\geq4$.
Suppose that $m$ is odd or $m\geq6$ with $(m,q)\ne(6,2)$ or $m=4$ with $q\geq4$.
Then, $G$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] $K=\widetilde A R$ is a proper subgroup of $\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$.
\end{itemize}
Let $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$ and $k=m-1$.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_q^{2m}$ with quadratic form $\mathcal Q$ and polar form $\beta(v,w)=\mathcal Q(v+w)-\mathcal Q(v)-\mathcal Q(w)$.
Next, let $\pi:\Omega^+_{2m}(q)\to G$ be the quotient map.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable and let $\widetilde A=\pi^{-1}(A)$.
Now, let $P_2$ be the maximal stabilizer of a totally singular $X\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}X=2$.
We have $P_2Y\ne G$ for every $Y<G$
\cite[Tables A.6--A.7]{LiXia}\cite[Theorem 4.2]{King2005}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we obtain that $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Moreover, for each maximal subgroup $M<G$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:max} an element $x\in G$ with $A\leq M^x$.

For odd $q$, choose the maximal stabilizer of $V=V_1\perp V_2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_1=3$.
For even $q$ and $m\geq5$, choose such a stabilizer with $V_1$ of minus type and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_1=4$ \cite[Theorem 4.3]{King2005}.
For $m=4$ and even $q$, use the maximal stabilizer of $\{V_1,V_2\}$ \cite[Theorem 4.7]{King2005}.
Both $V_i$ have minus type and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_i=4$.
Let $M$ be the chosen decomposition stabilizer.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose $y\in G$ with $A\leq M^y$.
We choose a lift $\widetilde y\in\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ of $y$ and replace $V_i$ by $\widetilde y^{-1}V_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Then, $\widetilde A$ stabilizes the chosen decomposition.
For $m=4$ and even $q$, each $g\in\widetilde A$ satisfies
$(gV_1,gV_2)=(V_1,V_2)$ or $(V_2,V_1)$.
If $p\nmid|B|$ and $K=AB^x$ is a subgroup, then each $p$-subgroup $P\leq K$ has $P^g\leq A$ for some $g\in K$.
Choose $\widetilde g\in\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ with $\pi(\widetilde g)=g$. Then, $\pi^{-1}(P)$ stabilizes $\widetilde gV_1\perp\widetilde gV_2$.

We choose a nondegenerate subspace $E\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}E=2k$. Let $D=E^\perp$, so $V=E\perp D$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}D=2$.
The space $E$ has minus type and $D$ is anisotropic.
On these spaces, choose Singer tori $T_E\leq\operatorname{SO}(E)$ and $T_D\leq\operatorname{SO}(D)$ with $|T_E|=q^k+1$ and $|T_D|=q+1$.
For their product, let $R_0=\{h_E\oplus h_D:h_E\in T_E,\ h_D\in T_D\}$ and $R=R_0\cap\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$.
If $q$ is odd, then $[R_0:R]=2$. If $q$ is even, then $R=R_0$.
Let $\pi_E:R\to\operatorname{O}(E)$ be $g\mapsto g|_E$.
For odd $q$, the spinor norm is surjective on $T_D$. Thus, every $h_E\in T_E$ has $h_D\in T_D$ with $h_E\oplus h_D\in R$.
We identify $E$ with $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2k}}$.
Then, $\pi_E(R)=\{M_\lambda:\lambda^{q^k+1}=1\}$ with $M_\lambda(v)=\lambda v$.
We have $|\pi_E(R)|=q^k+1$.
Let $\overline R$ be the image of $R$ in $G$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $A\overline R^x$ is a subgroup.
As $A\overline R^x\ne G$, we have $A\overline R^x<G$.
Choose a lift $\widetilde x\in\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ of $x$.
The inverse image of $A\overline R^x$ under $\pi$ is $K=\widetilde A R^{\widetilde x}<\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$.
Then, we replace $K,\widetilde A,A$ by
$\widetilde xK\widetilde x^{-1}$, $\widetilde x\widetilde A\widetilde x^{-1}$ and $xAx^{-1}$.
Also, replace $V_i$ by $\widetilde xV_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Then, $K=\widetilde A R$, and $\widetilde A$ stabilizes the transported decomposition.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] The only nonzero proper $R$-submodules of $V$ are $E$ and $D$.
\end{itemize}
Firstly, we show that $gE=E$ and $gD=D$ for $g\in K$.
We choose $c_0\in R$ in the primitive-divisor class prescribed in
\cite[Lemma 2.9 and Table 4]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
Let $\mathcal E=\{(4,2),\allowbreak(4,3),\allowbreak(4,4),\allowbreak(4,5),\allowbreak(5,2),\allowbreak(6,2),\allowbreak(7,2),\allowbreak(10,2),\allowbreak(11,2)\}$.
For $(m,q)\notin\mathcal E$, $c_0$ has order greater than $4k+1$ and an absolute primitive prime divisor.
The hypotheses omit $(4,2),(4,3),(6,2)$.
For $(m,q)\in\mathcal E$ under the hypotheses, we choose $\ell_0$ from
$$
 (m,q,\ell_0)\in\{(4,4,13),(4,5,7),(5,2,17),(7,2,13),(10,2,19),(11,2,41)\}.
$$
We have $\ell_0\mid|c_0|$ and $\operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(p)=2fk$, where $q=p^f$.
For $(m,q)\notin\mathcal E$, choose an absolute primitive divisor $\ell_0\mid|c_0|$.
We take $C_0=\langle c_0^{|c_0|/\ell_0}\rangle$.
Since $\operatorname{ord}_{\ell_0}(q)=2k$, $C_0$ acts irreducibly on $E$ and trivially on $D$.
Thus, $D$ is the unique $C_0$-submodule of $V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}D=2$.
The image $\{g|_D:g\in R\}$ is irreducible on $D$.
Thus, the only nonzero proper $R$-submodules of $V$ are $E$ and $D$.
Let $H\leq\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ with $R\leq H$, and suppose that $H$ acts reducibly on $V$.
As $H$ consists of isometries, we have $gE=E$ and $gD=D$ for every $g\in H$.

Suppose that $m,q$ are odd.
Suppose that $R\leq N_{\Omega^+_{2m}(q)}(\Omega_m(q^2))$, where $\Omega_m(q^2)$ acts linearly over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Since $\ell_0$ is odd and the normalizer quotient has order $2$, we have $C_0\leq\Omega_m(q^2)$.
Since $C_0$ acts irreducibly on $E$, its ring of commuting $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear maps is a field.
This field contains $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ and $\{r|_E:r\in R\}$, so $r|_E$ commutes with $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ for every $r\in R$.
For such $r$, choose $\tau_r\in\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{q^2}/\mathbb{F}_q)$ with $r(av)=\tau_r(a)r(v)$ for $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ and $v\in V$.
For $0\ne e\in E$, the restriction gives $a\,r(e)=r(ae)=\tau_r(a)r(e)$.
Since $r(e)\ne0$, we obtain that $\tau_r(a)=a$ for all $a\in\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Thus, $r$ is $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-linear on $V$.
Consequently, $r|_D=I_D$ or $-I_D$, as $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}D=1$.
As $|\{r|_D:r\in R\}|=q+1>2$, we obtain a contradiction.
Thus, $R\nleq N_{\Omega^+_{2m}(q)}(\Omega_m(q^2))$.
At $(m,q)=(7,2)$, the torus contains an element of order $195$.
The extra groups $A_{16}$, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(13)$ and $G_2(3).2$ do not.
A permutation of order $195$ requires at least $13+5+3$ points,
so $A_{16}$ has no element of order $195$.
Neither $|\operatorname{PSL}_2(13)|$ nor $|G_2(3).2|$ is divisible by $5$.
At $(m,q)=(10,2)$, the torus $R$ contains an element of order $513$.
The $3$-parts of $|\operatorname{PSL}_2(19)|$ and $|J_1|$ are smaller than $27$, so neither group contains $R$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] $K$ stabilizes $E$ and $D$.
\end{itemize}
For even $m$, we also consider $K\leq M_U=N_{\Omega^+_{2m}(q)}(\operatorname{SU}_m(q))$.
Let $J_1=K\cap\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$, so $J_1\unlhd K$.
The subgroup $J_1$ contains the torus of type $(k,1)$ and order $q^k+1$.
For ordered summands, a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$ is indecomposable by Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}.
It cannot stabilize the displayed decomposition.
For the unordered pair $\{V_1,V_2\}$, both summands have dimension $4$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
Since $q\geq4$, we have $|\operatorname{SU}_4(q)|_2=q^6>8q^4$.
The decomposition stabilizer has $2$-part at most $8q^4$.
Therefore, $J_1<\operatorname{SU}_m(q)$.
For $(m,q)\ne(4,5)$, $J_1$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$
\cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
Under the hypotheses, $(m,q)\notin\{(6,2),(4,2),(4,3)\}$.
At $(4,5)$, the extra $A_7$ has no element of order $63$.
As $C_0$ acts irreducibly on the complementary $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$-space of dimension $k$, the unitary line is unique.
Because $J_1\unlhd K$, $K$ stabilizes that line.
The underlying $\mathbb{F}_q$-space is $D$, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}D=2$.

For $m=4$, we compare $\overline R$ with the listed maximal subgroups $M<G$ of spin or adjoint unitary type.
Let $V=\mathbb{F}_q^8$.
For the spin type, we use the spin representation $\rho_s:\operatorname{Spin}_7(q)\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$.
For the unitary type, we use the adjoint representation $\rho_u:\operatorname{PSU}_3(q)\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$.
The unitary type requires $q\equiv2\pmod3$ \cite[Table 8.50]{BHR}.
Suppose that $\overline R\leq M$, and let $\overline C_0=\pi(C_0)$.
For the spin type, we have $|C_M(\overline C_0)|\leq q^3+1$.
For odd $q\geq5$, we have $|\overline R|=(q^3+1)(q+1)/4>q^3+1$.
For even $q\geq4$, we have $|\overline R|=(q^3+1)(q+1)>q^3+1$.
For the adjoint unitary type, we have $|C_M(\overline C_0)|\leq2(q^2-q+1)$.
Thus, $\overline R\nleq M$ for either type.
At $q=5$, the other listed groups have no element of odd order $63$.
For $A_{10}$, this follows by cycle lengths, and for $\operatorname{Sz}(8)$
by its order.
In $\Omega^+_8(2)$, an element $t$ of order $7$ has $2$ reciprocal irreducible constituents of dimension $3$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
Its fixed space is hyperbolic of dimension $2$.
Thus, $9\nmid|C_{\Omega^+_8(2)}(t)|$.
For a central quotient $\rho:\widetilde H\to H$ with $|\ker\rho|=2$, we have $|\rho(h)|=|h|$ whenever $h\in\widetilde H$ has odd order.
Therefore, $gE=E$ and $gD=D$ for $g\in K$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] We have $J\cap H<H$ for each nonabelian relative group $H=\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ or $\operatorname{SU}_b(Q)$.
\end{itemize}
For odd $q$, let
$K_0=\{g\in K:\det(g|_E)=\det(g|_D)=1\}$.
For even $q$ and $X=E,D$, let $D_X:\operatorname{O}(X)\to\mathbb{F}_2$ send $h$ to $\operatorname{rank}(h-I_X)\pmod2$.
We use $K_0=\{g\in K:D_E(g|_E)=D_D(g|_D)=0\}$.
Then, $K_0\unlhd K$ and $[K:K_0]\leq2$.
Let $\pi_E:K_0\to\operatorname{O}(E)$ be $g\mapsto g|_E$,
and let $J=\pi_E(K_0)$.
We have $\pi_E(R)\leq J$ and $|\pi_E(R)|=q^k+1$.
Moreover, $\ker\pi_E\leq\{I_E\}\times\operatorname{SO}(D)$ is central and has order prime to $p$.
By Bereczky's theorem \cite{Bereczky,Brookfield2014}, we use successive relative orthogonal groups $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ and unitary groups $\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ with odd $b$.
At each step, let $H_{\rm rel}\leq\operatorname{O}(E)$ be the chosen relative subgroup containing $\pi_E(C_0)$.
For $H_{\rm rel}$, let $F_0$ be its scalar field.
Next, let $H_{\rm lin}\unlhd H_{\rm rel}$ be its subgroup of $F_0$-linear maps.
Since $[H_{\rm rel}:H_{\rm lin}]\leq2k<\ell_0$, the image of $\pi_E(C_0)$ in $H_{\rm rel}/H_{\rm lin}$ is trivial.
Hence, $h|_E(av)=a(h|_E)(v)$ for $h\in C_0$, $a\in F_0$ and $v\in E$.
As $C_0$ acts irreducibly on $E$, we have $C_{\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{F}_q}(E)}(\{h|_E:h\in C_0\})\cong\mathbb{F}_{q^{2k}}$.
It contains $\pi_E(R)$ and $F_0$.
Thus, every element of $\pi_E(R)$ is $F_0$-linear.

By Lemmas \ref{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup} and \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, each relative orthogonal or special unitary group contains an indecomposable $p$-subgroup on $E$, trivial on $D$.
Thus, the indecomposable summands have dimensions $2k,1,1$.
By Krull--Schmidt, no direct summand has the required dimension $3$ or $4$.
For the unordered pair, choose $V=V_1\perp V_2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_i=4$ for $i=1,2$.
Let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of the relative group.
Let $\sigma:P\to S_2$ satisfy $\sigma(g)(i)=j$ when $gV_i=V_j$, and let $P_0=\ker\sigma$.
If some $g\in P$ satisfies $gV_1=V_2$, then $g^2\in P_0$.
The map $v\mapsto v+gv$ is an isomorphism $V_1^{P_0}\to V^P$.
Thus, $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_i^{P_0}=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V^P$ for $i=1,2$.
For a Sylow subgroup of the relative $\operatorname{SU}_3(q)$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_i^{P_0}=4$.
Thus, $P_0=1$. We obtain a contradiction.
For a Sylow subgroup of the relative $\Omega^-_6(q)$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V_i^{P_0}=3$ for $i=1,2$.
For $i=1,2$, let $P_i=\{g|_{V_i}:g\in P_0\}\leq\operatorname{O}(V_i)$.
Each $P_i$ fixes a hyperplane pointwise.
For each $i$, let $Y_i\leq V_i$ be a hyperplane fixed pointwise by $P_i$ and choose $0\ne v_i\in Y_i^\perp$.
As each $g\in P_i$ fixes $Y_i$ pointwise and is an isometry, it has the form $g(w)=w+a\beta(w,v_i)v_i$ for some $a\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
Since $g$ is an isometry, $a+a^2\mathcal Q(v_i)=0$.
This equation has at most $2$ solutions, so $|P_i|\leq2$.
Thus, $|P|\leq8$. This contradicts $|P|=q^6$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 5.} ] $R$ is normal in $K$ and $N_G(\overline R)/\overline R\cong C_{2k}$.
\end{itemize}
We check the relative small exceptions under the hypotheses on $(m,q)$.
For odd $m$, the integer $k$ is even.
At a relative unitary stage of odd dimension $b\geq3$, the field has order $Q=q^{k/b}$.
Since $k$ is even and $b$ is odd, $k/b$ is even.
Thus, $Q\geq q^2$ and $Q\notin\{2,3\}$.
For a relative $\Omega^-_4(Q)$ stage, we have $Q\geq q^2$.
By Dickson's theorem, the proper intersection lies in the nonsplit torus normalizer.
For even $m\geq6$, a relative $\operatorname{SU}_5(2)$ stage requires $(m,q)=(6,2)$.
The hypotheses omit that pair.
For $m=4$, both relative exceptions of dimension $6$ have $q<4$.

Let $H$ be the last normal intersection.
Since $H$ lies in the relative normalizer of $\pi_E(R)$, the Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup of $\pi_E(R)$ is the unique Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup of $H$.
By the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-odd-singer}, the Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup is characteristic in each successive normal intersection.
Let $R_{\ell_0}$ be the Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup of $R$.
By the preceding argument, $J$ has a unique Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup $J_{\ell_0}$.
As $\ker\pi_E$ is central and $\ell_0\nmid|\ker\pi_E|$, the group $\pi_E^{-1}(J_{\ell_0})$ has a unique Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup.
This subgroup is $R_{\ell_0}$, and every Sylow $\ell_0$-subgroup of $K_0$ lies in $\pi_E^{-1}(J_{\ell_0})$.
Thus, $R_{\ell_0}$ is characteristic in $K_0$.
Since $K_0\unlhd K$, we have $R_{\ell_0}\unlhd K$.
Moreover, $C_{\Omega^+_{2m}(q)}(R_{\ell_0})=R$.
Because $R\leq K$, we have $R\unlhd K$ and $A\leq N_G(\overline R)$.
In the field model $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2k}}$, the companion maps are
$v\mapsto v^{q^j}$.
For odd $q$, the determinant of $v\mapsto v^{q^j}$ on $E$ is $(-1)^j$.
For even $q$, its Dickson invariant is $j\pmod2$.
The companion map on $D$ must have determinant $(-1)^j$ or Dickson invariant $j\pmod2$, respectively.
For odd $q$, we multiply by $h_D\in T_D$ so that the map on $V$ has spinor norm $1$.
Therefore, $N_G(\overline R)/\overline R\cong C_{2k}$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 6.} ] $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid2(m-1)$.
\end{itemize}
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for $P_1$, $\widetilde A$ stabilizes a singular line $\Lambda\leq V$.
Since $D$ is anisotropic, we choose $v=e+d\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}$ with $0\ne e\in E$ and $d\in D$.
For $g\in\widetilde A\cap R$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{2k}}^*$ be its multiplier on $E$.
As $g\Lambda=\Lambda$, we have $gv=cv$ for some $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$.
Taking the projection on $E$, we obtain that $\lambda e=ce$, so $\lambda=c$.
Because $\lambda^{q^k+1}=1$, we have $c^2=1$.
Thus, $g|_E=I_E$ or $-I_E$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for a maximal isotropic parabolic, $\widetilde A$ stabilizes a totally singular $W\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=m$.
Suppose that $g\in\widetilde A\cap R$ has $g|_E=cI_E$ and $g|_D\ne cI_D$.
Since $g$ is semisimple and $c$ is not an eigenvalue of $g|_D$, we would have $W=(W\cap E)\oplus(W\cap D)$.
As $D$ is anisotropic and $W$ is totally singular, we would obtain that $W\cap D=0$ and $W\leq E$.
This contradicts $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=m$, because $E$ has Witt index $m-2$.
Thus, every element of $\widetilde A\cap R$ is a scalar on $V$.
Hence,
$A\cap\overline R=1, A\cong C_a, a\mid2(m-1)$.

Since $(m,q)\ne(6,2)$, we choose a primitive prime $\ell$ of $q^m-1$ by Zsigmondy's theorem.
We take $B=C_\ell$ in the corresponding linear torus of $G$.
As $\ell\geq m+1$, we have $\ell\nmid|A|$.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $x\in G$ with $L=AB^x\leq G$.
As $A$ and $B^x$ are abelian, $L$ is metabelian by It\^o's theorem.
If $\ell\mid|L'|$, then $B^x$ is the unique Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $L'$
and is normal in $L$.
Otherwise, $AL'$ is an $\ell$-free subgroup containing the Hall
subgroup $A$, so $AL'=A$.
Then, $A\unlhd L$.
Because $\ell\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(A)|$, the subgroup $B^x$ centralizes $A$.
Thus, $B^x\unlhd L$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 7.} ] $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group.
\end{itemize}
Let $r$ be an odd prime dividing $|A|$, and choose $c\in A$ of order $r$.
Since $r\mid m-1$ and $(r,2m)=1$, the element $c$ centralizes $B^x$.
Choose a lift $\widetilde c\in\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ of $c$ with $|\widetilde c|=r$.
Choose $\widetilde B_x\leq\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ of order $\ell$ with projective image $B^x$.
For $b\in\widetilde B_x$, the commutator $[\widetilde c,b]$ is a central element of $2$-power order.
Since $|\widetilde c|=r$ and this commutator is central, we have $[\widetilde c,b]^r=[\widetilde c^r,b]=1$.
As $r$ is odd, we obtain that $[\widetilde c,b]=1$.
For odd $m$, $\widetilde B_x$ has distinct reciprocal constituents $U_1,U_2$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U_i=m$.
We have $C_{\operatorname{SO}(V)}(\widetilde B_x)\cong\mathbb{F}_{q^m}^*$.
Because $p\nmid q^m-1$, we have $r\ne p$.
A nonidentity multiplier has degree $e\mid m$ and $e\mid r-1$,
so $e$ is odd and $e\leq(r-1)/2$.
Each eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\widetilde c|_D$ belongs to $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}^*$ and satisfies $\lambda^{q+1}=1$.
If $e=1$, then a nontrivial eigenvalue $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$ has odd order and $\lambda^{q+1}=\lambda^2\ne1$.
If $e\geq3$, then $e$ is odd, so $\lambda\notin\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$.
Thus, no nontrivial eigenvalue of $\widetilde c|_{U_i}$ is an eigenvalue of $\widetilde c|_D$.
Consequently, its eigenspace on $V$ lies in $E$ and has dimension at least
$\frac m e\geq\frac{2m}{r-1}>\frac{2(m-1)}r$.
But the nontrivial Singer companion of $\widetilde c$ has eigenvalue multiplicity $2(m-1)/r$ on $E$.

For even $m$, we have $C_{\operatorname{SO}(V)}(\widetilde B_x)\cong\operatorname{GU}_2(q^{m/2})$.
We identify $V$ with $\mathbb{F}_{q^m}^2$, on which this group acts linearly.
The possible dimensions of $\ker(\widetilde c-I_V)$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ are $0,m,2m$.
For the Singer companion, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(\widetilde c-I_V)=2(m-1)/r+d$ with $d\in\{0,2\}$.
For $m\geq6$, we have $0<\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(\widetilde c-I_V)<m$.
For $m=4$, the only prime is $r=3$.
If $p\ne3$, then fixed dimension $4$ requires $3\mid q^2+1$. We obtain a contradiction.
If $p=3$, then the unitary unipotent has Jordan type $2^4$.
The companion has type $3^2 1^2$, so the types differ.
Thus, $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 8.} ] We have $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
For odd $q$, choose $H\leq G$ from Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer} with $|N_G(H)|$ odd.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ such that $AH^y$ is a subgroup.
As $A$ is a cyclic $2$-group and $|H|$ is odd, we obtain from Burnside's theorem that $H^y\unlhd AH^y$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(H^y)$ and $A=1$.
For even $q$ and odd $m$, the normalizer of $B^x$ is odd.
The torus in $N_G(B^x)$ has order $q^m-1$, and its automizer has order dividing $m$.
A map sending the $2$ reciprocal summands to each other has Dickson invariant $m\pmod2=1$.
Thus, this map lies outside $\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$.
Because $B^x\unlhd L$, we have $A\leq N_G(B^x)$.
The group $A$ is a $2$-group and $N_G(B^x)$ is odd, so $A=1$.

Finally, suppose that $q$ and $m$ are even and $A\ne1$.
Let $t$ be the involution of $A$.
The field companion of $t|_E$ is $v\mapsto v^{q^k}$.
For $s\in T_D$, we have $(t|_D)s(t|_D)^{-1}=s^{-1}$.
By Hilbert 90, we have $\operatorname{rank}(t|_E-I_E)=k$ and $\operatorname{rank}(t|_D-I_D)=1$.
Thus, $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)=m$.
Take $H$ from Lemma \ref{lem:orthogonal-plus-odd-subgroup}.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AH^x$ is a subgroup.
Its Sylow $2$-subgroup is cyclic.
By Burnside's theorem, $H^x\unlhd AH^x$.
Thus, $t\in N_G(H^x)$ and $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)\leq m-1$. This contradicts $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_V)=m$.
