label: thm:orthogonal-plus-small
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] If $K\leq N_G(\operatorname{GU}_6(2))$, then $J<\operatorname{SU}_6(2)$.
\end{itemize}
Firstly, let $G=\Omega^+_{12}(2)$ and let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
We use $P_2$ and the stabilizer of $V_1\perp V_2$ from Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus}.
For $V=\mathbb{F}_2^{12}$, we require $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}V_1=4$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}V_2=8$.
Take $R=C_{33}\times C_3$.
Choose $u\in G$ such that $K=AR^u$ is a subgroup.
Replace $A,K$ by $uAu^{-1},uKu^{-1}$, so $K=AR$.
For each $2$-subgroup $P\leq K$, we choose $V=W_1\perp W_2$ with $PW_i=W_i$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W_1=4$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W_2=8$.
Now, we consider the maximal subgroup $M_U=N_G(\operatorname{GU}_6(2))<G$ with $K\leq M_U$.
Let $K_0=K\cap\operatorname{GU}_6(2)$ and $J=K\cap\operatorname{SU}_6(2)$.
We have $K_0,J\unlhd K$ and $[K:K_0]\leq2$.
Since $\det(R)=C_3$, the map $\det:K_0\to\{a\in\mathbb{F}_4^*:a^3=1\}$ is surjective.
We have $Z(\operatorname{SU}_6(2))\leq J$ and $C_{33}\leq J$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_6(2)$ is indecomposable on $V$.
Since every $2$-subgroup of $K$ stabilizes a decomposition $W_1\perp W_2$, we have $J<\operatorname{SU}_6(2)$.
Thus, the additional possibility in \cite[Lemma 2.6]{GuralnickMalle2012} is
$J\leq M_E=3.M_{22}<\operatorname{SU}_6(2)$.
The central quotient sends $M_E$ onto $M_{22}$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] In the $3.M_{22}$ and $\operatorname{GU}_5(2)$ cases, $K$ normalizes $R$.
\end{itemize}
If $J/C_3=M_{22}$, then $J=3.M_{22}$.
The natural representation of $3.M_{22}$ of dimension $6$ is absolutely irreducible.
Thus, $C_{\operatorname{GU}_6(2)}(3.M_{22})=\{\lambda I_6:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_4^*,\ \lambda^3=1\}$.
Since $\det(\lambda I_6)=\lambda^6=1$, every element of this centralizer has determinant $1$.
Let $Z_0=Z(3.M_{22})$.
Let $\psi:\operatorname{Aut}(3.M_{22})\to\operatorname{Aut}(M_{22})$ satisfy $\psi(\alpha)(gZ_0)=\alpha(g)Z_0$.
As $3.M_{22}$ is perfect, $\psi$ is injective.
We have $|\operatorname{Out}(3.M_{22})|\leq2$ \cite{Atlas1985}.
Thus, $\det(N_{\operatorname{GU}_6(2)}(3.M_{22}))=1$. This contradicts $\det(R)=C_3$.
If $J/C_3<M_{22}$, then we choose $L\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$ with $J/C_3\leq L$.
Suppose that $J/C_3<L$.
Since every proper subgroup of $L$ with order divisible by $11$ lies in $C_{11}\rtimes C_5$, the group $J/C_3$ has a unique Sylow $11$-subgroup.
The central kernel $C_3$ then yields a unique Sylow $11$-subgroup $S$ of $J$.
As $J\unlhd K$ and $[K:J]\mid6$, we have $S\unlhd K$, and $S$ is Sylow in $K$.
Because $C_G(S)=R$, we obtain that $K\leq N_G(R)$.

Suppose that $J/C_3=L$.
Since the Schur multiplier of $L$ has order $2$, $J=C_3\times L$ \cite{Atlas1985}.
The characteristic derived subgroup $L$ is normal in $K$.
The nontrivial absolutely irreducible $L$-modules in characteristic $2$ have dimensions $5,5,10,12,12$ \cite[p.~7]{BrauerAtlas1995}.
Therefore, $L$ has no simple module of dimension $6$ over $\mathbb{F}_4$.
The $\mathbb{F}_4L$-module $\mathbb{F}_4^6$ has composition factors of dimensions $5$ and $1$.
A nonsplit extension of these factors has different socle and top dimensions.
As $\mathbb{F}_4^6$ is Hermitian self-dual, we have a direct sum of the $2$ factors.
The fixed line is unique and nondegenerate.
For a singular-line parabolic $P<\operatorname{GU}_6(2)$, we have $11\nmid|P|$.
Thus, $K$ stabilizes the unique $L$-fixed unitary line and its perpendicular complement.
Over $\mathbb{F}_2$, we choose $V=E\perp D$ with $E$ of minus type and $D$ anisotropic.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}E=10$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}D=2$.

For the decomposition $V=E\perp D$ stabilized by $K$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}E=10$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}D=2$.
Let
$$
 K_0=\{g\in K:g|_E\text{ and }g|_D\text{ are }\mathbb{F}_4\text{-linear}\}\unlhd K.
$$
For the relative exception in $\operatorname{GU}_5(2)$, let $L=\operatorname{PSL}_2(11)$ and $M=C_3\times L$.
By the relative subgroup classification, we have $\{g|_E:g\in K_0\}\leq M$.
Let $\pi_L:K_0\to L$ be the composite of $g\mapsto g|_E$
and $M\to L$, $(c,h)\mapsto h$.
If $\pi_L(K_0)<L$, then $\pi_L(K_0)\leq C_{11}\rtimes C_5$, so this image has a unique Sylow $11$-subgroup.
As $\ker\pi_L\leq C_3^2$ is central, $K_0$ has a unique Sylow $11$-subgroup $S$.
Since $K_0\unlhd K$ and $[K:K_0]\leq2$, we have $S\unlhd K$.
Because $C_G(S)=R$, we obtain that $K\leq N_G(R)$.
Suppose that $\pi_L(K_0)=L$.
As $[K:K_0]\leq2$ and $|\ker\pi_L|\mid9$, we have
$|K|\mid2\cdot9\cdot660=11880$.
Let $A_0=A\cap K_0$. Because $R\leq K_0$, we have $K_0=A_0R$.
As $\pi_L(R)=C_{11}$, the index of $\pi_L(A_0)$ in $L$ is $1$ or $11$.
Thus, $\pi_L(A_0)$ is $L$ or $A_5$.
The central kernel is a subgroup of $C_3^2$.
As the Schur multiplier of $A_5$ has order $2$, the inverse image in $A_0$
of an $A_5$ subgroup of $\pi_L(A_0)$ contains a subgroup isomorphic to $A_5$.

Next, we choose $V=(U\oplus U^*)\perp W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}U=5$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W=2$.
On this decomposition, take $B=C_{31}$ acting irreducibly on $U,U^*$ and trivially on the hyperbolic space $W$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AB^x$ is a subgroup.
As $31\nmid11880$ and $|A|\mid11880$, the Sylow $31$-count in $AB^x$ divides $11880$ and is $1$ modulo $31$.
Only the divisor $1$ has this property, so $B^x$ is normal.
Since $\operatorname{Aut}(B^x)$ is abelian and $A_5$ is perfect, the subgroup $A_5\leq A$ centralizes $B^x$.
For $U_x=x^{-1}U$ and $W_x=x^{-1}W$, the centralizer on $U_x\oplus U_x^*$ is $\operatorname{GL}_1(32)$.
Moreover, $\operatorname{SO}(W_x)=\operatorname{SO}_2^+(2)=1$.
Thus, $A_5\leq C_G(B^x)=C_{31}$, a contradiction.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $G=\Omega^+_{12}(2)$ and $K\leq N_G(R)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Suppose that $K\leq N_G(R)$.
By the argument for $P_1$ and the maximal isotropic parabolic in Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus}, we have $A\cap R=1$.
Thus, $A$ is cyclic with $|A|\mid10$.
At $(m,q)=(6,2)$, Zsigmondy's exception at exponent $6$ requires a different comparison.
We choose $V=U\perp W$ with $U,W$ of minus type.
For $U,W$, we require $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}U=8$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}W=4$.
Take $B=C_{17}\leq\Omega(U)$ irreducible on $U$ and trivial on $W$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x\leq G$.
The Sylow $17$-count divides $10$ and is $1$ modulo $17$.
Thus, $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
Suppose that $5\mid|A|$, and choose $a\in A$ with $|a|=5$.
Since $|N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)|$ divides $8$, the element $a$ centralizes $B^x$.
For $U_x=x^{-1}U$ and $W_x=x^{-1}W$, we have
$C_G(B^x)=C_{17}\times\Omega(W_x)$.
Thus, $a|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$.
In $N_G(R)$, the field companion of $a|_E$ has $2$ cycles of length $5$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}\ker(a|_E-I_E)=2$.
As $|\operatorname{SO}(D)|=3$, we also have $a|_D=I_D$.
Therefore, $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}\ker(a-I_V)=4$.
This contradicts $a|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$, because $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_2}U_x=8$.
Hence, $A$ is cyclic of $2$-power order.
Suppose that $A\ne1$, and let $t$ be its involution.
Take $H$ from Lemma \ref{lem:orthogonal-plus-odd-subgroup}.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $AH^x$ is a subgroup.
By Burnside's theorem, $H^x\unlhd AH^x$.
Thus, $t\in N_G(H^x)$.
The involution $t$ has rank $6$, but every involution in $N_G(H^x)$ has rank at most $5$.
We obtain a contradiction.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] $M$ stabilizes $V=E\perp D$ or normalizes $\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$.
\end{itemize}
Now, let $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega^+_8(3)$ and let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $\pi:\Omega^+_8(3)\to G$ be the quotient map and $\widetilde A=\pi^{-1}(A)$.
We use $P_2$ and the stabilizer of $V_1\perp V_2$ from Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus}. For every $Y<G$, we have $P_2Y\ne G$.
We have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}V_1=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}V_2=5$.
Since $\operatorname{SO}_3(3)$ and $\operatorname{SO}_5(3)$ are
of orders not divisible by $7$, we have $7\nmid|A|$.
The torus $R$ of signed type $(-3,-1)$ has order $56$
in $\Omega^+_8(3)$ and order $28$ projectively.
Let $\overline R=\pi(R)$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $u\in G$ such that $K=A\overline R^u$ is a subgroup.
Then, we choose a lift $\widetilde u\in\Omega^+_8(3)$ of $u$. Let $\widetilde K=\pi^{-1}(K)$.
Then, we replace $A,K$ by $uAu^{-1},uKu^{-1}$.
Correspondingly, we replace $\widetilde A,\widetilde K$ by $\widetilde u\widetilde A\widetilde u^{-1},\widetilde u\widetilde K\widetilde u^{-1}$ and $V_i$ by $\widetilde uV_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Then, $\widetilde K=\widetilde A R<\Omega^+_8(3)$, and $\widetilde A V_i=V_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Since $|R|=56$, we have $|\widetilde K|_3=|\widetilde A|_3$.
For every $3$-subgroup $P\leq\widetilde K$, Sylow's theorem permits a choice of $g\in\widetilde K$ with $P^g\leq\widetilde A$.
Thus, $P$ stabilizes $gV_1\perp gV_2$, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}gV_1=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}gV_2=5$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.9 and Table 4]{GuralnickMalle2012}, we choose a maximal subgroup $M<\Omega^+_8(3)$ with $\widetilde K\leq M$.
No line $L_0\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}L_0=1$ satisfies $rL_0=L_0$ for every $r\in R$.
In $\operatorname{Spin}_7(3)$, a primitive element of order $7$ has centralizer
order $28$, and the extra $2.\Omega^+_8(2)$ has centralizer at most $28$.
For an element $s\in\Omega^+_8(2)$ of order $7$, the module $\mathbb{F}_2^8$ has reciprocal constituents of dimension $3$.
The fixed space $\ker(s-I)$ is hyperbolic of dimension $2$.
Its orthogonal centralizer has order $14$, doubled at most in $2.\Omega^+_8(2)$.
As $R\leq\widetilde K\leq M$, we have $M\not\cong\operatorname{Spin}_7(3)$ and $M\not\cong2.\Omega^+_8(2)$.
Thus, $M$ stabilizes a nondegenerate decomposition $V=E\perp D$ or normalizes $\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$.
In the decomposition alternative, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}E=6$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}D=2$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 5.} ] If $M$ normalizes $\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$, then $|A|\mid192$ or $\widetilde K D=D$ for some nondegenerate $D\leq V$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}D=2$.
\end{itemize}
In the unitary case, let $K_0=\widetilde K\cap\operatorname{GU}_4(3)$
and $J=\widetilde K\cap\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$.
We have $[\widetilde K:K_0]\leq2$ and $[K_0:J]\leq2$.
For $\det:\operatorname{GU}_4(3)\cap\Omega^+_8(3)\to\{a\in\mathbb{F}_9^*:a^4=1\}$,
we have image $\{1,-1\}=C_2$ and $\det(R)=C_2$.
Since $R\leq K_0$, we have $C_{28}\leq J$ and $Z(\operatorname{SU}_4(3))=C_4\leq J$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, a Sylow $3$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$ is indecomposable on $V$.
Since every $3$-subgroup of $\widetilde K$ stabilizes a decomposition of dimensions $3$ and $5$, we have $J<\operatorname{SU}_4(3)$.
Thus, the exceptional projective images of $J$ are $A_7$ and $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$.

If the projective image of $J$ is $A_7$, then its derived subgroup satisfies $J'\cong2.A_7$.
By \cite[Proposition 4.5.5(ii)]{BHR}, we have $N_{\operatorname{CGU}_4(3)}(J')=J'\{\lambda I_4:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_9^*\}$.
Thus, we have $N_{\operatorname{GU}_4(3)}(J')=J'\{\lambda I_4:\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_9^*,\lambda^4=1\}$.
Since $J'$ is perfect and $\lambda^4=1$, every element of $N_{\operatorname{GU}_4(3)}(J')$ has determinant $1$. This contradicts $\det(R)=\{1,-1\}$.
If the projective image of $J$ is $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$, then the quotient $N_{\operatorname{GU}_4(3)}(J)/C_4$
has order at most $2|\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)|$
\cite[Proposition 4.5.6]{BHR}.
We have an image of $R$ of order $14$ in $N_{\operatorname{GU}_4(3)}(J)/C_4$.
As $K_0=A_0R$ with $A_0=\widetilde A\cap K_0$, the image of $A_0$ has index at most $14$ in a group containing $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$.
Every proper subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$ has index at least $21$
\cite{Atlas1985}.
Thus, the image of $A_0$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$. This contradicts $7\nmid|A_0|$.

A proper exceptional image containing $7$ lies in $\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$
or a smaller $C_7\rtimes C_3$ subgroup.
Thus, $|J|\mid4\cdot168$.
We have $[\widetilde K:K_0]\leq2$ and $[K_0:J]\leq2$. Since $|\ker\pi|=2$, we have $|K|\mid1344$.
As $7\nmid|A|$, we have $|A|\mid192$.
Suppose that $J$ stabilizes a nondegenerate unitary line $D_0$ over $\mathbb{F}_9$.
Let $C_7$ be the Sylow $7$-subgroup of $R$.
Because $C_7$ acts irreducibly on $D_0^\perp$ over $\mathbb{F}_9$, $D_0$ is the unique $C_7$-stable line.
As $C_7\leq J$ and $JD_0=D_0$, it follows that $D_0$ is the unique $J$-stable line.
For $g\in\widetilde K$, the relation $gJg^{-1}=J$ shows that $gD_0$ is $J$-stable.
Thus, $gD_0=D_0$ for every $g\in\widetilde K$.
The underlying $\mathbb{F}_3$-space $D$ has $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}D=2$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 6.} ] We have $|A|\mid192$.
\end{itemize}
We choose $V=E\perp D$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}E=6$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}D=2$.
For this decomposition, let $K_0=\{g\in\widetilde K:\det(g|_E)=\det(g|_D)=1\}\unlhd\widetilde K$,
$A_0=\widetilde A\cap K_0$ and $J=\{g|_E:g\in K_0\}\leq\operatorname{SO}(E)$.
Since $R\leq K_0$ and $\widetilde K=\widetilde A R$, we have $K_0=A_0R$.
The group $J$ contains the Singer torus $C_{28}$ in $\operatorname{SO}^-_6(3)$.
For the action on $E$, let $\pi_E:K_0\to J$ send $g$ to $g|_E$.
Restriction to $D$ is injective on $\ker\pi_E$ and takes values in $\Omega(D)$.
Since $|\Omega(D)|\leq2$, we have $|\ker\pi_E|\leq2$.
Let $J_0=J\cap\Omega^-_6(3)$. Then, $[J:J_0]\leq2$.
Under $\Omega^-_6(3)=\operatorname{SU}_4(3)/\langle -I\rangle$, the inverse image of $J_0$ contains $C_{28}$.
Suppose that $J_0=\Omega^-_6(3)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup}, choose a $3$-subgroup $P\leq J_0$ indecomposable on the $\mathbb{F}_3$-space $E$.
Since $|\ker\pi_E|\leq2$, a Sylow $3$-subgroup $\widehat P$ of $\pi_E^{-1}(P)$ maps isomorphically onto $P$.
Moreover, $\widehat P$ acts trivially on $D$, because $|\operatorname{SO}(D)|$ is $2$ or $4$.
Thus, the indecomposable $\mathbb{F}_3\widehat P$-summands of $V=E\perp D$ have dimensions $6,1,1$.
By Krull--Schmidt, no direct summand has dimension $3$.
This contradicts $\widehat P\leq\widetilde K$ and the decomposition property for its $3$-subgroups.
Therefore, $J_0<\Omega^-_6(3)$.

If the projective image of $J_0$ is $A_7$, then $J_0'\cong A_7$.
In this case, $E\cong\{(x_1,\ldots,x_7)\in\mathbb{F}_3^7:\sum_{i=1}^7x_i=0\}$ as an $\mathbb{F}_3J_0'$-module.
The group $J_0'$ acts by permuting the $7$ coordinates.
Moreover, the $\mathbb{F}_3J_0'$-module $E$ is absolutely irreducible \cite[Tables 4.2 and 8.34]{BHR}.
Thus, $C_{\operatorname{O}(E)}(J_0')=\{I_E,-I_E\}$.
Since $C_{\operatorname{Aut}(A_7)}(C_7)=C_7$, an element of order $7$ has centralizer
order at most $14$ in $N_{\operatorname{O}(E)}(J_0')$.
Thus, $N_{\operatorname{O}(E)}(J_0')$ cannot contain the Singer torus $C_{28}$.
If the projective image equals $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$, then the orthogonal normalizer
adds at most a factor $2$ \cite[Table 8.34]{BHR}.
Modulo the scalar $C_2$ of the orthogonal normalizer, the Singer image has order $14$.
As every proper subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$ has index at least $21$, the image of $A_0$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$.
This contradicts $7\nmid|A_0|$.
For proper exceptional images, we have $|J_0|\mid2\cdot168$.
For the unitary line stabilizer, identify $E$ with $\mathbb{F}_9^3$ over $\mathbb{F}_3$.
We also consider $C_{28}\leq M_3=C_4\times\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)<\operatorname{GU}_3(3)$
\cite[Tables 8.6--8.7]{BHR}\cite{Bereczky}.
A Sylow $3$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_3(3)$ is indecomposable on $E$.
On $V=E\perp D$, it has no direct summand of dimension $3$ over $\mathbb{F}_3$.
From the plane kernel and component indices, we have $|A|\mid192$ in both cases.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 7.} ] If $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega^+_8(3)$, then $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
We choose $V=(U\oplus U^*)\perp W$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}U=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_3}W=2$.
Take $B=C_{13}$ irreducible on $U,U^*$ and trivial on the hyperbolic space $W$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x\leq G$.
As only the divisor $1$ of $192$ is $1$ modulo $13$, we have $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
We have $C_G(B^x)=C_{13}$, and $N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)$ is cyclic of order dividing $6$.
Since $|A|\mid192$, we have $A\cap C_G(B^x)=1$.
Thus, the quotient map is injective on $A$, so $A$ is cyclic of order dividing $6$.
Suppose that $3\mid|A|$, and choose $a\in A$ with $|a|=3$.
Choose $\widetilde x\in\Omega^+_8(3)$ with $\pi(\widetilde x)=x$.
Let $\widetilde a\in\Omega^+_8(3)$ be the unique lift of $a$ with $|\widetilde a|=3$.
From the action on $\widetilde x^{-1}U$, $\widetilde x^{-1}U^*$ and $\widetilde x^{-1}W$, we obtain Jordan type $3^2 1^2$ for $\widetilde a$.
We take $C_5$ as in Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus} and choose $y\in G$ such that $AC_5^y$ is a subgroup.
By It\^o's theorem and the normality argument in Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus}, we have $C_5^y\unlhd AC_5^y$.
Because $|N_G(C_5^y)/C_G(C_5^y)|$ divides $4$, we have $a\in C_G(C_5^y)$.
Let $\widetilde C_5\leq\Omega^+_8(3)$ satisfy $\pi(\widetilde C_5)=C_5^y$ and $|\widetilde C_5|=5$.
As $|\ker\pi|=2$, we have $\widetilde a\in C_{\Omega^+_8(3)}(\widetilde C_5)$.
We have $C_{\operatorname{SO}_8(3)}(\widetilde C_5)\cong\operatorname{GU}_2(9)$.
A nonidentity unipotent in this group has Jordan type $2^4$ on $V=\mathbb{F}_3^8$.
Because $2^4\ne3^2 1^2$, we have $3\nmid|A|$.
Now, $|A|\mid2$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer}, choose an odd-order subgroup $H\leq G$ with $|N_G(H)|$ odd.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, we conclude that $A=1$.
head: environment

label: cor:orthogonal-plus-all
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:orthogonal-plus-all}
For every $m\geq4$ and every prime power $q$, the group
$\mathrm{P}\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$\mathrm{P}\Omega^+_{2m}(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We obtain the conclusion from Theorems \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus} and \ref{thm:orthogonal-plus-small}.
For $\Omega^+_8(2)$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
head: environment

label: lem:orthogonal-odd-singer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonal-odd-singer}
Let $G=\Omega_{2m+1}(q)$ with $m\geq3$ and $q$ odd.
If $A<G$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, then $A$ lies in a
Singer normalizer $N_G(T)$ with $|T|=(q^m+1)/2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the lemma into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] If $K\leq N_1^-$ and $(m,q)\ne(3,3)$, then $T^x$ is normal in $K$.
\end{itemize}
Let $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$, so $q=p^f$.
Let $P_2$ stabilize a totally singular $X\leq V=\mathbb{F}_q^{2m+1}$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}X=2$.
The subgroup $P_2$ is maximal.
For every $Y<G$, we have $P_2Y\ne G$
\cite[Table A.4]{LiXia}\cite[Theorem 4.2]{King2005}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we obtain that $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
For each maximal subgroup $M<G$, we choose $x\in G$ with $A\leq M^x$ by Lemma \ref{lem:max}.
Choose $M$ to stabilize an anisotropic space of dimension $2$ \cite[Theorem 4.3]{King2005}.
Then, $A$ stabilizes $V=U\perp W$, with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=2m-1$.
Take a Singer torus $T$ of order $(q^m+1)/2$.
We choose $x\in G$ such that $K=AT^x$ is a subgroup.
Since $AT^x\ne G$, we have $K<G$.
Let $L=V^{T^x}$ and $E=L^\perp$. Then, $V=E\perp L$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}E=2m$.
The group $T^x$ acts irreducibly on $E$, and $L$ is a nondegenerate line.
As $|K|_p=|A|_p$, every $p$-subgroup $P\leq K$ satisfies $P^g\leq A$ for some $g\in K$.
Thus, $P$ stabilizes $gU\perp gW$.

We choose a maximal subgroup $M_7<G$ with $K\leq M_7$.
Let $N_1^- =\operatorname{Stab}_G(L)$.
For $m\geq4$, the only maximal subgroup $M<G$ with $T^x\leq M$ is
$N_1^-$
\cite[Lemma 2.7]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
Thus, $M_7=N_1^-$ when $m\geq4$.
For $(m,q)\notin\{(3,3),(3,5)\}$, the primitive-part class in \cite[Lemma 2.7]{GuralnickMalle2012} exists and lies in $T$.
Suppose that $K\leq N_1^-$. Let $J=K\cap\Omega^-(E)\unlhd K$.
Then, $T^x\leq J$.
For $J$, we use the normal base intersections from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}.
At each relative $\Omega^-_{2a}(Q)$ stage, the intersection contains the Singer torus of order $(Q^a+1)/2=(q^m+1)/2$.
At each unitary stage $\operatorname{GU}_b(Q)$ with odd $b$, adjoin $Z(\operatorname{GU}_b(Q))$.
Since $v_2(Q^b+1)=v_2(Q+1)$, we then have the unitary Singer torus of order $Q^b+1$.
As $|Z(\operatorname{GU}_b(Q))|=Q+1$ and $p\nmid Q+1$, adjoining $Z(\operatorname{GU}_b(Q))$ does not change the Sylow $p$-subgroups.
By Lemmas \ref{lem:orthogonal-minus-two-subgroup} and \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}, each relative classical group contains an indecomposable $p$-subgroup on $E$.
On $V$, its indecomposable summands have dimensions $2m$ and $1$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
Thus, there is no direct summand of dimension $2$.
The small odd-field exceptions require original $(m,q)=(3,3)$
\cite[Theorem 2.1.7]{Brookfield2014}.
When $(m,q)\ne(3,3)$ and $K\leq N_1^-$, choose a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{2m}-1$.
Let $T_\ell$ be the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $T^x$.
By the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}, $T_\ell$ is characteristic in $J\unlhd K$.
Thus, $T^x=C_G(T_\ell)\unlhd K$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] If $m=3$ and $q\geq5$, then $T^x$ is normal in $K$.
\end{itemize}
For $m=3$, we use the maximal subgroup list in
\cite[Tables 8.39--8.40]{BHR}.
A primitive $\Phi_6$ element in $G_2(q)$ has cyclic centralizer
of order $q^2-q+1$.
This is smaller than $|T|=(q^3+1)/2$, so $G_2(q)$ cannot contain $T$.
We check the primitive-element centralizer in the unitary normalizer in characteristic $3$ from \cite[Lemma 2.7]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
On the irreducible adjoint module $V=\mathbb{F}_q^7$ of $\operatorname{PSU}_3(q)$,
the scalar centralizer in $\operatorname{SO}_7(q)$ is trivial.
Now, let $q=3^f$. Next, we choose an absolute primitive divisor $\ell$
of $3^{6f}-1$ in the displayed primitive class.
Since $q=3^f$ and $(3,q+1)=1$, the diagonal outer quotient of $\operatorname{PSU}_3(q)$ is trivial.
Next, let $c$ be a generator of the subgroup of order $\ell$ in the primitive torus.
For this element, the graph and field automorphisms normalizing $\langle c\rangle$ induce maps $c\mapsto c^{3^i}$ with $0\leq i<2f$, modulo the inner Singer Weyl subgroup.
Moreover, an inner Singer Weyl generator sends $c$ to $c^{-q}$, where $-q\equiv3^{4f}\pmod\ell$.
The inner Singer Weyl subgroup has exponents $0,2f,4f$ modulo $6f$,
so only $i=0$ among $0\leq i<2f$ centralizes the primitive element modulo that subgroup.
Thus, the primitive-element centralizer in $\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{PSU}_3(q))$ has order $q^2-q+1$
and cannot contain $T$.
Let $J_u\leq G$ be a unitary subgroup from the maximal list acting reducibly on $V$.
For this $J_u$, let $C_\ell\leq J_u$ be its primitive subgroup and $L_u=V^{C_\ell}$.
Since $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=6$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}V=7$, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}L_u=1$.
Since $J_u$ is reducible and $C_\ell$ is irreducible on $L_u^\perp$, a nonzero proper $J_u$-submodule is $L_u$ or $L_u^\perp$.
As $J_u$ consists of isometries, we have $gL_u=L_u$ for $g\in J_u$.
Thus, $J_u\leq N_1^-$.
For a Ree normalizer, the primitive-element centralizer is cyclic of order $q\pm\sqrt{3q}+1\leq q^2-q+1$.
Moreover, the torus quotient has order dividing $6$.
For its field quotient, the exponents satisfy $0\leq i<f$.
Since $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(3)=6f$, we have $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(3^i)=6f/(6f,i)>6$ for $0<i<f$.
Thus, no nonidentity field automorphism can centralize the primitive element after multiplication by a torus representative.
At $q=3$, let $R(3)=\operatorname{PSL}_2(8)\rtimes C_3$.
For $s\in R(3)$ with $|s|=7$, we have $C_{R(3)}(s)\cong C_7$.
Thus, no Ree normalizer contains $T$
\cite[Tables 8.42--8.43]{BHR}.
For $q\geq7$, the remaining case is $K\leq N_1^-$.
At $q=5$, we also consider the possibility that the maximal subgroup $M_7<G$ with $K\leq M_7$ has one of the types
$$
 A_8,\  C_2^6\rtimes A_7,\  \operatorname{Sp}_6(2),\  \operatorname{PSU}_3(3)\rtimes C_2
$$
\cite[Table 2]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
Neither $A_8$ nor $C_2^6\rtimes A_7$ has an element of odd order divisible by $9$.
As $\operatorname{ord}_9(2)=6$, every $s\in\operatorname{Sp}_6(2)$ with $|s|=9$ acts irreducibly on $\mathbb{F}_2^6$.
Thus, $|C_{\operatorname{Sp}_6(2)}(s)|=9$, so this centralizer has no element of order $7$.
For a regular $s\in\operatorname{PSU}_3(3)$ with $|s|=7$, we have $|C_{\operatorname{PSU}_3(3)}(s)|=7$.
Consequently, its centralizer in $\operatorname{PSU}_3(3)\rtimes C_2$ has order dividing $14$.
Since $|T^x|=63$, these facts show that none of the listed types contains $T^x$.
Therefore, $K\leq N_1^-$ at $(m,q)=(3,5)$.
Let $Q$ be the Sylow $7$-subgroup of $T^x$.
By the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}, $Q$ is characteristic in $J\unlhd K$.
Thus, $T^x=C_G(Q)\unlhd K$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] If $(m,q)=(3,3)$ and $M_7\cong S_9$, then $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
\end{itemize}
Now, we consider $(m,q)=(3,3)$.
By $A\leq P_2^y$ for some $y\in G$, we know that $A$ is a $\{2,3\}$-group.
Thus, $5\nmid|K|$.
In $C_2^6\rtimes A_7$, a $7$-cycle fixes no nonidentity sign vector
$(\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_7)$ with $\prod_i\varepsilon_i=1$.
Since its centralizer in $A_7$ is $C_7$, its centralizer in $C_2^6\rtimes A_7$ is also $C_7$.
For $c\in\operatorname{Sp}_6(2)$ with $|c|=7$, the module $\mathbb{F}_2^6$ has $2$ reciprocal irreducible constituents of dimension $3$.
Thus, $C_{\operatorname{Sp}_6(2)}(c)\cong C_7$.
As neither centralizer has an involution, neither subgroup type contains $T^x=C_{14}$.
Therefore, $M_7=N_1^-$ or $M_7\cong S_9$.

Suppose that $M_7\cong S_9$.
We identify $M_7$ with $S_9$, so $K\leq S_9$.
An element of $T^x$ of order $14$ has cycle type $(7)(2)$,
so $K$ contains a transposition.
A primitive subgroup of $S_9$ containing a transposition equals $S_9$, contrary to $5\nmid|K|$.
A transitive imprimitive group of degree $9$ has blocks of size $3$,
which cannot accommodate an element of order $7$.
Thus, $K$ is intransitive.
Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the $2$ points outside the $7$-cycle.
Since $(\alpha\ \beta)\in K$, a $K$-orbit contains both points or neither point.
Thus, the $K$-orbit containing the $7$-cycle cannot have size $8$.
It follows that $K\leq S_7\times S_2$.
For this subgroup of $S_7\times S_2$, let $\pi_7:K\to S_7$ send $(g,h)$ to $g$.
Since $\pi_7(K)$ contains a $7$-cycle, its action of prime degree $7$ is transitive and primitive.
If $\pi_7(K)$ contained a single $3$-cycle, then we would have $A_7\leq\pi_7(K)$ by Jordan's theorem \cite{JonesCycles}.
This contradicts $5\nmid|K|$.
Thus, every element of order $3$ in $\pi_7(K)$ has type $3^2 1$.
As the kernel of $\pi_7$ has order at most $2$, we identify each such $a$ with its unique lift $(a,1)\in K$ of order $3$.
Next, choose $y\in S_7\times\{1\}\leq M_7$ with $a^y$ a generator of a $C_3$ complement in $C_7\rtimes C_3$.
As $\operatorname{ord}_7(3)=6$, $C_7$ has $6$ distinct nontrivial eigenlines and a fixed line on $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_3^7$.
The complement permutes the $6$ eigenlines in $2$ $3$-cycles.
Each weighted cycle has Jordan block $J_3$ in characteristic $3$.
Thus, each element $a$ of order $3$ has Jordan form $J_3+J_3+J_1$ on $V=\mathbb{F}_3^7$.
It has no invariant direct summand of dimension $2$.
This contradicts the decomposition $gU\perp gW$ stabilized by $\langle a\rangle$.
Hence, $A$ is a $2$-group.
Because $|K|$ has only the prime divisors $2$ and $7$, we have $K$ soluble by Burnside's theorem.
As $\pi_7(K)$ is soluble and primitive, we have $\pi_7(K)\leq\operatorname{AGL}_1(7)$.
Because $3\nmid|K|$, we have $\pi_7(K)\leq C_7\rtimes C_2$.
The Sylow $7$-subgroup is normal in $K$.
Let $S$ be the normal Sylow $7$-subgroup of $K$.
As $C_G(S)=T^x$, we have $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] If $(m,q)=(3,3)$ and $K\leq N_1^-$, then $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
\end{itemize}
Finally, suppose that $(m,q)=(3,3)$ and $K\leq N_1^-$.
Let $J=K\cap\Omega^-_6(3)\unlhd K$.
By the indecomposability argument in Step 1, we have $J<\Omega^-_6(3)$.
As $5\nmid|K|$, we have $5\nmid|J|$.
Since $[K:J]\leq2$, every element of $A$ of order $3$ lies in $J$.
Since $J<\Omega^-_6(3)$, we choose a maximal subgroup $M_6<\Omega^-_6(3)$ with $J\leq M_6$.
As $T^x=C_{14}\leq J$, $M_6$ is isomorphic to one of $\operatorname{SU}_3(3)\times C_2,2\times A_7,2.\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$
\cite[Tables 8.33--8.34]{BHR}.
For the unitary type, identify $E$ with $\mathbb{F}_9^3$ over $\mathbb{F}_3$.
We identify $M_6$ with $\{g\in\operatorname{GU}_3(3):\det g\in\{1,-1\}\}=\operatorname{SU}_3(3)\times C_2$.
Let $C_4=Z(\operatorname{GU}_3(3))$ and $T_U=T^xC_4$, so $|T_U|=28$.
We have $JC_4<\operatorname{GU}_3(3)$.
Otherwise, $JC_4$ would contain an indecomposable Sylow $3$-subgroup of $\operatorname{SU}_3(3)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-unitary-sylow}.
Every proper subgroup $H<\operatorname{GU}_3(3)$ with $T_U\leq H$ lies in $N_{\operatorname{GU}_3(3)}(T_U)$ or $C_4\times\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$
\cite{Bereczky,Brookfield2014}.
For $M_6\cong C_2\times A_7$, we identify $M_6$ with $C_2\times A_7$.
Let $\pi_A:C_2\times A_7\to A_7$ send $(c,h)$ to $h$.
Because $5\nmid|\pi_A(J)|$, the image has no single $3$-cycle by Jordan's theorem.
For $M_6\cong2.\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$, let $\pi_L:2.\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)\to\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$ be the central quotient.
Then,
we have $5\nmid|\pi_L(J)|$ and $\pi_L(J)<\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$.
Thus, $\pi_L(J)$ lies in
$\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$ \cite{Atlas1985}.
For every element $a\in J$ of order $3$, we choose a conjugating element $y$.
For the unitary type, we choose $y\in\operatorname{GU}_3(3)$ acting as $I_L$ on $L$.
For $M_6$ of type $C_2\times A_7$ or $2.\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$, we choose $y\in M_6$.
In each case, $a^y$ lies in a $C_3$ complement of $C_7\rtimes C_3$.
Thus, $a$ has Jordan form $J_3+J_3+J_1$ on $V=\mathbb{F}_3^7$.
As $\langle a\rangle$ cannot stabilize a direct summand of dimension $2$, $3\nmid|A|$.
Because the only prime divisors of $|K|$ are $2$ and $7$, $K$ is soluble.
If $J\leq N_{\operatorname{GU}_3(3)}(T_U)$, then its Sylow $7$-subgroup lies in the cyclic torus and is unique.
For $J\leq C_4\times\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$, let $\pi_2:C_4\times\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)\to\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$ send $(c,h)$ to $h$.
In this case, let $J_{\rm im}=\pi_2(J)$.
For $M_6\cong C_2\times A_7$, let $J_{\rm im}=\pi_A(J)$.
For $M_6\cong2.\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$, let $J_{\rm im}=\pi_L(J)$.
Because $K$ is soluble, $J_{\rm im}$ is soluble in each of the $3$ cases.
As $7\mid|J_{\rm im}|$, its action of degree $7$ is transitive and hence primitive.
By the preceding argument for degree $7$, $J_{\rm im}$ has a unique Sylow $7$-subgroup.
The central kernels have order prime to $7$, so $J$ also has a unique Sylow $7$-subgroup.
Let $Q$ be the unique Sylow $7$-subgroup of $J$, with $C_G(Q)=T^x$.
Because $Q$ is characteristic in $J\unlhd K$ and $[K:J]\leq2$, $Q$ is a normal Sylow $7$-subgroup of $K$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
head: environment

label: thm:orthogonal-odd
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:orthogonal-odd}
Let $q$ be odd and $m\geq3$.
Then, $\Omega_{2m+1}(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$\Omega_{2m+1}(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G=\Omega_{2m+1}(q)$ and $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Lemma \ref{lem:orthogonal-odd-singer}, we have $A\leq N_G(T)$ for a Singer torus $T$.
We choose $V=E\perp L$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}E=2m$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}L=1$.
The torus $T$ acts irreducibly on $E$ and fixes $L$ pointwise.
Next, on $E=\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}$, let $M_\lambda(v)=\lambda v$ for $\lambda\in E^*$. We take $S_0=\{M_\lambda:\lambda^{q^m+1}=1\}$.
Then, we have $S_0\leq\operatorname{SO}(E)$ and $|S_0|=q^m+1$.
Let $\iota:S_0\to\operatorname{SO}(V)$ send $h$ to $h\oplus I_L$.
By the spinor calculation in Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-minus-odd}, we have $T=\iota(S_0^2)$.
Let $F:E\to E$ satisfy $F(v)=v^q$.
Since $\det F=-1$, the map $F\oplus(-I_L)$ has determinant $1$.
Choose $h\in S_0$ so that $\iota(h)(F\oplus(-I_L))$ has trivial spinor norm.
The map $\theta:N_G(T)\to\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}/\mathbb{F}_q)$
takes $g\in N_G(T)$ to the field automorphism in the semilinear restriction $g|_E$.
By the preceding construction, we have $g_0\in N_G(T)$ with $\theta(g_0)(v)=v^q$ for $v\in E$.
Hence, $\theta$ is surjective and $\ker\theta=T$.
Therefore, $N_G(T)/T=C_{2m}$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} for $P_1$, $A$ stabilizes a singular line $\Lambda\leq V$.
Since $L$ is nondegenerate, we choose $v=e+l\in\Lambda\setminus\{0\}$ with $0\ne e\in E$ and $l\in L$.
For $a\in A\cap T$, let $M_\lambda=a|_E$.
As $a\Lambda=\Lambda$, we have $av=cv$ for some $c\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$.
Taking the projection on $E$, we obtain that $\lambda e=ce$, so $\lambda=c$.
Because $\lambda^{q^m+1}=1$, we have $c^2=1$.
Thus, $a|_E=I_E$ or $-I_E$, and $a|_L=I_L$.
Consequently, $|A\cap T|\leq2$.
The possible involution of $A\cap T$ is $t=(-I_E)\oplus I_L\in Z(N_G(T))$.
As $A\cap T\leq Z(N_G(T))$ and $A/(A\cap T)$ is cyclic, $A$ is abelian.
The odd Sylow subgroups of $A$ are cyclic of orders dividing $m$,
and the Sylow $2$-subgroup has rank at most $2$.

We take a primitive prime divisor $\ell$ of $q^{2m-2}-1$.
Next, we choose a nondegenerate subspace $U\leq V$ of minus type with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U=2m-2$. Let $W=U^\perp$, so $V=U\perp W$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W=3$.
Take $B=C_\ell$ irreducible on $U$ and trivial on $W$.
Since $\ell\geq2m-1>m$ and $\ell\geq5$, we have $\ell\nmid|A|$.
We choose $x\in G$ such that $H=AB^x$ is a subgroup.
As $A$ and $B^x$ are abelian, we conclude from It\^o's theorem that $H'$ is abelian.
If $\ell\mid|H'|$, then the Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $B^x$ of the abelian group $H'$ is characteristic.
Thus, $B^x\unlhd H$.
Otherwise, $AH'$ is $\ell$-free and contains $A$, so $AH'=A$ and $A\unlhd H$.
The odd Sylow subgroups of $A$ are cyclic with primes at most $m$, so their automorphism groups have no prime divisor greater than $m$.
For the Sylow $2$-subgroup of rank at most $2$, the automorphism group has no prime divisor other than $2$ or $3$.
Since $\ell>m$ and $\ell\geq5$, we obtain that $\ell\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(A)|$.
Thus, $B^x$ centralizes $A$, and $B^x\unlhd H$.

Let $a\in A$ have odd prime order $r$.
Since $|A\cap T|\leq2$, we have $\theta(a)\ne1$.
Let $\alpha:N_G(B^x)\to\operatorname{Aut}(B^x)$ satisfy $\alpha(g)(b)=gbg^{-1}$.
As $|N_G(B^x)/C_G(B^x)|$ divides $2m-2$, the order of $\alpha(a)$ divides both $r$ and $2m-2$.
Since $r\mid m$ is odd, $a$ centralizes $B^x$.
Let $U_x=x^{-1}U$, so $B^x$ is irreducible on $U_x$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U_x=2m-2$.
If $r=p$, then $a|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$.
As $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}U_x^\perp=3$ and $a|_{U_x^\perp}$ is unipotent, we have $\operatorname{rank}(a-I_V)\leq2$.
Because $\theta(a)\ne1$, the operator $a|_E$ has $2m/p$ Jordan blocks of length $p$.
Thus, $\operatorname{rank}(a|_E-I_E)=2m(p-1)/p\geq4$.
This is impossible.

Suppose that $r\ne p$.
Since $\theta(a)\ne1$, every nonidentity eigenvalue of $a$ has multiplicity $2m/r$.
Moreover, the eigenvalue $1$ has multiplicity $2m/r+1$.
As $a$ centralizes $B^x$, the restriction $a|_{U_x}$ is a multiplier of degree at most $r-1$.
If $a|_{U_x}\ne I_{U_x}$ and $r<m$, then a nonidentity eigenvalue has multiplicity at least $(2m-2)/(r-1)>2m/r$.
We have a contradiction.
If $r=m$ is prime, then we have $r\nmid q^{m-1}+1$ by Fermat's theorem.
Thus, $a|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$.
If $a|_{U_x}=I_{U_x}$, then we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(a-I_V)\geq2m-2>2m/r+1$.
This contradicts the preceding multiplicity of eigenvalue $1$.
Thus, $A$ is a $2$-group.

If $T$ is odd, then $A\cap T=1$ and $A$ is cyclic.
By Corollary \ref{cor:split-odd-involutions}, we conclude that $A=1$.
If $T$ is even, then $m$ is odd and $q\equiv3\pmod4$.
The Sylow $2$-subgroup of $\theta(A)$ has order at most $2$, so $|A|\leq4$.
If $A$ is cyclic, then we conclude that $A=1$ by Corollary \ref{cor:split-odd-involutions}.
If $A$ is isomorphic to $C_2\times C_2$, then the torus involution $t\in A\cap T$ has fixed dimension $1$.
For every other involution $s\in A$,
$s|_E(v)=cv^{q^m}$ for $v\in E$ and $c\in\mathbb{F}_{q^{2m}}^*$ with $c c^{q^m}=1$.
By Hilbert 90, we have $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(s|_E-I_E)=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}\ker(s|_E+I_E)=m$.
Since $\det(s|_E)=(-1)^m=-1$ and $\det s=1$, we have $s|_L=-I_L$.
Thus, $\dim\ker(s-I_V)=m\ne1=\dim\ker(t-I_V)$.
As conjugation in $G$ does not change fixed-space dimensions, no $g\in G$ satisfies $t^g=s$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer}, we choose a $p$-subgroup $H\leq G$ with $|N_G(H)|$ odd.
However, by Lemma \ref{lem:odd-normalizer-fusion}, we would have $t^g=s$ for some $g\in G$. We obtain a contradiction.
Hence, $A=1$.

label: lem:alternating-affine-restriction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-affine-restriction}
Let $H\leq S_{\Omega}$ and let $\Delta\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy $h\Delta=\Delta$ for every $h\in H$.
Suppose that $|\Delta|=p$ is prime and $p\nmid|H^\Delta|$.
Let $\xi_0:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_p$ be a bijection with $c_{\xi_0}(H^\Delta)\leq\operatorname{AGL}_1(p)$.
There exist $v\in\mathbb{F}_p$ and a bijection $\xi:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_p$ satisfying $\xi(\delta)=\xi_0(\delta)-v$ for every $\delta\in\Delta$.
The homomorphism $\theta=\mu_p\circ c_\xi\circ\pi_\Delta:H\to\mathbb{F}_p^*$ satisfies $\ker\theta=\ker\pi_\Delta$.
For $D=\theta(H)$, the integer $d=|D|=|H^\Delta|$ divides $p-1$.
Moreover, $c_\xi(H^\Delta)=\{u\mapsto cu\mid c\in D\}$.
For $d=1$, every point of $\Delta$ is fixed by $H$.
For $d>1$, $\xi^{-1}(0)$ is the unique $H$-fixed point in $\Delta$.
For $u\in\mathbb{F}_p^*$, the $H$-orbit of $\xi^{-1}(u)$ is $\xi^{-1}(uD)$ and has size $d$.
If $X\subseteq\Omega$ satisfies $hX=X$ for every $h\in H$ and $|X|\geq|\Omega\setminus\Delta|+2$, then $d\leq|X|$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\ker\mu_p$ has order $p$ and $p\nmid|H^\Delta|$, we have $\ker\mu_p\cap c_{\xi_0}(H^\Delta)=1$.
Thus, $c_{\xi_0}(H^\Delta)$ is cyclic and has order $m=|H^\Delta|$ dividing $p-1$.
For $m>1$, we choose $h\in H^\Delta$ with $H^\Delta=\langle h\rangle$.
We have $c_{\xi_0}(h)(u)=au+b$ with $a\ne1$.
As $av+b=v$ for $v=b/(1-a)$, the bijection $\xi(\delta)=\xi_0(\delta)-v$ satisfies $c_\xi(h)(u)=au$.
For $m=1$, we take $v=0$ and $\xi=\xi_0$.
The coordinate change $u\mapsto u-v$ sends $u\mapsto au+b$ to $u\mapsto au+b+(a-1)v$.
Consequently, $c_\xi(H^\Delta)\leq\operatorname{AGL}_1(p)$ and $\mu_p$ is injective on $c_\xi(H^\Delta)$.
We obtain that $\ker\theta=\ker\pi_\Delta$ and $|D|=m=d$.
Because $c_\xi(H^\Delta)$ consists of the maps $u\mapsto cu$ with $c\in D$, the fixed points and orbits have the required forms.

Suppose that $hX=X$ for every $h\in H$ and $|X|\geq|\Omega\setminus\Delta|+2$.
Then, $|X\cap\Delta|\geq2$.
We choose $u\in\mathbb{F}_p^*$ with $\xi^{-1}(u)\in X\cap\Delta$.
Since $hX=X$ for every $h\in H$, we have $\xi^{-1}(uD)\subseteq X$.
Therefore, $d\leq|X|$.

label: prop:alternating-involutions
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:alternating-involutions}
For every $n\geq7$, the group $A_n$ has no ordinary
$A_n$-permutable subgroup of order $2$.
For $n\geq14$, $A_n$ has no nontrivial ordinary
$A_n$-permutable cyclic $2$-subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the proposition into the following steps.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] If $c\in A_n$ is an odd cycle of length $n$ or $n-1$, then every involution in $N_{A_n}(\langle c\rangle)$ fixes at most $n/3+1$ points.
\end{itemize}
Let $L=n$ when $n$ is odd, and $L=n-1$ when $n$ is even.
Let $C\leq A_n$ be generated by an $L$-cycle.
For this cyclic subgroup, we have $N_{S_n}(C)=C_L\rtimes\operatorname{Aut}(C_L)$,
with the point outside the cyclic orbit fixed when $n$ is even.
An involution $t\in N_{S_n}(C)$ fixes a proper divisor of $L$ points
on the cyclic orbit.
For each prime $p\mid L$, let $p^a$ denote the $p$-part of $L$.
On the factor $C_{p^a}\leq C_L$, the multiplier of $t$ is $1$ or $-1$.
When the multiplier is $1$, the component contributes its order to the number of fixed points.
When the multiplier is $-1$, the component contributes $1$ point.
Since $L$ is odd, every proper divisor of $L$ is at most $L/3$.
Thus, every involution in $N_{A_n}(C)$ has at most $n/3+1$ fixed points.
For an involution in $A_n$, the number $f$ of fixed points satisfies $f\equiv n\pmod4$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, a generator of an ordinary $A_n$-permutable subgroup of order $2$ must satisfy both bounds.

We construct subgroups $B\leq A_n$ for which no involution in $N_{A_n}(B)$ has the cycle type of an involution in $N_{A_n}(C)$.
For this construction, let $H=C_7\rtimes C_3=\langle a,b\rangle$ act affinely on $7$ points.
We take $b^{-1}ab=a^2$.
We claim that every automorphism of $H$ acts trivially on $H/H'\cong C_3$.
To prove the claim, let $\varphi\in\operatorname{Aut}(H)$.
We choose $1\leq u\leq6$, $0\leq v\leq6$ and $e\in\{1,2\}$ with $\varphi(a)=a^u$ and $\varphi(b)=a^vb^e$.
Since $\varphi(b)^{-1}\varphi(a)\varphi(b)=\varphi(a)^2$, we have $2^e\equiv2\pmod7$.
Therefore, $e=1$.

We choose $r$ copies of $H$ on disjoint orbits of length $7$.
Let $\chi:H\to\mathbb{F}_3$ satisfy $\chi(a)=0$ and $\chi(b)=1$.
For $1\leq i\leq r$, let $\chi_i:H^r\to\mathbb{F}_3$ satisfy $\chi_i(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\chi(h_i)$.
For $\Lambda\subseteq\operatorname{Hom}(H^r,\mathbb{F}_3)\setminus\{0\}$ with distinct kernels,
add $1$ orbit $\mathbb{F}_3$ for each $\lambda\in\Lambda$.
On the orbit indexed by $\lambda$, an element $h\in H^r$ sends $t$ to $t+\lambda(h)$.
Let $\rho:H^r\to A_n$ be the permutation homomorphism with $n-7r-3|\Lambda|$ additional fixed points.
Since each copy of $H$ acts faithfully on its $7$ points, we have $\ker\rho=1$.
Let $B=\rho(H^r)$.
Since $g\in N_{S_n}(B)$ maps $B$-orbits to $B$-orbits of equal length, $g$ permutes the orbits of length $7$.
Hence, $g$ also permutes the factors of $H^r$.
For the induced automorphism, let $\varphi_g:H^r\to H^r$ satisfy $\varphi_g(h)=\rho^{-1}(g\rho(h)g^{-1})$ for $h\in H^r$.
Let $\sigma\in S_r$ be the permutation of the $r$ factors induced by $\varphi_g$.
For $1\leq i\leq r$, we have $\chi_{\sigma(i)}\circ\varphi_g=\chi_i$.
Each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ satisfies $\ker(-\lambda)=\ker\lambda$.
Suppose that the kernels in $\Lambda$ have trivial stabilizer under permutations of the $r$ coordinates.
Then, $\sigma=1$ for every $g\in N_{S_n}(B)$.
By $\chi_{\sigma(i)}\circ\varphi_g=\chi_i$, we have $\chi_i\circ\varphi_g=\chi_i$ for $1\leq i\leq r$.
Since each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ is an $\mathbb{F}_3$-linear combination of the $\chi_i$, we have $\lambda\circ\varphi_g=\lambda$.
Because the kernels are distinct, $g$ maps each orbit indexed by $\lambda\in\Lambda$ to itself.
On that orbit, $g$ commutes with $u\mapsto u+1$.
The centralizer of this $3$-cycle has order $3$.
Consequently, every involution in $N_{S_n}(B)$ fixes all $3$ points on each of these orbits.
Let $t\in N_{S_n}(B)$ be an involution.
On each orbit of length $7$, $t$ normalizes $C_7$ and fixes at least $1$ point.
Thus, $t$ fixes at least $r+3|\Lambda|$ points.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] For $n\geq20$, $A_n$ has no ordinary $A_n$-permutable subgroup of order $2$.
\end{itemize}
Suppose that $n\geq30$.
Let $n=10r+3k+\ell$ with $r=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\geq3$.
Then, $0\leq k\leq3$ and $0\leq\ell\leq2$.
We use $\Lambda_0=\{\chi_1\}\cup\{\chi_i+\chi_{i+1}\mid1\leq i<r\}$.
Then, we add the first $k$ characters in the list
$\chi_1+\chi_2+\chi_3,\chi_1+\chi_2-\chi_3,\chi_1-\chi_2+\chi_3$.
For $\lambda=\sum_i c_i\chi_i$, let $I(\lambda)=\{i:c_i\ne0\}$.
Since $I(\chi_1)=\{1\}$ is the only singleton among the sets $I(\lambda)$, a coordinate permutation stabilizing the kernels in $\Lambda$ fixes $1$.
The sets $I(\chi_i+\chi_{i+1})=\{i,i+1\}$ form the path $1,2,\ldots,r$.
As an automorphism of the path $1,2,\ldots,r$ fixing $1$ fixes every vertex, the coordinate stabilizer is trivial.
Because $|\Lambda|=r+k$, the action uses $10r+3k$ points.
We let $B$ fix the $\ell$ unused points.
Every involution normalizing $B$ fixes at least $4r+3k$ points.
As $r\geq3$ and $\ell\leq2$, we have $3(4r+3k)-n-3=2r+6k-\ell-3>0$.
This contradicts $f\leq n/3+1$ for involutions in $N_{A_n}(C)$.

For $20\leq n\leq22$, we take $r=2$ and $\Lambda=\{\chi_1,\chi_1+\chi_2\}$.
We fix the unused points.
By the bound $r+3|\Lambda|$, every involution in $N_{S_n}(B)$ fixes at least $8$ points.
For $n=20,21$, we have $n/3+1<8$, contrary to the bound from $N_{A_n}(C)$.
For $n=22$, we have $f\leq8$ and $f\equiv2\pmod4$.
Thus, $f\leq6$.
For $23\leq n\leq29$, we also add $\chi_1-\chi_2$ to $\Lambda$.
Then, every involution normalizing $B$ fixes at least $11$ points, greater than $n/3+1$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] For $7\leq n\leq19$, $A_n$ has no ordinary $A_n$-permutable subgroup of order $2$.
\end{itemize}
For $14\leq n\leq18$, let $m=n-10$ when $n$ is odd and $m=n-11$ when $n$ is even.
Let $\rho_m:H\times C_m\to A_n$ have disjoint orbits $\Omega_7,\Xi_3,\Gamma_m$ of lengths $7$, $3$ and $m$.
On $\Omega_7$, the factor $H$ has its affine action.
In addition, $H$ acts on $\Xi_3$ through $H/H'\cong C_3$.
On $\Gamma_m$, the factor $H$ acts trivially and $C_m$ acts regularly.
For the action of $C_m$ on the other points, we take every point of $\Omega_7\cup\Xi_3$ to be fixed.
For even $n$, we add $1$ point fixed by $\rho_m(H\times C_m)$.
Let $B=\rho_m(H\times C_m)$.
Every element of $N_{S_n}(B)$ maps $\Xi_3$ to itself.
For $n=14$, the centre $Z(B)$ fixes $\Xi_3$ pointwise.
Since $Z(B)$ is transitive on the other orbit of length $3$, no element of $N_{S_n}(B)$ sends either orbit to the other.
When $n=17,18$, the image $B^{\Omega_7}$ is nonabelian and $B^{\Gamma_7}$ is cyclic.
Hence, every element of $N_{S_n}(B)$ maps each orbit of length $7$ to itself.
Every normalizing involution fixes at least $5$ points for odd $n$
and $6$ for even $n$.
For $n=14,15,16,17,18$, the fixed-point bounds from $N_{A_n}(C)$ allow only $f=2,3,4,1,2$ in that order.
For $n=19$, the cyclic normalizer has no even involution.

For $n\in\{7,8,11,12\}$, we add $1$ to the proper divisors of $L$ when $n$ is even.
None of the possible values of $f$ satisfies $f\equiv n\pmod4$.
For $n=9,10,13$, the fixed-point bounds from $N_{A_n}(C)$ allow only $f=1,2,1$ in that order.
We use $B=\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)$ on $7$ points and fix the rest.
The unique $B$-orbit of length $7$ on triples is the Fano plane.
Since $N_{S_7}(B)$ permutes the $B$-orbits on triples of equal length, every element of $N_{S_7}(B)$ maps the Fano plane to itself.
As the automorphism group of the Fano plane is $B$, we have $N_{S_7}(B)=B$.
An involution in $B$ moves $4$ points.
Together with the permutations of the fixed points, an even
normalizing involution has at most $2$ transpositions for $n=9,10$
and $4$ for $n=13$.
Thus, neither possible number of transpositions agrees with the required cycle type.
Consequently, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers} that $A_n$ has no ordinary $A_n$-permutable subgroup of order $2$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] For $n\geq14$, $A_n$ has no nontrivial ordinary $A_n$-permutable cyclic $2$-subgroup.
\end{itemize}
Suppose that $n\geq14$ and $A$ is a nontrivial cyclic $2$-subgroup that is ordinary $A_n$-permutable.
For $n=19$, we choose $y\in A_n$ such that $AC^y$ is a subgroup.
By Burnside's normal-complement theorem, we have $C^y\unlhd AC^y$.
The involution of $A$ then lies in $N_{A_n}(C^y)$, a contradiction.
For $n\ne19$, the constructed subgroup $B$ has odd order.
We choose $x,y\in A_n$ such that $AB^x$ and $AC^y$ are subgroups.
Both products have cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroups.
By Burnside's normal-complement theorem, we have $B^x\unlhd AB^x$ and $C^y\unlhd AC^y$.
Let $t$ be the unique involution of $A$.
Then, $t\in N_{A_n}(B^x)\cap N_{A_n}(C^y)$.
The fixed-point bounds for those $2$ normalizers are incompatible.
Therefore, no nontrivial cyclic $2$-subgroup $A$ is ordinary $A_n$-permutable.
head: environment

label: prop:alternating-twenty-four
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G=A_{24}$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
Let $M=(S_6\times S_{18})\cap G$, a maximal subgroup.
By \cite[Theorem D]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq M^x$ for some $x\in G$.
Thus, $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
For each maximal subgroup $M<G$, there exists $x_M\in G$ with $A\leq M^{x_M}$.
We use the imprimitive subgroup $(S_3\wr S_8)\cap G$.
The order of $A$ divides $(3!)^8\,8!$, so $11$ and $23$ do not divide $|A|$.
Let $B$ be generated by a $23$-cycle.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $K=AB^x$ is a subgroup.
As $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$, we have $K<G$.
We have $11\nmid|K|$.
The $K$-orbit containing the $23$-cycle has size $23$ or $24$.

Let $\Delta$ be the $K$-orbit containing $\operatorname{supp}(B^x)$.
Suppose that $|\Delta|=23$.
Then, $K$ fixes the point outside $\Delta$ and acts primitively on $\Delta$.
By \cite[Theorem 1.2]{JonesCycles}, $K^\Delta$ is affine or projective or $K^\Delta\cong M_{23}$ or $K^\Delta$ contains the alternating group on $\Delta$.
Since $11\mid|M_{23}|$ and $11\mid|A_{23}|$, neither $K^\Delta\cong M_{23}$ nor $A_{23}\leq K^\Delta$ is possible.
The projective equation $(q^a-1)/(q-1)=23$ has no solution with $q$ a prime power and $a\geq2$.
For $a\geq5$, the degree is at least $31$.
For $a=4$ and $q=2$, the degree is $15$.
For $a=4$ and $q\geq3$, the degree is at least $40$.
For $a=3$, we would have $q(q+1)=22$.
For $a=2$, we would have $q=22$.
As $22$ is not a prime power, this equality is impossible.
Therefore, we choose a bijection $\xi:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_{23}$ with $c_\xi(K^\Delta)\leq\operatorname{AGL}_1(23)$.
Because $K$ fixes the outside point, every element of $K^\Delta$ is even.
Thus, $|K^\Delta|$ divides $23\cdot11$.
As $11\nmid|K|$ and $B^x\leq K$, we have $K=B^x$ and $A=1$.

Suppose that $|\Delta|=24$.

A nontrivial block system in degree $24$ has at most $12$ blocks, each of size at most $12$.
Since $|B^x|=23$, each block would be fixed setwise by $B^x$.
No block could contain the support of its $23$-cycle.
Therefore, $K$ is primitive.
By Jones's list, either $K$ is affine or $A_{24}\leq K$ or $K\in\{\operatorname{PSL}_2(23),\operatorname{PGL}_2(23),M_{24}\}$.
An affine degree is a power of a prime.
As $24$ is not a prime power, $K$ is not affine.
The orders of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(23)$, $\operatorname{PGL}_2(23)$ and $M_{24}$ are divisible by $11$.
A group containing $A_{24}$ contradicts $K<G$.
Therefore, $K$ cannot be transitive on all $24$ points.
head: environment

label: thm:alternating-prime-plus-one
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alternating-prime-plus-one}
Let $p\geq7$ be prime.
Then, $A_{p+1}$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$A_{p+1}$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}, we have the conclusion for $p=7,11$.
By Proposition \ref{prop:alternating-twenty-four}, we have the conclusion for $p=23$.
Assume that $p\geq13$ and $p\ne23$.
Let $n=p+1$ and $G=A_n$, and let $1<A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
To use Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose the maximal set stabilizer $M=(S_6\times S_{n-6})\cap G$.
By \cite[Theorem D]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Hence, $A\leq M^x$ for some $x\in G$, and $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
In particular, $p\nmid|A|$.

We choose a bijection $\eta:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\mathbf P^1(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
Let $H=\eta^{-1}\operatorname{PSL}_2(p)\eta\leq G$, using the natural action on $\mathbf P^1(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
By \cite[proof of Corollary 3.2]{BurnessLiebeckShalevDepth}, $H$ is maximal in $G$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ with $AH^y$ a subgroup.
As $AH^y\ne G$ and $H$ is maximal, we have $A\leq H^y$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max} and $AY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$, we have a point fixed by $A$.
We replace $A$ by $A^{y^{-1}}\leq H$.
Because $A$ fixes a point, $A$ lies in a Borel subgroup $P=C_p\rtimes C_{(p-1)/2}$ of $H$.
As $p\nmid|A|$, we choose $z\in P$ and a split torus $T\leq P$ with $|T|=(p-1)/2$ and $A^z\leq T$.
Thus, $A$ is cyclic of order $d$.
As $A\leq T^{z^{-1}}$, every nonidentity element of $A$ fixes precisely the $2$ common eigenlines of $T^{z^{-1}}$ in the action on $\mathbf P^1(\mathbb{F}_p)$.
Thus, every point outside those $2$ fixed points has trivial stabilizer in $A$.
Consequently, all other $A$-orbits have length $d$.

Let $M_3=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\{1,2,3\})$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we choose $h\in G$ with $A\leq M_3^h$.
Then, $\Gamma=h^{-1}\{1,2,3\}$ satisfies $a\Gamma=\Gamma$ for every $a\in A$, and $|\Gamma|=3$.
Since $A$ has only $2$ fixed points and every other orbit has length $d$, we have $d\leq3$.
If $d=2$, then Proposition \ref{prop:alternating-involutions} contradicts ordinary permutability of $A$.
Suppose that $d=3$. Let $B$ be generated by a $5$-cycle.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The subgroup has order $15$, so it is cyclic.
Let $a$ generate $A$ and let $b$ generate $B^x$.
Because $ab=ba$ and $|a|=3$ is prime to $|b|=5$, we have $a|_{\operatorname{supp}(b)}=1$.
This contradicts the $2$ fixed points of $a$.
Thus, $A=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:alternating-prime-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-prime-support}
Let $p\geq13$ be prime and $1\leq k\leq8$.
Let $A<A_{p+k}$ be ordinary $A_{p+k}$-permutable.
Then, $p\nmid|A|$. For each maximal subgroup $M<A_{p+k}$, there exists $y\in A_{p+k}$ with $A\leq M^y$.
The subgroup $A$ fixes a point and has an invariant subset of each size at most $(p+k)/2$.
Let $C=\langle c\rangle$, where $c$ is a $p$-cycle in $A_{p+k}$.
If $AC^x$ is a subgroup for $x\in A_{p+k}$,
then $A\operatorname{supp}(c^x)=\operatorname{supp}(c^x)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n=p+k$.
Let $M=(S_6\times S_{n-6})\cap A_n$, a maximal subgroup.
By \cite[Theorem D]{LPS}, we have $MY\ne A_n$ for every $Y<A_n$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq M^x$ for some $x\in A_n$.
Thus, $AY\ne A_n$ for every $Y<A_n$.
For each maximal subgroup $M<A_n$, there exists $y\in A_n$ with $A\leq M^y$.
The stabilizer of $\{1,\ldots,k+1\}$ has order $(k+1)!(p-1)!/2$,
so $p\nmid|A|$.
By the point and set stabilizers, we have an $A$-fixed point.
We also have an $A$-invariant subset of each size below $n/2$.
When $n$ is even, we choose $y\in A_n$ with $A\leq((S_{n/2}\wr C_2)\cap A_n)^y$.
Let $\Omega_1,\Omega_2$ be its blocks, labelled so that an $A$-fixed point $\alpha$ lies in $\Omega_1$.
Since $g\alpha=\alpha$ for every $g\in A$, we have $g\Omega_i=\Omega_i$ for $i=1,2$.
Thus, $A$ has an invariant subset of size $n/2$.
Consequently, every $A$-orbit has size at most $\lceil n/2\rceil$.

Let $\Delta$ be the orbit of $K=AC^x$ containing $\operatorname{supp}(c^x)$.
If $|\Delta|>p$, then choose a $C^x$-fixed point $\alpha\in\Delta$.
Since $K=AC^x$ and $C^x$ fixes $\alpha$, we have $\Delta=\{a(\alpha):a\in A\}$.
As $p\geq13$ and $k\leq8$, we have $|\Delta|>p>\lceil(p+k)/2\rceil$.
This contradicts the $A$-orbit bound.
Hence, $|\Delta|=p$ and $A\Delta=\Delta=\operatorname{supp}(c^x)$.
head: environment

label: thm:alternating-prime-plus-two
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alternating-prime-plus-two}
Let $p\geq7$ be prime.
Then, $A_{p+2}$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$A_{p+2}$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p=7,11$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Assume that $p\geq13$, and let $A<G=A_{p+2}$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-prime-support}, we have $p\nmid|A|$.
We also have $A$-invariant sets of sizes $3$ and $4$.
Let $C_p$ be generated by a $p$-cycle.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $K=AC_p^x$ is a subgroup.
The support $\Delta$ of $C_p^x$ is a $K$-orbit of size $p$.
Every element of $\ker\pi_\Delta$ is an even permutation on the $2$ points outside $\Delta$.
Thus, $\ker\pi_\Delta=1$ and $\pi_\Delta:K\to S_{\Delta}$ is injective.
The primitive group $K^\Delta$ has subgroup $A^\Delta$ of index $p$.
Let $L\lhd K^\Delta$ with $p\mid|L|$. As $p\nmid|A^\Delta|$, we have $L\nleq A^\Delta$.
The $L$-orbits on $K^\Delta/A^\Delta$ have equal length dividing $p$.
Hence, $L$ is transitive on $K^\Delta/A^\Delta$ and $[L:L\cap A^\Delta]=p$.

By \cite[Theorem 1.2(1)]{JonesCycles}, $K^\Delta$ is affine or $L=\operatorname{soc}(K^\Delta)$ is nonabelian simple.
If $K^\Delta$ is not affine, then $L\cong A_p$ or $L$ is projective or Mathieu.
For $L\cong A_p$ or $L\cong M_{23}$, we have $[L:L\cap A^\Delta]=p$.
The subgroup $L\cap A^\Delta$ is a natural point stabilizer \cite[Theorem 1.1]{JonesSezer}.
The natural point stabilizer has orbits of lengths $1$ and $p-1$.
With only $2$ outside points, $A$ cannot have an invariant subset of size $4$.
For a projective group, let $L=\operatorname{PSL}_b(q)$, where
$p=(q^b-1)/(q-1)$.
The subgroup $L\cap A^\Delta$ stabilizes a point or a hyperplane
\cite[Theorem 1.1 and the following paragraph]{JonesSezer}.
The orbits of a projective point stabilizer have lengths $1$ and $p-1$.
With only $2$ outside points, $A$ cannot have an invariant subset of size $4$.
For $b\geq3$, a hyperplane stabilizer has orbit lengths $(q^{b-1}-1)/(q-1)$ and $q^{b-1}$.
Both lengths are at least $4$.
The $2$ outside points cannot form an invariant subset of size $3$.
For $b=2$, the point and hyperplane stabilizers coincide.

Thus, $K^\Delta$ is affine.
Since $p\nmid|A|$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} a bijection $\xi:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_p$ for the action of $A$ on $\Delta$.
Let $\theta=\mu_p\circ c_\xi\circ(\pi_\Delta|_A):A\to\mathbb{F}_p^*$, $D=\theta(A)$ and $d=|D|$.
We have $\ker\theta=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$ and $A^\Delta\cong D\cong C_d$ with $d\mid p-1$.
As $\pi_\Delta|_A$ is injective, we have $\ker\theta=1$ and $A\cong C_d$.
We choose an $A$-invariant set $X_0$ with $|X_0|=4$.
Because $|\{1,\ldots,p+2\}\setminus\Delta|=2$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} that $d\leq4$.
For $d=2,4$, Proposition \ref{prop:alternating-involutions} contradicts ordinary permutability of $A$.
If $d=3$, then $A$ fixes the $2$ outside points.
A generator of $A$ has exactly $3$ fixed points.
Let $B$ be generated by a $5$-cycle.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The subgroup has order $15$, so it is cyclic.
Let $a$ generate $A$ and let $b$ generate $B^x$.
Because $ab=ba$ and $|a|=3$ is prime to $|b|=5$, we have $a|_{\operatorname{supp}(b)}=1$.
This contradicts the $3$ fixed points of $a$.
Therefore, $A=1$.
head: environment

label: thm:alternating-prime-plus-three
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alternating-prime-plus-three}
Let $p\geq7$ be prime.
Then, $A_{p+3}$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$A_{p+3}$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $p=7$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
Since $A_{14}=A_{13+1}$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-one} for $p=11$.
Assume that $p\geq13$, and let $A<G=A_{p+3}$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-prime-support}, we have $p\nmid|A|$.
We also have $A$-invariant sets of every size at most $(p+3)/2$.
For $M=(S_2\wr S_{(p+3)/2})\cap G$, there exists $y\in G$ with $A\leq M^y$.
A $3$-cycle cannot act within a block of size $2$.
Moving $3$ such blocks moves at least $6$ points.
Therefore, $A$ contains no single $3$-cycle.

Let $C_p$ be generated by a $p$-cycle.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AC_p^x$ a subgroup.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-prime-support}, $\Delta=\operatorname{supp}(C_p^x)$ is a $K$-orbit of size $p$.
The subgroup $A^\Delta$ has index $p$ in the primitive group $K^\Delta$.
By \cite[Theorem 1.2(1)]{JonesCycles}, $K^\Delta$ is affine or $L=\operatorname{soc}(K^\Delta)$ is nonabelian simple.
Suppose that $L=\operatorname{soc}(K^\Delta)$ is nonabelian simple.
As $L\unlhd K^\Delta$ and $p\nmid|A^\Delta|$, the $L$-orbits on $K^\Delta/A^\Delta$ have length $p$. Thus, $[L:H]=p$ for $H=L\cap A^\Delta$.
For $L\cong A_p$ or $L\cong M_{23}$, we obtain from \cite[Theorem 1.1]{JonesSezer} that $H$ is a natural point stabilizer.
For projective $L$, $H$ is a point or hyperplane stabilizer.
The point stabilizers have orbit lengths $1$ and $p-1$.
With only $3$ outside points, these orbits cannot form an $A$-invariant subset of size $5$.
Let $q$ be a prime power and $b\geq3$.
A hyperplane stabilizer in $\operatorname{PSL}_b(q)$ has orbit lengths $h=(q^{b-1}-1)/(q-1)$ and $q^{b-1}$.
If $h\geq5$, then neither orbit can meet an invariant subset of size $4$.
The $3$ outside points cannot form such a subset.
The only smaller possibility with $b\geq3$ and $p\geq13$ is $(b,q)=(3,3)$.
Then, $p=13$ and the orbit lengths are $4$ and $9$.
With only $3$ outside points, $A$ cannot have an invariant subset of size $8$.
For $b=2$, the point and hyperplane stabilizers coincide.

Thus, $K^\Delta$ is affine.
Since $p\nmid|A|$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} a bijection $\xi:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_p$ for the action of $A$ on $\Delta$.
Let $\theta=\mu_p\circ c_\xi\circ(\pi_\Delta|_A):A\to\mathbb{F}_p^*$, $D=\theta(A)$ and $d=|D|$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction}, we have $\ker\theta=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$ and $A^\Delta\cong D\cong C_d$ with $d\mid p-1$.
Let $A_0=\ker\theta=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$.
As $A_0=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$, every element of $A_0$ fixes $\Delta$ pointwise and acts evenly on the $3$ outside points.
Consequently, every nonidentity element of $A_0$ is a single $3$-cycle.
Since $A$ contains no such element, we have $A_0=1$ and $A\cong C_d$.
We choose an $A$-invariant set $X_0$ with $|X_0|=5$.
Because $|\{1,\ldots,p+3\}\setminus\Delta|=3$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} that $d\leq5$.
For $d=2,4$, Proposition \ref{prop:alternating-involutions} contradicts ordinary permutability of $A$.

If $d=3$, then an invariant subset of size $2$ requires an $A$-fixed outside point.
Since $A$ has order $3$, it fixes all $3$ outside points.
A generator then has exactly $4$ fixed points.
Let $B$ be generated by a $5$-cycle.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The subgroup has order $15$, so it is cyclic.
Hence, a generator of $A$ centralizes $B^x$.
On the $5$ points moved by $B^x$, the centralizer of $B^x$ has order $5$.
Because the generator has order $3$, it fixes those $5$ points.
We have a contradiction.
If $d=5$, then the outside action is again trivial.
Let $B$ be generated by the product of $2$ disjoint $3$-cycles.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The subgroup has order $15$, so it is cyclic.
The centralizer of the $2$ cycles on their support of size $6$ has order $18$.
Thus, a generator of $A$ of order $5$ fixes $6$ points.
This contradicts the $4$ fixed points of a generator of $A$.
Therefore, $A=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:alternating-small-products
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-small-products}
Let $K$ be a finite group.
If $|K|$ divides $12d\cdot13\cdot17$ with $1\leq d\leq6$, then
the Sylow $13$- and $17$-subgroups of $K$ are normal.
If $|K|$ divides $4d\cdot11\cdot13$ with $1\leq d\leq7$, then
the Sylow $11$- and $13$-subgroups of $K$ are normal.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The order formulas for finite simple groups show that the only possible
nonabelian composition factor in the first case is $A_5$.
In contrast, if $|K|\mid4d\cdot11\cdot13$ with $1\leq d\leq7$, then $K$ has no nonabelian composition factor.
We can also compare each possible simple order with the divisibility bounds using \cite{BreuerSimpleOrders}.
For this comparison, we have $12d\cdot13\cdot17\leq15912$ for $d\leq6$ and $4d\cdot11\cdot13\leq4004$ for $d\leq7$.
In the first case, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(16)$ requires divisibility by $2^4\cdot3\cdot5$.
Similarly, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(17)$ requires divisibility by $2^4\cdot3^2$.
Since neither number divides an allowed $12d$, neither group can be a composition factor.
For every other nonabelian simple group $S$ of order at most $15912$, we have $|S|\nmid12d\cdot13\cdot17$ for $1\leq d\leq6$.

Let $\ell$ be one of the primes in the lemma.
If $\ell\nmid|K|$, then its Sylow $\ell$-subgroup is trivial.
Suppose that $\ell\mid|K|$.
We induct on $|K|$ using a minimal normal subgroup $N$.
Since $\ell\mid|K|$ and $\ell^2\nmid|K|$, we have $v_\ell(|K|)=1$.
If $N$ is an $\ell$-group, then $N$ is a normal Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $K$.
Otherwise, an elementary abelian $N$ has rank at most $4$ in characteristic $2$.
The rank is at most $2$ in characteristic $3$ and at most $1$ in every other characteristic.
Neither $\operatorname{GL}_4(2)$ nor $\operatorname{GL}_2(3)$ has order divisible by $\ell$.
For $N=C_r$ with $r$ prime, we have $\operatorname{Aut}(N)=\mathbb{F}_r^*$ and $\ell\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(N)|$.
As $5^2\nmid|K|$, a nonabelian $N$ must be isomorphic to $A_5$.
The group $\operatorname{Aut}(N)\cong S_5$ has no element of order $\ell$.
Thus, a Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $P$ centralizes $N$.
By induction, $PN/N$ is normal in $K/N$.
The inverse image of $PN/N$ under $K\to K/N$ is $NP=N\times P$, in which $P$ is characteristic.
Hence, $P\lhd K$, as required.
head: environment

label: thm:alternating-prime-plus-four-five
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alternating-prime-plus-four-five}
Let $p\geq7$ be prime and $k\in\{4,5\}$.
Then, $A_{p+k}$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
$A_{p+k}$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] $A^\Delta$ is cyclic and $|A^\Delta|\leq k+2$.
\end{itemize}
For $p=7$, we use Proposition \ref{prop:finite-tables}.
For $p=11$, we use Theorems \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-two} and \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-three}.
For $n=15,16$, we take $p=13$.
Assume that $p\geq13$.
For these degrees, let $n=p+k$ and $G=A_n$.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-prime-support}, we have $p\nmid|A|$.
The subgroup $A$ fixes a point and has invariant sets of each size at most $n/2$.
Let $C_p$ be generated by a $p$-cycle.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AC_p^x$ a subgroup.
The support $\Delta$ of $C_p^x$ is a $K$-orbit of size $p$,
and $A^\Delta$ has index $p$ in $K^\Delta$.
As in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-three}, we use \cite[Theorem 1.2(1)]{JonesCycles} and \cite[Theorem 1.1]{JonesSezer}.
Each alternating, Mathieu or projective point stabilizer has orbit lengths $1$ and $p-1$.
With only $k$ outside points, $A$ cannot have an invariant subset of size $k+2$.
Let $q$ be a prime power and $b\geq3$.
A hyperplane stabilizer in $\operatorname{PSL}_b(q)$ has orbit lengths $h=(q^{b-1}-1)/(q-1)$ and $q^{b-1}$.
When $h\geq k+2$, neither orbit can meet an $A$-invariant subset of size $k+1$.
The $k$ outside points cannot form such a subset.
The smaller cases are $p=13$, and also $p=31$ when $k=5$.
For $p=13$ and $n=17$, we use \cite{YG}.
For $n=18$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-one}.
For $(p,k)=(31,5)$, the projective orbits have sizes $6$ and $25$.
With only $5$ outside points, $A$ cannot have an invariant subset of size $12$.
Thus, $K^\Delta$ is affine.
As $p\nmid|A|$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} a bijection $\xi:\Delta\to\mathbb{F}_p$ for the action of $A$ on $\Delta$.
Let $\theta=\mu_p\circ c_\xi\circ(\pi_\Delta|_A):A\to\mathbb{F}_p^*$, $D=\theta(A)$ and $d=|D|$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction}, we have $\ker\theta=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$ and $A^\Delta\cong D\cong C_d$ with $d\mid p-1$.
Let $A_0=\ker\theta=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$.
As $A_0=\ker(\pi_\Delta|_A)$, every element of $A_0$ fixes $\Delta$ pointwise and acts evenly on the $k$ outside points.
Thus, $A_0$ is isomorphic to a subgroup of $A_k$.
We choose an $A$-invariant set $X_0$ with $|X_0|=k+2$.
Because $|\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\Delta|=k$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-affine-restriction} that $d\leq k+2$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] The map $\pi_\Delta|_A:A\to A^\Delta$ is injective.
\end{itemize}
For $k=4$, we have $|A|\mid12d$.
A nontrivial $A_0$ contains a single $3$-cycle or an involution $u$ with $|\operatorname{supp}(u)|=4$.
For $k=5$, we choose $y\in G$ with $A\leq((S_2\wr S_{n/2})\cap G)^y$.
An element of order $3$ or $5$ moving the blocks of size $2$ moves at least $6$ or $10$ points.
Thus, $A$ contains no single $3$-cycle or $5$-cycle.
As $A_0$ acts evenly on $5$ points, $A_0$ is a $2$-group of order at most $4$.
Therefore, $|A|\mid4d$.
A nontrivial $A_0$ contains an involution $u$ with $|\operatorname{supp}(u)|=4$.

For $k=4$, let $n=13a+17b+j$ with $a,b\geq0$ and $0\leq j\leq2$.
For $k=5$, let $n=11a+13b+j$ with $a,b\geq0$ and $0\leq j\leq3$.
For the first prime length, we choose a product of $a$ disjoint cycles.
For the second prime length, we choose a product of $b$ disjoint cycles on the other points.
Let $B$ be generated by these $2$ permutations.
We let $B$ fix the $j$ unused points and omit a generator when its coefficient is zero.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
By Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-small-products}, every Sylow subgroup of $B^x$ is normal in $AB^x$.
Suppose that $A_0\ne1$.
We choose $u\in A_0$ with $|u|\in\{2,3\}$ and $|\operatorname{supp}(u)|\in\{3,4\}$.
Since every Sylow subgroup of $B^x$ is normal in $AB^x$, $u$ normalizes $B^x$.
As $|\operatorname{supp}(u)|\leq4$, the element $u$ maps each orbit of prime length of $B^x$ to itself.
A nontrivial affine automorphism on an orbit moves at least $10$ points, so $u$ induces none.
For each orbit of prime length $\Gamma$ of $B^x$, we have $u|_\Gamma\in C_{S_{\Gamma}}((B^x)^\Gamma)$.
The centralizer $C_{S_{\Gamma}}((B^x)^\Gamma)$ has order $11,13$ or $17$, so $u|_\Gamma=1$.
Thus, $\operatorname{supp}(u)$ lies in the $j$ fixed points of $B^x$.
This contradicts $|\operatorname{supp}(u)|>j$.
Consequently, $A_0=1$.

The first degree representation holds for every $n\geq90$. For every residue modulo $13$, we have a representative $17b+j\leq102$.
We may take $0\leq b\leq6$ and $0\leq j\leq2$.
For the interval $90\leq n\leq101$, we verify the integer representations directly.
Among smaller degrees $p+4$ with $p$ prime, only $n\in\{21,23,33,63\}$ lack the representation $n=13a+17b+j$.
For the prime degree $23$, we use \cite{YG}.
For the other degrees, we use Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-two} with $21=19+2$, $33=31+2$ and $63=61+2$.
For the second representation, we use the residues $13b+j$ modulo $11$.
For every $n\geq55$, we have $n=11a+13b+j$ with $a\geq0$, $0\leq b\leq4$ and $0\leq j\leq3$.
The interval $44\leq n\leq54$ is checked directly.
Below $44$, only degree $18$ lacks the required representation
among the degrees $p+5$ with $p$ prime under consideration.
For $n=18$, we use Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-prime-plus-one}.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] We have $|A|\notin\{2,3,4,6\}$.
\end{itemize}
Now, $A$ is cyclic of order $d\leq k+2\leq7$.
For $d=2,4$, Proposition \ref{prop:alternating-involutions} contradicts ordinary permutability of $A$.
For $d=3,6$, let $B$ be generated by the product of $2$ disjoint $5$-cycles.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
If $|AB^x|=15$, then the Sylow $5$-subgroup is normal.
For $|AB^x|=30$, Sylow's theorem allows $1$ or $6$ Sylow $5$-subgroups.
Suppose that $|AB^x|=30$ and $AB^x$ has $6$ Sylow $5$-subgroups.
Their nonidentity elements number $24$, leaving exactly the $6$ elements of $A$.
Let $\Sigma$ be the set of the $24$ nonidentity elements in Sylow $5$-subgroups of $AB^x$.
As $g\Sigma g^{-1}=\Sigma$ for every $g\in AB^x$ and $A=AB^x\setminus\Sigma$, we have $A\unlhd AB^x$.
Let $P$ be a Sylow $5$-subgroup of $AB^x$.
Because $A\unlhd AB^x$ and $5\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(A)|$, we have $[P,A]=1$.
As $AB^x=AP$, it follows that $P\unlhd AB^x$.
This contradicts the $6$ Sylow $5$-subgroups.
Therefore, $B^x\unlhd AB^x$.
We choose $c\in A$ with $|c|=3$.
As $B^x\unlhd AB^x$ and $3\nmid|\operatorname{Aut}(B^x)|=4$, we have $c\in C_G(B^x)$.
Let $B^x=\langle b\rangle$ and let $\Sigma=\operatorname{supp}(b)$.
Because $cb=bc$, we have $c\Sigma=\Sigma$.
We have $|\Sigma|=10$ and $|C_{S_{\Sigma}}(b|_\Sigma)|=50$.
As $3\nmid50$, we have $c|_\Sigma=\operatorname{id}_\Sigma$.
Because $c$ has at most $k+1\leq6$ fixed points, we obtain a contradiction.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] We have $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
For $d=5$ and $k=4$, an element of order $5$ fixes the $4$ outside points.
For $k=5$, an $A$-invariant subset of size $2$ cannot meet an outside orbit of length $5$.
As $\Delta$ has only $1$ $A$-fixed point, such an outside orbit would leave no invariant subset of size $2$.
Thus, $A$ fixes all points outside $\Delta$.
Let $B$ be generated by the product of $3$ disjoint $3$-cycles.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The product has order $15$, so it is cyclic.
The centralizer of the $3$ cycles on their support of size $9$ has order $162$.
Thus, a generator of $A$ of order $5$ fixes $9$ points.
This contradicts the bound of at most $k+1\leq6$ fixed points for a generator of $A$.

Finally, $d=7$ requires $k=5$ and $p\geq29$.
The action has at least $4$ orbits of length $7$ and $6$ fixed points.
Let $B$ be generated by the product of $3$ disjoint $3$-cycles.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AB^x$ a subgroup.
The product has order $21$, so $A$ is its normal Sylow $7$-subgroup.
Let $b$ generate $B^x$, so $|b|=3$ and $|\operatorname{supp}(b)|=9$.
Moving $3$ $A$-orbits of length $7$ would move $21$ points.
Thus, $b$ maps each $A$-orbit of length $7$ to itself.
If $bab^{-1}\ne a$ for a generator $a$ of $A$, then $b$ moves $6$ points on each such orbit.
As there are at least $4$ such orbits, $b$ would move at least $24$ points.
Therefore, $b$ centralizes $A$.
On each orbit of length $7$, $b$ lies in its cyclic centralizer of order $7$.
Because $|b|=3$, $b$ fixes each such orbit pointwise.
Then, $\operatorname{supp}(b)$ lies in the $6$ $A$-fixed points, contradicting its size $9$.
Thus, $d=1$ and $A=1$.

label: lem:alternating-finite-products
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-finite-products}
Let $J$ be a finite group.
The Sylow $\ell$-subgroups of $J$ are normal if
$|J|\mid2520d\ell$, where $1\leq d\leq9$ and $\ell\in\{47,59\}$.
The Sylow $23$-subgroups of $J$ are normal if $|J|\mid20160d\cdot23\cdot29$,
where $1\leq d\leq10$.
Suppose that $1\leq d\leq10$ and $C,B_{23},B_{29}\leq J$.
Assume that $J=C(B_{23}\times B_{29})$ and $|C|\mid20160d$.
Assume also that $|B_{23}|=23$ and $|B_{29}|=29$.
Then, $B_{29}$ is normal in $J$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
When $|J|\mid2520d\ell$, the possible nonabelian simple composition factors are
$A_5,A_6,A_7,A_8,\allowbreak\operatorname{PSL}_2(7),\allowbreak\operatorname{PSL}_2(8),\allowbreak\operatorname{PSL}_3(4)$.
Their automorphism orders are
$120,\allowbreak1440,\allowbreak5040,\allowbreak40320,\allowbreak336,\allowbreak1512,\allowbreak241920$.
None is divisible by $47$ or $59$, and
$|S|^2\nmid2520d\ell$ for every displayed simple group $S$.
When $|J|\mid20160d\cdot23\cdot29$, the further possibilities are $A_9,\operatorname{PSU}_3(3),\operatorname{PSp}_4(3),\operatorname{PSL}_2(29)$.
Their automorphism orders in this order are $362880,12096,51840,24360$.
From the order formulas for finite simple groups, we obtain the displayed lists of $S$ by divisibility.
We can also use the list in \cite{BreuerSimpleOrders}.
In particular, we have the bounds $1338120$ when $|J|\mid2520d\ell$ and $134467200$ when $|J|\mid20160d\cdot23\cdot29$.
In the second case, a minimal normal subgroup with several nonabelian simple factors is $A_5^2$ or $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)^2$.
We have $|\operatorname{Aut}(A_5^2)|=2\cdot120^2$ and $|\operatorname{Aut}(\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)^2)|=2\cdot336^2$.
For every displayed simple group $S$, we have
$|S|^3\nmid20160d\cdot23\cdot29$.

In the first case, an elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup $C_r^a$ satisfies $a\leq6$ for $r=2$.
In addition, we have $a\leq4$ for $r=3$ and $a\leq2$ for $r\in\{5,7\}$.
For the second case, only the bound at $r=2$ changes, to $a\leq9$.
For the displayed bounds on $a$, the orders $|\operatorname{GL}_a(r)|$ are prime to $47,59$
in the first case and to $23,29$ in the second.
For other primes $r$, the rank is at most $1$.
For the primes $\ell$ in the lemma, we have $v_\ell(|J|)\leq1$.
We also have $23\nmid28$ and $29\nmid22$.
A Sylow $\ell$-subgroup centralizes every minimal
normal subgroup of order prime to $\ell$.
The only possible nonabelian minimal normal subgroup whose order
is divisible by a prime $\ell$ in the lemma is $\operatorname{PSL}_2(29)$.

We induct on $|J|$ for $\ell\in\{47,59\}$.
For $\ell=23$ with $|J|\mid20160d\cdot23\cdot29$, we also induct on $|J|$.
If $\ell\nmid|J|$, then its Sylow $\ell$-subgroup is trivial.
Suppose that $\ell\mid|J|$, so $v_\ell(|J|)=1$.
We choose a minimal normal subgroup $N$.
If $N$ is an $\ell$-group, then $N$ is a normal Sylow $\ell$-subgroup of $J$.
Otherwise, a Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $P$ centralizes $N$.
By induction, we have $PN/N\unlhd J/N$.
The inverse image of $PN/N$ under $J\to J/N$ is $NP=N\times P$, in which $P$ is characteristic.
Hence, $P\lhd J$.

Suppose that $J=CB_{29}$ with $|C|\mid20160d$.
We choose a minimal normal subgroup $N$ of $J$.
If $N$ is a $29$-group, then $N=B_{29}$ and $B_{29}\unlhd J$.
Suppose that $29\nmid|N|$.
Then, $B_{29}$ centralizes $N$.
We have $J/N=(CN/N)(B_{29}N/N)$ and $|CN/N|\mid20160d$.
By induction, $B_{29}N/N\unlhd J/N$.
The inverse image of $B_{29}N/N$ under $J\to J/N$ is $N\times B_{29}$. Its Sylow $29$-subgroup $B_{29}$ is characteristic.
Therefore, $B_{29}\unlhd J$.
The only other possibility is $N\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(29)$.
Since $v_{29}(|J|)=1$, we have $B_{29}\leq N$.
Thus, $J=CN$ and $[N:N\cap C]=[J:C]=29$.
By Dickson's classification \cite[Tables 8.1--8.2]{BHR}, every proper subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(29)$ has order at most $\max\{29\cdot28/2,30,60\}=406$.
A subgroup of index $29$ would have order $(29^2-1)/2=420>406$, a contradiction.
Thus, $B_{29}$ is normal in every such product.

In the mixed product, $B_{23}\lhd J$.
Let $\rho:J\to J/B_{23}$ be the quotient map.
By the preceding argument, we have $\rho(B_{29})\lhd J/B_{23}$.
The inverse image $\rho^{-1}(\rho(B_{29}))$ is $B_{23}\times B_{29}$ and is normal in $J$.
Since $B_{29}$ is characteristic in $B_{23}\times B_{29}$, we have $B_{29}\lhd J$.
