label: lem:e7-primitive-regular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:e7-primitive-regular}
Let $q\geq2$ be a prime power and $s\in\{14,18\}$.
Let $\ell$ be a primitive prime divisor of $q^s-1$.
The group $E_7(q)$ has a torus $T_s$ of order $(q+1)\Phi_s(q)/(2,q-1)$.
Let $\mathbf T_s$ be the algebraic torus containing $T_s$ in the adjoint algebraic group $\mathbf G$ of type $E_7$.
For every $B\leq T_s$ with $|B|=\ell$, we have $C_{\mathbf G}(B)^\circ=\mathbf T_s$.
The quotient $N_{E_7(q)}(T_{14})/T_{14}$ has order prime to $3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the simply connected algebraic group of type $E_7$ and the root lattice $\Lambda$ of type $E_7$.
The lattice has rank $7$ and determinant $2$.
Moreover, every root has squared length $2$.
For the Weyl group action, a Coxeter element $w_{18}$ has characteristic polynomial
$\Phi_{18}(X)(X+1)$, and $w_{18}^9=-I$.
For $w_{14}$, use minus a Coxeter element on the $A_6$ chain
$1,3,4,5,6,7$ in the Bourbaki diagram.
The characteristic polynomial of $w_{14}$ is $\Phi_{14}(X)(X+1)$.
No root lies in the negative eigenline of either element.
For $w_{18}$, the claim follows from the root orbits of length
$18$. For the $A_6$ chain, no root is perpendicular to all $6$ roots.

Choose a generator $b$ of the subgroup of order $\ell$ and $\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^*$ with $|\zeta|=\ell$.
Since $\det\Lambda=2$ and $\ell$ is odd, a nonzero $v\in\Lambda/\ell\Lambda$ satisfies $\alpha(b)=\zeta^{(\alpha,v)}$ for every root $\alpha$.
We have $w_sv=qv$ or $w_sv=q^{-1}v$ modulo $\ell$.
Suppose that $(\alpha,v)=0\pmod\ell$.
Then, $(w_s^j\alpha,v)=0\pmod\ell$ for every integer $j$.
The component of $\alpha$ in $\ker\Phi_s(w_s)\leq\Lambda\otimes\mathbb Q$ is nonzero and has degree $6$.
Thus, the rational span $U$ of the $w_s$-orbit of $\alpha$ has dimension $6$ or $7$.
We choose a basis of roots from the orbit and let $\Lambda_0$ be
the lattice they generate.
The saturation $S=\Lambda\cap U$ of $\Lambda_0$ has integral Gram determinant
at least $1$.
By Hadamard's inequality, we have $[S:\Lambda_0]\leq8$ in dimension $6$.
As $\det\Lambda=2$ in dimension $7$, we also have $[S:\Lambda_0]\leq8$.
Because $\ell\geq19$, the chosen basis roots span $S$ modulo $\ell$.
The lattice pairing is nonsingular modulo $\ell$.
If $\dim U=7$, then we obtain that $v=0$.
If $\dim U=6$, then the annihilator of $U$ is the negative eigenline.
But the Weyl eigenvalue on $v$ has order $s$, and is not $-1$.
This contradicts the Weyl eigenvalue on $v$.

From the $2$ characteristic polynomials, we obtain the torus orders.
For $w_{14}$, we have the rational linear centralizer algebra $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{14})\times\mathbb Q$.
Its unit group $\mathbb Q(\zeta_{14})^*\times\mathbb Q^*$ has torsion subgroup of order $28$.
Since the Weyl centralizer is finite, its order is prime to $3$.
Thus, $N_{E_7(q)}(T_{14})/T_{14}$ has order prime to $3$.
Let $\widetilde G=E_7(q)_{\rm sc}$ be the finite group obtained from the simply connected algebraic group.
Let $\eta:\widetilde G\to E_7(q)$ be the central quotient, with $|\ker\eta|=(2,q-1)$.
For $B\leq T_s$ of order $\ell$, the subgroup $\eta^{-1}(B)$ has a unique Sylow $\ell$-subgroup $\widetilde B$.
The map $\eta|_{\widetilde B}:\widetilde B\to B$ is an isomorphism.
head: environment

label: thm:e7
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] For $p=\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q$, we have $|A|_p<q^9$.
\end{itemize}
Let $G=E_7(q)$.
For the algebraic group containing $G$, let $\mathbf G$ be the adjoint group of type $E_7$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$, with $G\leq\mathbf G(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$.
To specify the central quotient, let $\widetilde{\mathbf G}$ be the simply connected algebraic group of type $E_7$.
Let $\kappa_0:\widetilde{\mathbf G}\to\mathbf G$ be the central isogeny with $\ker\kappa_0=Z(\widetilde{\mathbf G})$.
On finite groups, $\kappa_0$ induces the central quotient $\eta:\widetilde G=E_7(q)_{\rm sc}\to G$.
Next, let $d=(2,q-1)$ and $e=(3,q+1)$.
Let $f=q^6-q^3+1$ and $r=f/e$.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
Now, we take the cyclic torus $T=T_{18}$.
Then, we have $|T|=(q+1)f/d$.
Let $M$ be the unique maximal subgroup of $G$ with $T\leq M$.
For this subgroup, we have $L={}^2E_6(q)_{\rm sc}\unlhd M$
\cite[Proposition 2.11 and Table 6]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
The intersection $T_0=T\cap L$ is a cyclic torus of order $f$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AT^x$ a subgroup.
By \cite[Proposition 4.2]{LiXia}, we have $TY\ne G$ for every $Y<G$.
Thus, $AT^x<G$ and $A\leq M^x$.

The subgroup $C=\operatorname{PSL}_2(q^7)\rtimes C_7$ is maximal for every $q$
\cite[Theorem 1.1 and Table 4.1]{CravenE7}.
From the group orders, we have
$$
 \frac{|M||C|}{|G|}
 =\frac{14(q+1)(q^9+1)(q^5+1)}
 {d q^{20}(q^{10}-1)(q^{18}-1)}
 <448q^{-33}<1.
$$
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ with $AC^y$ a subgroup.
As $|M||C|<|G|$, we have $AC^y<G$.
By maximality of $C$, we have $A\leq C^y$.
In particular,
$|A|_p\leq q^7(7)_p<q^9$.
Because $7<q^2$, the strict bound $|A|_p<q^9$ also holds when $p=7$.
Every prime divisor of $r$ is primitive for exponent $18$.
The only possible nonprimitive divisor of $f$ is $3$,
and $v_3(f)=1$ when $e=3$.
Hence, $(r,|C|)=1$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] $A$ normalizes $T$.
\end{itemize}
Choose $z\in G$ with $AT^z\leq M^z$.
Replacing $A,y$ by $A^{z^{-1}},y z^{-1}$, let $K=AT\leq M$.
Let $J=K\cap L$.
Since $L\unlhd M$ and $K\leq M$, we have $J\unlhd K$ and $T_0\leq J$.
Let $\kappa:L\to L/Z(L)$ be the central quotient map and let $\overline J=\kappa(J)$.
As $|\overline J|_p\leq|J|_p\leq|A|_p<q^9<q^{36}=|L/Z(L)|_p$, we have $\overline J<L/Z(L)$ and $J<L$.
Let $M_1$ be the unique maximal subgroup of $L/Z(L)$ with $\kappa(T_0)\leq M_1$.
By uniqueness of $M_1$, we have $\overline J\leq M_1$. Moreover, $L_1\unlhd M_1$, where $L_1=\operatorname{PSU}_3(q^3)$.
Let $J_1=\overline J\cap L_1$.
To use the unitary group, let $\kappa_1:\operatorname{SU}_3(q^3)\to\operatorname{PSU}_3(q^3)$ be the standard quotient.
We have a cyclic torus $\widetilde T_1\leq\kappa_1^{-1}(J_1)$ with $|\widetilde T_1|=f=q^6-q^3+1$.
Also, $|\kappa_1^{-1}(J_1)|_p<q^9$.
By Bereczky's theorem \cite{Bereczky}\cite[Theorem 2.1.7]{Brookfield2014}, we have $J_1\leq N_{\operatorname{PSU}_3(q^3)}(\kappa_1(\widetilde T_1))$.
Since $q^3\geq8$, Bereczky's theorem has no small exception.

The subgroup $\overline R$ of order $r$ is $O_{3'}(J_1)$,
and is characteristic in $J_1$.
Since $L_1\unlhd M_1$ and $\overline J\leq M_1$, we have $J_1\unlhd\overline J$.
Thus, $\overline R\unlhd\overline J$ and $\overline J$ lies in the corresponding Singer normalizer of $L/Z(L)$.
Let $X=(\kappa|_J)^{-1}(\overline R)$.
By the choice of $X$, the map $\kappa|_X:X\to\overline R$ is surjective, with central kernel $X\cap Z(L)$ of order dividing $3$.
By Schur--Zassenhaus, we choose a Hall $3'$-subgroup $R_1$ of $X$.
For every Hall $3'$-subgroup $R_2$ of $X$, we choose $z\in\ker(\kappa|_X)$ with $R_1^z=R_2$.
Since $\ker(\kappa|_X)\leq Z(X)$, we have $R_2=R_1$.
The unique Hall $3'$-subgroup is $R\leq T_0$ of order $r$.
Consequently, $R\unlhd J$ and $J/R$ is a $3$-group.
By Lemma \ref{lem:e7-primitive-regular}, we have $C_L(R)=T_0$.
Thus, $R=O_{3'}(J)$.
Since $R=O_{3'}(J)$ and $J\unlhd K$, we have $R\unlhd K$.
Let $\mathbf T$ be the algebraic torus containing $T$.
A subgroup of $R$ of primitive prime order has connected algebraic centralizer $\mathbf T$ by Lemma \ref{lem:e7-primitive-regular}.
As $R\leq T$, we obtain that $C_{\mathbf G}(R)^\circ=\mathbf T$.
Consequently, $K\leq N_G(T)$ and $A\leq N_G(T)$.
We have $N_G(T)/T\cong C_{18}$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] We have $|A\cap T|\mid9$ and $|A|\mid162$.
\end{itemize}
We now bound $U=A\cap T$.
Since $A\leq C^y$ and $(r,|C|)=1$, the subgroup $U$ lies in the Hall $r'$-subgroup $V$ of $T$.
Let $\mathbf D\leq\widetilde{\mathbf G}$ be the algebraic torus of dimension $1$ centralizing the $E_6$ derived Levi.
For its rational points, let $\widetilde D=\mathbf D(\mathbb{F}_q)\leq\widetilde G$.
Let $\rho:\widetilde{\mathbf G}\to\operatorname{GL}(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}W)$ be the minuscule representation on $W=\mathbb{F}_q^{56}$.
For this representation, the $\mathbf D$-weight spaces $W_j\leq\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_q}W$ satisfy
$\dim W_1=\dim W_{-1}=27$ and $\dim W_3=\dim W_{-3}=1$.
Next, let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_7$ be the simple roots in Bourbaki's numbering.
To describe $\mathbf D$, we take twice the seventh fundamental coweight
$$
 \tau(\lambda)=\prod_{i=1}^7\alpha_i^\vee(\lambda^{c_i}),
 \  (c_1,\ldots,c_7)=(2,3,4,6,5,4,3).
$$
The map $\tau:\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^*\to\mathbf D$ has image $\mathbf D$.
Then, $\rho(\tau(\lambda))|_{W_j}=\lambda^j I$.
We have $\ker\eta=\langle \tau(-1)\rangle$.
For the rational points, let $F$ be the Frobenius endomorphism on $\widetilde{\mathbf G}$.
On $\mathbf D$, we have $F(\tau(\lambda))=\tau(\lambda^{-q})$.
Therefore, $\widetilde D=\{\tau(\lambda):\lambda^{q+1}=1\}$.
Thus, $D=\eta(\widetilde D)\leq T$ has order $(q+1)/d$.
Since $f=er$ and $\gcd(r,q+1)=1$, the Hall $r'$-subgroup $V$ of $T$ has order $(q+1)e/d$.
Because $D\leq T$ and $|D|=(q+1)/d$, we have $D\leq V$ and $[V:D]=e$.
The index $[V:D]=e$ accounts for the possible central factor $3$ in $E_6$.

Since $T$ is abelian and $A/(A\cap T)$ is cyclic, $A$ is soluble.
Let $P$ be the maximal parabolic subgroup with $E_6$ Levi subgroup.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $z\in G$ with $AP^z$ a subgroup.
As $A$ is soluble and $P^z<G$, we have $AP^z\ne G$ by \cite[Proposition 4.2]{LiXia}.
Hence, $A\leq P^z$.
We have a subspace $W_0\leq W$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_q}W_0=1$ and $\rho(\eta^{-1}(A))W_0=W_0$.
For $g\in A\cap D$, choose $\lambda$ with $\lambda^{q+1}=1$ and $\widetilde g=\tau(\lambda)$ satisfying $\eta(\widetilde g)=g$.
The eigenvalue of $\rho(\widetilde g)|_{W_0}$ is $\lambda^j\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$,
where $j\in\{1,-1,3,-3\}$.
Since $\lambda^j\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$ and $\lambda^{q+1}=1$, we have $\lambda^j=\lambda^{qj}=\lambda^{-j}$.
Thus, $\lambda^{2j}=1$.
After the quotient by $\langle \tau(-1)\rangle$, the order of $g$ divides $|j|$.
As $A\cap D$ is cyclic, we have $|A\cap D|\mid3$.
Because $U\leq V$ and $[V:D]=e\mid3$, we have $[U:U\cap D]\mid3$.
Hence, $|U|\mid9$.
Since $A/U$ is a subgroup of $C_{18}$, we have $|A|\mid162$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] We have $|A|\leq2$ and $A=1$ for odd $q$.
\end{itemize}
We take a primitive prime $\ell$ of $q^{14}-1$ and
$B=C_\ell$ in $T_{14}$.
The prime $\ell$ exists for every $q$, and $\ell\equiv1\pmod{14}$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AB^x\leq G$.
Let $n_\ell$ be the number of Sylow $\ell$-subgroups of $K$.
Note that $|A|\mid162$. Thus, $n_\ell\mid162$ and $n_\ell\equiv1\pmod\ell$.
If $n_\ell>1$, then $n_\ell\in\{2,3,6,9,18,27,54,81,162\}$.
Because $\ell\mid n_\ell-1$, we would have $\ell\in\{2,5,7,13,17,23,53\}$.
But no prime in that set is $1$ modulo $14$.
Therefore, $n_\ell=1$. Hence, $B^x\unlhd K$ and $A\leq N_G(B^x)$.
We obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:e7-primitive-regular} that $C_{\mathbf G}(B^x)^\circ=\mathbf T_{14}^x$.
As $B^x\unlhd K$, we have $A\leq N_G(T_{14}^x)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:e7-primitive-regular}, the quotient $N_G(T_{14}^x)/T_{14}^x$ has order prime to $3$.
Thus, a Sylow $3$-subgroup $Q$ of $A$ lies in $T_{14}^x$ and is cyclic.
Let $\mathbf D_{14}$ be the algebraic torus of dimension $1$ centralizing the $A_6$ subgroup with rational points $\operatorname{SU}_7(q)^x$.
Because $3\nmid\Phi_{14}(q)$, we have $Q\leq\mathbf D_{14}\cap G$.
Every element of $Q$ has algebraic centralizer
dimension at least $49$.
If $p=3$, then $3\nmid|T_{14}|$.
Hence, $Q=1$.

Suppose that $p\ne3$ and $Q\ne1$, and let $c$ have order $3$ in $Q$.
If $Q\cap T\ne1$, then the cyclic group $Q$ has its unique subgroup of order $3$ in $Q\cap T$.
Therefore, $c\in U\leq V$.
If $e=1$, then $V=D$.
If $e=3$, then $3\mid|D|$.
Since $V$ is cyclic, every $h\in V$ with $|h|=3$ lies in $D$.
The rational lift of $c$ of order $3$ is $\tau(\lambda)$ with $|\lambda|=3$.
For a root $\beta$ outside the $E_6$ subsystem, we have $\beta(\tau(\lambda))=\lambda^2$ or $\lambda^{-2}$.
Thus, $C_{\mathbf G}(c)^\circ=E_6T_1$.
The rational centralizer $C_G(c)$ is unitary.
Every prime dividing $|C_G(c)|$ divides
$$
 (q+1)q^{36}(q^2-1)(q^5+1)(q^6-1)(q^8-1)(q^9+1)(q^{12}-1).
$$
Since $14$ divides none of $2,6,8,12,2\cdot1,2\cdot5,2\cdot9$, no primitive divisor of $q^{14}-1$ divides $|C_G(c)|$.
But $c$ centralizes $B^x$, a contradiction.

Thus, $Q\cap T=1$.
Let $\omega_{18}:N_G(T)/T\to\langle w_{18}\rangle\leq W(E_7)$ be the rational Weyl group identification for $T$.
Let $\nu_{18}:N_G(T)\to\langle w_{18}\rangle$ satisfy $\nu_{18}(g)=\omega_{18}(gT)$.
Since $Q\cap T=1$ and $|c|=3$, we have $\nu_{18}(c)\in\{w_{18}^6,w_{18}^{12}\}$.
Let $\mathbf T$ be the algebraic torus containing $T$.
For the Cartan part, we have a fixed space of dimension $1$ for $\operatorname{Ad}(c)|_{\operatorname{Lie}(\mathbf T)}$.
In addition, on the root spaces, $\nu_{18}(c)$ has $42$ cycles of length $3$.
As $|c|=3$, each cycle contributes $1$ fixed dimension.
The centralizer of $c$ is smooth, so we obtain that
$\dim C_{\mathbf G}(c)=43$.
This contradicts the previous lower bound $49$.
We conclude that $Q=1$, so $A$ is trivial or has order $2$.
For odd $q$, $|A|=2$ contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:split-root-normalizer}.
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 5.} ] We have $A=1$ for even $q$.
\end{itemize}
Suppose that $q$ is even.
Let $E\rtimes\operatorname{SL}_3(3)\leq F_4(2)$ be the subgroup in Lemma \ref{lem:f4-odd-normalizer}, with $E\cong C_3^3$.
We use the chain $F_4(2)\leq E_6(2)\leq E_7(2)\leq E_7(q)$.
For the first inclusion, we realize $F_4(2)$ inside the subgroup of $E_6(2)$ fixed by its graph automorphism.
The inclusion $F_4(2)\to E_6(2)$ sends $g$ to $g$.
Next, we realize $E_6(2)$ as the derived $E_6$ Levi subgroup of $E_7(2)$.
The inclusion $E_6(2)\to E_7(2)$ sends each root element $x_\alpha(t)$ to $x_\alpha(t)$ for $t\in\mathbb{F}_2$.
Finally, the inclusion $E_7(2)\to E_7(q)$ sends each root element $x_\alpha(t)$ to $x_\alpha(t)$ for $t\in\mathbb{F}_2$.
For the subgroup used below, let $B=E\rtimes C_{13}$, of order $351$.
The characteristic subgroup $O_3(B)=E$ is not toral in $\mathbf G$.
Otherwise, the induced automorphism of $E$ of order $13$ would lie in
a Weyl quotient, whereas $13\nmid|W(E_7)|$
\cite[Proposition 5.1]{AnDietrichLitterick}.
For the unique class of subgroups $E\cong C_3^3$ not contained in an algebraic torus, we have
$\dim C_{\mathbf G}(E)=3, N_{\mathbf G}(E)/C_{\mathbf G}(E)\cong\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$
\cite[Proposition 6.1 and Table 3]{AnDietrichLitterick}.
Let $u\in N_G(B)$ have order $2$.
Because $E=O_3(B)$ is characteristic in $B$, we have $u\in N_{\mathbf G}(E)$.
The coset $uC_{\mathbf G}(E)$ normalizes the image of $C_{13}$ in $N_{\mathbf G}(E)/C_{\mathbf G}(E)\cong\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$.
Since $N_{\operatorname{SL}_3(3)}(C_{13})=C_{13}\rtimes C_3$ has odd order, the coset $uC_{\mathbf G}(E)$ is the identity.
Therefore, $u$ centralizes $E$.

As $|E|=27$ is prime to the characteristic, $C_{\mathbf G}(E)$ is smooth
\cite[Theorem 13.9]{MilneAlgebraicGroups}.
Let $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(\mathbf G)$, of dimension $133$. Thus, $\dim\mathfrak g^E=3$.
For $\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(E,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_2^*)$, let
$\mathfrak g_\chi=\{X\in\mathfrak g:\operatorname{Ad}(e)X=\chi(e)X\text{ for all }e\in E\}$.
For $s\in\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$ and $e\in E$, let $\chi^s(e)=\chi(s^{-1}es)$.
As $\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$ induces its natural action on $E\cong\mathbb{F}_3^3$, it is transitive on the $26$ characters $\chi\ne1$.
Hence, $\dim\mathfrak g_\chi=5$ for $\chi\ne1$.
For an involution $u$ centralizing $E$, we have $\operatorname{Ad}(u)\mathfrak g_\chi=\mathfrak g_\chi$ for every $\chi$.
As $u^2=1$ and the characteristic is $2$, we have $(\operatorname{Ad}(u)-I)^2=0$.
On each $\mathfrak g_\chi$, the image of $\operatorname{Ad}(u)-I$ lies in its kernel.
By rank-nullity, the rank on $\mathfrak g_\chi$ is at most $\lfloor\dim\mathfrak g_\chi/2\rfloor$.
Consequently, $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(u)-I)\leq1+26\lfloor5/2\rfloor=53$.
Because $T$ is odd, each involution of $N_G(T)$ maps to $w_{18}^9=-I$ in $N_G(T)/T\cong C_{18}$.
The rational Tits representatives split the Weyl group in characteristic $2$.
Let $n$ represent $w_{18}^9$.
As squaring is bijective on $T$, for each involution $t\in N_G(T)$ there exists $z\in T$ with $t^z=n$.
On the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak t$, we have $\operatorname{Ad}(n)|_{\mathfrak t}=I$.
For each root $\alpha$, we have $\operatorname{Ad}(n)\mathfrak g_\alpha=\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$.
The $126$ root spaces form $63$ pairs $\{\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}\}$.
Hence, $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t)-I)=63$ for every involution $t\in N_G(T)$.

If $|A|=2$, then write $A=\langle t\rangle$ and choose $x_1\in G$ with $K=AB^{x_1}$ a subgroup.
Since $[K:B^{x_1}]=2$, we have $t\in N_G(B^{x_1})$ and $t^{x_1^{-1}}\in N_G(B)$.
As $t^{x_1^{-1}}$ is conjugate to $t$, we have $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t^{x_1^{-1}})-I)=63$.
But $t^{x_1^{-1}}\in N_G(B)$ requires $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t^{x_1^{-1}})-I)\leq53$, a contradiction.
Thus, $A=1$ for every even $q$ as well.

label: lem:e8-primitive-regular
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:e8-primitive-regular}
Let $q\geq2$ be a prime power and $d\in\{20,24\}$.
Let $\ell$ be a primitive prime divisor of $q^d-1$.
There are a torus $S\leq E_8(q)$ and a subgroup $B\leq S$ with $|S|=\Phi_d(q)$ and $|B|=\ell$.
Moreover, $N_{E_8(q)}(B)\leq N_{E_8(q)}(S)$ and $|N_{E_8(q)}(S)|=d\Phi_d(q)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Weyl group has a regular element $w_d$ with irreducible
characteristic polynomial $\Phi_d(X)$ and centralizer $C_d$
\cite[Corollary 4.3 and Table 3]{SpringerRegular}.
For this Weyl element, let $S$ be the corresponding rational torus, with $|S|=\Phi_d(q)$.
Since Zsigmondy's theorem has no exception at either degree, we take $B=C_\ell\leq S$.
Since $\ell\equiv1\pmod d$, we have $\ell\geq41$ for $d=20$
and $\ell\geq73$ for $d=24$.

Let $\Lambda$ be the unimodular $E_8$ root lattice.
Let $\zeta\in\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q^*$ have order $\ell$, and let $b$ generate $B$.
Since $\Lambda$ is unimodular, we represent $b$ by a nonzero $v\in\Lambda/\ell\Lambda$ with $\alpha(b)=\zeta^{(\alpha,v)}$ for every root $\alpha$.
As $v$ represents a rational point of $S$, we have $w_dv=qv$ or $w_dv=q^{-1}v$.
If $\alpha|_B=1$, then $(w_d^j\alpha,v)=0\pmod\ell$ for every integer $j$ and either Weyl eigenvalue.
Because $\Phi_d(X)$ is irreducible of degree $8$, the roots $\alpha,w_d\alpha,\ldots,w_d^7\alpha$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$.
Each has Euclidean norm $\sqrt2$.
The sublattice they generate has index at most
$(\sqrt2)^8=16$
by Hadamard's inequality and unimodularity.
Thus, the $8$ roots $\alpha,w_d\alpha,\ldots,w_d^7\alpha$ span $\Lambda$ modulo $\ell$.
As every chosen root annihilates $v$, we would have $v=0$.
This contradicts the choice of $v$.
For every root $\alpha$, we have $\alpha|_B\ne1$.
The connected algebraic centralizer of $B$ is the underlying torus of $S$.
Every $g\in N_{E_8(q)}(B)$ normalizes the algebraic torus containing $S$.
Hence, $N_{E_8(q)}(B)\leq N_{E_8(q)}(S)$, of order $d\Phi_d(q)$.
head: environment

label: thm:e8
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G=E_8(q)$.
For its algebraic realization, let $\mathbf G$ be the group of type $E_8$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$, with $G=\mathbf G(\mathbb{F}_q)$.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
We first choose the Coxeter torus $T\leq G$, of order
$t_T=\Phi_{30}(q)=q^8+q^7-q^5-q^4-q^3+q+1$.
The unique maximal subgroup $M<G$ with $T\leq M$ is the soluble normalizer $T\rtimes C_{30}$
\cite[Proposition 2.11 and Table 6]{GuralnickMalle2012}.
By \cite[Proposition 4.2]{LiXia}, we have $G\ne XY$ whenever $X,Y<G$ and at least one of $X,Y$ is soluble.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AT^x$ a subgroup.
Because $T$ is soluble, $AT^x<G$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(T^x)$.
In particular, $A$ is soluble.
Replacing $T$ by $T^x$, assume that $A\leq N_G(T)$.

Let $P$ be the standard maximal parabolic subgroup with $E_7$ Levi subgroup.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ with $AP^y$ a subgroup.
As $A$ is soluble and $P^y<G$, we have $AP^y\ne G$ by the cited product condition.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $A\leq P^y$.
The order of $P$ is
$|P|=q^{120}(q-1)\prod_{d\in\{2,6,8,10,12,14,18\}}(q^d-1)$.
A nonprimitive prime divisor of $\Phi_{30}(q)$ would belong to $\{2,3,5\}$.
For a nonprimitive divisor $\ell\in\{2,3,5\}$, we would need $\operatorname{ord}_\ell(q)=30/\ell$.
But $30/\ell\nmid\ell-1$ for every $\ell\in\{2,3,5\}$.
Consequently, every prime dividing $\Phi_{30}(q)$ is primitive for exponent $30$.
Hence, $(t_T,|P|)=1$ and $A\cap T=1$.
Let $w\in W(E_8)$ be the Coxeter element associated with $T$.
Let $\omega_T:N_G(T)/T\to\langle w\rangle$ be the rational Weyl group identification.
For $g\in N_G(T)$, let $\nu_T(g)=\omega_T(gT)$.
Because $A\cap T=1$, the homomorphism $\nu_T:N_G(T)\to\langle w\rangle$ is injective on $A$.
Thus, $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid30$.

For $d\in\{20,24\}$, let $B_d=C_{\ell_d}$ be the subgroup in Lemma \ref{lem:e8-primitive-regular}.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $z_d\in G$ with $K_d=AB_d^{z_d}\leq G$.
Let $n_{\ell_d}$ be the number of Sylow $\ell_d$-subgroups of $K_d$.
By Sylow's theorem, $n_{\ell_d}\mid|A|$ and $n_{\ell_d}\equiv1\pmod{\ell_d}$.
As $|A|\leq30<\ell_d$, we have $n_{\ell_d}=1$.
Thus, $B_d^{z_d}\unlhd K_d$ and $A\leq N_G(B_d^{z_d})$.
Now,
$\Phi_{20}(q)=q^8-q^6+q^4-q^2+1, \Phi_{24}(q)=q^8-q^4+1$.
As $\Phi_{20}(q)\equiv1\pmod3$ and $3\nmid20$, the order $20\Phi_{20}(q)$ is prime to $3$.
Because $\Phi_{24}(q)\equiv1\pmod5$ and $5\nmid24$, the order $24\Phi_{24}(q)$ is prime to $5$.
Therefore, $|A|=1$ or $2$.
For odd $q$, we have $A=1$ by Corollary \ref{cor:split-odd-involutions}.

Suppose that $q=2^f$ and $|A|=2$.
We use the rational subgroup chain
$F_4(2)\leq E_6(2)\leq E_8(2)\leq E_8(q)$.
To specify the inclusions, we realize $F_4(2)$ as a subgroup of $E_6(2)$ fixed by its graph automorphism
\cite[Table 9]{CravenExceptional}.
The inclusion map $F_4(2)\to E_6(2)$ sends $g$ to $g$.
Next, we realize $E_6(2)$ by the split $E_6$ root subsystem of $E_8(2)$.
The inclusion $E_6(2)\to E_8(2)$ sends each root element $x_\alpha(t)$ to $x_\alpha(t)$ for $t\in\mathbb{F}_2$.
Finally, the inclusion $E_8(2)\to E_8(q)$ sends each root element $x_\alpha(t)$ to $x_\alpha(t)$ for $t\in\mathbb{F}_2$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:f4-odd-normalizer}, we have $E\rtimes S\leq F_4(2)$.
We take $E=C_3^3$ and $S=\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$ with a faithful action on $E$.
Then, we take $C=C_{13}\leq S$ and let $B=E\rtimes C$.

The group $S$ induces an automorphism of $E$ of order $13$, and $13\nmid|W(E_8)|=696729600$.
By \cite[Proposition 5.1]{AnDietrichLitterick}, $E$ is not contained in an algebraic torus of $\mathbf G$.
Since $S$ is transitive on $E\setminus\{1\}$, all nonidentity elements of $E$ are conjugate in $\mathbf G$.
Thus, $E\cong C_3^3$ belongs to class $(3^3)_b$.
We have $C_{\mathbf G}(E)=E\times G_2$ and $N_{\mathbf G}(E)/C_{\mathbf G}(E)=\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$ \cite[Proposition 6.1 and Table 3]{AnDietrichLitterick}.
The subgroup $S$ maps onto $N_{\mathbf G}(E)/C_{\mathbf G}(E)$.

Every involution $u\in N_G(B)$ normalizes $E=O_3(B)$.
We take $\rho:N_{\mathbf G}(E)\to\operatorname{Aut}(E)$ with $\rho(n)(e)=nen^{-1}$.
Then, $\rho(u)\in N_{\rho(S)}(\rho(C))\cong C_{13}\rtimes C_3$.
Since $\rho$ is a homomorphism and $u^2=1$, we have $\rho(u)^2=1$.
As $|C_{13}\rtimes C_3|$ is odd, we have $\rho(u)=1$.
Therefore, $u$ centralizes $E$.
Let $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(\mathbf G)$ and $V=\mathfrak g$, the adjoint module of dimension $248$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$.
As $|E|$ is prime to the characteristic, $\operatorname{Ad}|_E:E\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is semisimple
and $C_{\mathbf G}(E)$ is smooth
\cite[Theorem 13.9]{MilneAlgebraicGroups}.
Thus, $\dim V^E=14$.
For $\chi\in\operatorname{Hom}(E,\overline{\mathbb{F}}_2^*)$, let
$V_\chi=\{v\in V:\operatorname{Ad}(e)v=\chi(e)v\text{ for all }e\in E\}$.
For $s\in S$ and $e\in E$, let $\chi^s(e)=\chi(s^{-1}es)$.
Because $S=\operatorname{SL}_3(3)$ is transitive on the $26$ characters $\chi\ne1$, we have $\dim V_\chi=(248-14)/26=9$.
We have $\operatorname{Ad}(u)V_\chi=V_\chi$ for every $\chi$.
For a space $W_0$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_2$ with $\dim W_0=n$, let $t\in\operatorname{GL}(W_0)$ be an involution.
Then, $(t-I_{W_0})^2=0$, so $\operatorname{im}(t-I_{W_0})\leq\ker(t-I_{W_0})$.
By rank-nullity, $\operatorname{rank}(t-I_{W_0})\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor$.
Hence,
$\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(u)-I) \leq7+26\cdot4=111$.

Write $A=\langle t\rangle$.
Then, $\nu_T(t)=w^{15}=-I$, where $w$ is the Coxeter element associated with $T$.
In characteristic $2$, the Tits representatives form a copy of the Weyl group.
Let $n$ represent $w^{15}$.
Since $n$ commutes with the Coxeter representative, we have $n\in N_G(T)$.
As $|T|$ is odd, we choose $z\in T$ with $t^z=n$ by Schur--Zassenhaus.
On the Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak t$ with $\dim\mathfrak t=8$, we have $\operatorname{Ad}(n)|_{\mathfrak t}=I$.
For each root $\alpha$, we have $\operatorname{Ad}(n)\mathfrak g_\alpha=\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$.
The $240$ root spaces form $120$ pairs $\{\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}\}$.
Hence, $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t)-I)=120$.

Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x_1\in G$ with $K=AB^{x_1}$ a subgroup.
As $[K:B^{x_1}]=2$, we have $t\in N_G(B^{x_1})$ and $t^{x_1^{-1}}\in N_G(B)$.
We have $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t^{x_1^{-1}})-I)=\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t)-I)$.
Hence, $\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{Ad}(t^{x_1^{-1}})-I)=120\leq111$, a contradiction.
Therefore, $A=1$ for even $q$ also.

label: thm:large-ree
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:large-ree}
Let $q=2^{2n+1}$ with $n\geq1$.
Then, ${}^2F_4(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary
${}^2F_4(q)$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof of the theorem into the following steps.

\setlist[itemize]{leftmargin=4em,labelsep=.5em,topsep=.2\baselineskip,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt}
\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 1.} ] $A$ is cyclic and $|A|\mid4$.
\end{itemize}
Let $G={}^2F_4(q)$ and $s=\sqrt{2q}$.
By \cite[Proposition 4.2]{LiXia}, we have $G\ne XY$ whenever $X,Y<G$ and at least one of $X,Y$ is soluble.
We take cyclic tori $T_+$ and $T_-$ of orders $t_\pm=q^2+q+1\pm s(q+1)$.
By \cite[Proposition 2.11 and Table 6]{GuralnickMalle2012}, the unique maximal subgroup $M<G$ with $T_+\leq M$ is $N_G(T_+)$.
We have $N_G(T_+)/T_+\cong C_{12}$.
By \cite[Theorem 20]{WilsonSuzukiRee}, both $N_G(T_-)=T_-\rtimes C_{12}$ and $\operatorname{Sz}(q)\wr S_2$ are maximal.
Both $t_\pm$ are odd and prime to $3(q+1)$.
Their greatest common divisor divides $2s(q+1)$ and is $1$.

Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $AT_+^x$ a subgroup.
As $T_+^x$ is soluble, we have $AT_+^x<G$ by the cited condition on $X,Y<G$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(T_+^x)$ and $A$ is soluble.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $y\in G$ with $A N_G(T_-)^y$ a subgroup.
As $A$ is soluble, we have $A N_G(T_-)^y<G$ by the cited condition on $X,Y<G$.
By maximality of $N_G(T_-)$, we have $A\leq N_G(T_-)^y$.
Consequently, $|A|\mid12$.
Because $A\cap T_+^x=1$, the subgroup $A$ is cyclic.
The maximal subgroup $\operatorname{Sz}(q)\wr S_2$ has order prime to $3$.
As $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $z\in G$ such that $A(\operatorname{Sz}(q)\wr C_2)^z$ is a subgroup.
Because $A$ is soluble, we have $A(\operatorname{Sz}(q)\wr C_2)^z\ne G$.
By maximality, we have $A\leq(\operatorname{Sz}(q)\wr C_2)^z$.
Hence, $3\nmid|A|$ and $|A|\in\{1,2,4\}$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 2.} ] Every $2$-subgroup $P\leq G$ with $u\in P$ lies in $U$.
\end{itemize}
The group has $2$ involution classes $\mathcal I_s$ and $\mathcal I_b$.
For these classes, the centralizer orders are $q^{12}(q^2+1)(q-1)$ and $q^{10}(q^2-1)$ \cite[Table A.2]{HimstedtHuang2009}.
To identify the involutions in $N_G(T_+)$, we choose $t_0\in N_G(T_+)$ with $|t_0|=2$ and $t_0^{-1}rt_0=r^{-1}$ for every $r\in T_+$.
Then, $t_0\in\mathcal I_b$ by \cite[Corollary 4.4]{BurnessThomasFixity}.
Since $T_+$ is odd and $N_G(T_+)/T_+\cong C_{12}$,
for each involution $t\in N_G(T_+)$ there exists $z\in T_+$ with $t^z=t_0$.
For $|A|\in\{2,4\}$, the unique involution of $A$ belongs to $\mathcal I_b$.
We next construct a unipotent subgroup for $|A|\in\{2,4\}$.
Let $\theta=2^n$ and let $U$ be a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $G$.
For $1\leq i\leq12$, we use the rational root maps $\alpha_i:\mathbb{F}_q\to U$ from \cite[Section 2]{HimstedtHuang2009}.
Every $g\in U$ has a unique ordered expression $g=\alpha_1(t_1)\cdots\alpha_{12}(t_{12})$ with $t_i\in\mathbb{F}_q$.
For $1\leq i\leq12$, let $t_i:U\to\mathbb{F}_q$ send $g$ to $t_i$ in that expression.
For $i\in\{1,4,5,6\}$, multiplication satisfies
$$
 \alpha_i(t)\alpha_i(u)
 =\alpha_i(t+u)\alpha_{j(i)}(tu^{2\theta}), (j(1),j(4),j(5),j(6))=(2,8,12,11).
$$
For $i\notin\{1,4,5,6\}$, we have $\alpha_i(t)\alpha_i(u)=\alpha_i(t+u)$.
The corrected commutator relations are in \cite[Table 1]{HimstedtHuang2009}.

We take $u=\alpha_1(1)\alpha_3(1)$ and $C=\langle u\rangle$.
Then, we collect the factors and obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
 v=u^2&=\alpha_2(1)\alpha_4(1)\alpha_5(1)
              \alpha_7(1)\alpha_{11}(1)\alpha_{12}(1),\\
 u^4&=\alpha_7(1)\alpha_8(1)\alpha_9(1)\alpha_{12}(1),\\
 u^8&=\alpha_{12}(1), u^{16}=1.
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, $|C|=16$, and the unique involution $u^8$ of $C$ belongs to $\mathcal I_s$
\cite[Table A.4]{HimstedtHuang2009}.
Let $\mathbf G$ be the algebraic group of type $F_4$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_2$ containing $G$.
In the root numbering of \cite[Section 2]{HimstedtHuang2009}, the roots $r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$ are simple and $r_6=r_2+r_3$.
Since $\alpha_1(1)=x_3(1)x_2(1)x_6(1)$ and $\alpha_3(1)=x_4(1)x_1(1)$,
the $4$ absolute simple-root coordinates of $u$ are all $1$.
As the $4$ simple-root coordinates are nonzero, we obtain from Steinberg's criterion \cite[Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.3, pp.~54--55]{SteinbergRegular} that $u$ is regular unipotent and belongs to a unique algebraic Borel subgroup $\mathbf B$.
No restriction on the characteristic is required in the cited criterion.
Let $R_u(\mathbf B)$ be the unipotent radical of $\mathbf B$.
By the root maps, we have $U=R_u(\mathbf B)\cap G$.
If a finite $2$-subgroup $P\leq G$ contains $u$, then $P\leq U^g$ for some $g\in G$.
Because $u\in\mathbf B^g$ and $\mathbf B$ is unique, we have $\mathbf B^g=\mathbf B$.
Therefore, $U^g=R_u(\mathbf B^g)\cap G=U$ and $P\leq U$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 3.} ] Every involution in $C_U(u^2)$ belongs to $\mathcal I_s$.
\end{itemize}
We claim that every involution in $U$ centralizing $v$ belongs to $\mathcal I_s$.
To prove the claim, let $g=\alpha_1(t_1)\cdots\alpha_{12}(t_{12})\in C_U(v)$ be an involution.
In each row, we use the zero equations from the preceding rows.
For a row labelled by $\alpha_i$, the coordinate function is $t_i:U\to\mathbb{F}_q$.
We use $t_i(gv)=t_i(vg)$ in a row with $gv=vg$.
In addition, in a row with $g^2=1$, we use $t_i(g^2)=0$.
In the last column, every listed expression equals $0$.
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{1.12}{1.12}
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
Condition & Coordinate & Required zero\\\hline
$g^2=1$ & $\alpha_2$ & $t_1^{2\theta+1}$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_6$ & $t_3$\\
$g^2=1$ & $\alpha_8$ & $t_4^{2\theta+1}$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_7$ & $t_2$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_9$ & $t_5$\\
$g^2=1$ & $\alpha_{11}$ & $t_6^{2\theta+1}$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_{10}$ & $t_7+t_8$\\
$g^2=1$ & $\alpha_{12}$ & $t_7t_8$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_{11}$ & $t_9$\\
$gv=vg$ & $\alpha_{12}$ & $t_{10}$\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
By the seventh row, we have $t_7=t_8$.
By the eighth row, we have $t_7=t_8=0$.
Thus, $g=\alpha_{11}(t_{11})\alpha_{12}(t_{12})$.
If $t_{11}\ne0$, then let $x=\alpha_3(t_{12}/t_{11})\in U$.
Then, $g^x=\alpha_{11}(t_{11})$.
By torus scaling, we choose $h\in N_G(U)$ with $g^{xh}=\alpha_{11}(1)$.
If $t_{11}=0$, then we choose $h\in N_G(U)$ with $g^h=\alpha_{12}(1)$ by torus scaling.
Both representatives belong to $\mathcal I_s$.
Hence, every involution $g\in C_U(v)$ belongs to $\mathcal I_s$.

\begin{itemize}
\item[{\bf Step 4.} ] We have $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Firstly, suppose that $|A|=2$ and write $A=\langle a\rangle$.
The element $a$ lies in $\mathcal I_b$, whereas the involution of $C$ lies in $\mathcal I_s$.
Consequently, $A\cap C^x=1$ for every $x\in G$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $H=AC^x$ a subgroup of order $32$.
Replacing $H,A,a$ by $H^{x^{-1}},A^{x^{-1}},a^{x^{-1}}$, assume that $H=AC$.
Since $u$ is regular, $H\leq U$.
As $[H:C]=2$, $C\lhd H$.
Thus, $a^{-1}ua=u^k$ with $k\in\{1,7,9,15\}$ modulo $16$.
By the first square constraint, we have $t_1(a)=0$.
By the commutator relations, only elements of $\alpha_1(\mathbb{F}_q)$ can change $t_2(g)$ when conjugating $g\in U$.
Because $t_1(a)=0$ and $t_2(u)=0$, we have $t_2(a^{-1}ua)=0$.
But $t_2(u^k)=((k-1)/2)\cdot1_{\mathbb{F}_q}$ for odd $k$.
As $\operatorname{char}\mathbb{F}_q=2$, we obtain $k\equiv1\pmod4$.
Therefore, $k\in\{1,9\}$.
Because $k\in\{1,9\}$, we have $a^{-1}va=u^{2k}=u^2=v$.
By the calculation in $C_U(v)$, we have $a\in\mathcal I_s$.
This contradicts $a\in\mathcal I_b$.

Now, suppose that $|A|=4$ and $A=\langle a\rangle$.
Since the unique involutions of $A$ and $C$ lie in different $G$-classes, we have $A\cap C^x=1$ for every $x\in G$.
Because $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $H=AC^x$ a subgroup of order $64$.
Replacing $H,A,a$ by $H^{x^{-1}},A^{x^{-1}},a^{x^{-1}}$, assume that $H=AC\leq U$.
Let $\rho:H\to S_{H/C}$ satisfy $\rho(h)(gC)=hgC$ for $h,g\in H$.
As $[H:C]=4$, the image $\rho(H)\leq S_4$ is a $2$-group of order at most $8$.
Thus, $\operatorname{Core}_H(C)$ has order at least $8$.
The cyclic subgroup $\operatorname{Core}_H(C)$ has characteristic subgroup $\langle v\rangle$ of order $8$.
Consequently, $\langle v\rangle\unlhd H$.
Since $\langle v\rangle\unlhd H$, conjugation by $a$ induces an automorphism of $\langle v\rangle\cong C_8$.
As $\operatorname{Aut}(C_8)$ has exponent $2$, we have $a^{-2}va^2=v$.
By the calculation in $C_U(v)$, we have $a^2\in\mathcal I_s$.
This contradicts $a^2\in\mathcal I_b$.
For $|A|=2$ and $|A|=4$, we have obtained contradictions from $AC^x\leq G$.
Therefore, $A=1$ throughout the family.

label: thm:ree
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite{LPS}, we have $G\ne XY$ for all $X,Y<G$.
We use the maximal torus normalizers of orders $6(q+3^{m+1}+1)$ and $6(q-3^{m+1}+1)$
\cite[proof of Theorem 1, Case II]{GT23}.
Since the $2$ torus orders are coprime, we obtain the following bound.
By Lemma \ref{lem:max}, we have $|A|\mid6$
for any proper ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup $A$.

We first construct an odd-order torus $D$ with $3\nmid|N_G(D)|$.
Let $s=3^m$ and $d=(q-1)/2$.
We use $V=\mathbb{F}_q^7$ and the split torus $H=\{h(\lambda):\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^*\}$.
For $\lambda\in\mathbb{F}_q^*$, we have
$$
 h(\lambda)=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda^s,\lambda^{1-s},\lambda^{2s-1},1,
                  \lambda^{1-2s},\lambda^{s-1},\lambda^{-s}).
$$
The normalizer $N_G(H)$ is dihedral of order $2(q-1)$
\cite[Proposition 3.1(9)]{Baarnhielm2014}. Let $D$ be the subgroup of $H$
of order $d$. Since $4s-2<d$ for $s\geq3$, the $7$ displayed exponents are distinct modulo $d$.
Hence, a generator of $D$ has $7$ distinct eigenvalues. The centralizer of this generator fixes the first and
last coordinate lines. Their common stabilizer in $G$ is $H$
\cite[Proposition 3.2]{Baarnhielm2014}. Thus, $C_G(D)=H$ and $N_G(D)\leq N_G(H)$.
We have $3\nmid|N_G(H)|$.

Suppose that $|A|=3$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AD^x$ a subgroup.
We have $|K|=3d$.
As $D^x$ has odd order and index $3$ in $K$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:index3} that $D^x\unlhd K$.
Thus, $A\leq N_G(D^x)$.
Because $3\nmid|N_G(D^x)|$, we have a contradiction.

Suppose that $|A|=6$.
Since $A$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ with $K=AD^x$ a subgroup.
Since $\gcd(|A|,|D|)=1$, we have $|K|=6d$.
For the regular action of $K$ on itself, the sign homomorphism $\epsilon:K\to\{1,-1\}$ sends $g$ to $\operatorname{sgn}(k\mapsto gk)$, where $k\in K$.
An involution acts as $3d$ transpositions, so $\epsilon$ is nontrivial.
As $\epsilon(K)=\{1,-1\}$, the kernel $L=\ker\epsilon$ has order $3d$.
Moreover, every subgroup of $K$ of odd order has trivial image under $\epsilon$ and lies in $L$.
Hence, $D^x\leq L$.
We also have a subgroup $R\leq A\cap L$ of order $3$.
As $|D|$ is odd and $[L:D^x]=3$, we obtain from Lemma \ref{lem:index3} that $D^x\unlhd L$.
Thus, $R\leq N_G(D^x)$.
Because $|R|=3$ and $3\nmid|N_G(D^x)|$, we have a contradiction.

Now, suppose that $|A|=2$. We construct a cyclic subgroup
$B$ of order $9$ with $|N_G(B)|$ odd.
For this construction, let $U$ be a Sylow $3$-subgroup and let $e=3^{m+1}$.
We use the coordinates $U=\{u(a,b,c):(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{F}_q^3\}$
\cite[(3.10)--(3.13)]{Baarnhielm2014}.
They satisfy
$$
\begin{aligned}
 u(a,b,c)^{-1}
   &=u(-a,-b-a^{e+1},-c-ab+a^{e+2}),\\
 u(a,b,c)^{u(v,w,z)}
   &=u(a,b-av^e+va^e,\,*).
\end{aligned}
$$
Only the first $2$ coordinates in the second formula are used below.
For conjugation by the involution $j=h(-1)$, we have
$u(a,b,c)^j=u(-a,b,-c)$.
In addition, every element $u(a,b,c)$ with $a\ne0$ has order $9$.
Moreover, distinct Sylow $3$-subgroups intersect trivially and
$N_G(U)=U\rtimes H$ \cite[Proposition 3.1(2), (5), (6)]{Baarnhielm2014}.
Consequently, $N_G(B)\leq N_G(U)$ for every nontrivial $B\leq U$.
The cyclic group $H$ has unique involution $j$.
For each involution $g\in U\rtimes H$, we choose $y\in U$ with $g^y=j$ by Schur--Zassenhaus.

Write $\operatorname{Tr}=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_3}:\mathbb{F}_q\to\mathbb{F}_3$.
Since $\operatorname{Tr}:\mathbb{F}_q\to\mathbb{F}_3$ is surjective, we choose $\beta\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)\ne\operatorname{Tr}(1)$.
Let $u=u(1,\beta,0)$ and $B=\langle u\rangle$.
For $y=u(v,w,z)\in U$, the second coordinate of $u^y$ is $\beta-v^e+v$.
As $\operatorname{Tr}(v^e)=\operatorname{Tr}(v)$, we have $\operatorname{Tr}(\beta-v^e+v)=\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)$.

Suppose that $g\in N_G(B)$ is an involution.
Choose $y\in U$ with $g^y=j$, and let $u'=u^y=u(1,b,c)$.
Then, $j\in N_G(\langle u'\rangle)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(b)=\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)$.
Since $u'^j=u(-1,b,-c)$, we have $j\notin C_G(u')$.
As $|j|=2$ and $\langle u'\rangle\cong C_9$, we have $j^{-1}u'j=u'^{-1}$.
By comparing the second coordinates, we obtain that $b=-b-1$.
Because the characteristic is $3$, we have $b=1$. But $b=1$ contradicts
$\operatorname{Tr}(b)=\operatorname{Tr}(\beta)\ne\operatorname{Tr}(1)$.

Thus, $N_G(B)$ contains no involution.
For $|A|=2$, Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers} contradicts ordinary permutability of $A$.
Hence, $A=1$.
head: environment

label: lem:subgroup-products
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:subgroup-products}
Let $H_1,\ldots,H_s$ represent the conjugacy classes of subgroups
of $G$. Let $h_i=|H_i|$ and
$S_k=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,s\}:\exists x\in G,\ H_i^x\leq H_k\}$.
Suppose that $H_i$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.
For every $j\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$, there exist $k\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$ and $d\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $i,j\in S_k$, $d=h_i h_j/h_k$ and $d\mid\gcd(h_i,h_j)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $H_i$ is ordinary $G$-permutable, we choose $x\in G$ such that $K=H_iH_j^x$ is a subgroup.
We choose $z\in G$ and $k$ with $K^z=H_k$.
As $H_i^z\leq H_k$ and $H_j^{xz}\leq H_k$, we have $i,j\in S_k$.
We have $d=h_i h_j/h_k=|H_i\cap H_j^x|\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Hence, $d\mid\gcd(h_i,h_j)$.
head: environment

label: prop:finite-tables
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:finite-tables}
Let $G$ be a group in the following list $$
\begin{gathered}
 A_7,\ldots,A_{13}, \operatorname{PSU}_4(2), \operatorname{PSU}_4(3), \operatorname{PSL}_4(3),\\
 \operatorname{PSp}_4(5), \operatorname{PSp}_6(2), G_2(3), G_2(4), {}^3D_4(2), \Omega^+_8(2).
\end{gathered}
$$
Then, $G$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup.
In $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(4)$, the proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable
subgroups are $\langle t\rangle$ with $|t|=2$ and $|C_G(t)|=256$.
For any $2$ such involutions $t,u$, there exists $x\in G$ with $t^x=u$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first read the lists $S_k$ and the orders $h_k$ from TomLib.
For each $i$ with $1<H_i<G$, we search for an index $j$ for which no $k$ satisfies Lemma \ref{lem:subgroup-products}.
For each pair $(i,j)$ found in the search, we save $i,j,h_i,h_j$.
Then, we examine every $k$ with $i,j\in S_k$.
If $h_k\mid h_i h_j$, then we verify that $(h_i h_j/h_k)\nmid\gcd(h_i,h_j)$.
If $h_k\nmid h_i h_j$, then $h_i h_j/h_k$ is not an integer.
Consequently, $H_i$ is not ordinary $G$-permutable for each pair $(i,j)$ found in the search.

In the following table, we include the trivial subgroup and $G$ in the number of subgroup classes.
In each column headed ``Remaining classes'', we list the classes $i$ with $1<H_i<G$
satisfying the condition in Lemma \ref{lem:subgroup-products} for every $j$.
In addition, class indices refer to the corresponding TomLib table.
\begin{center}
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{6pt}
\renewcommand{1.12}{1.12}
\begin{tabular}{|l|r|r|l|r|r|}
\hline
$G$ & \shortstack{Subgroup\\classes} & \shortstack{Remaining\\classes} & $G$ & \shortstack{Subgroup\\classes} & \shortstack{Remaining\\classes}\\\hline
$G_2(3)$ & $433$ & none & $A_{12}$ & $2537$ & none\\
$G_2(4)$ & $4300$ & none & $A_{13}$ & $4558$ & none\\
${}^3D_4(2)$ & $2867$ & none & $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ & $116$ & none\\
$A_5$ & $9$ & $2$ & $\operatorname{PSU}_4(3)$ & $381$ & none\\
$A_6$ & $22$ & $2$ & $\operatorname{PSL}_4(3)$ & $817$ & none\\
$A_7$ & $40$ & none & $\operatorname{PSp}_4(4)$ & $496$ & $2$\\
$A_8$ & $137$ & none & $\operatorname{PSp}_4(5)$ & $307$ & none\\
$A_9$ & $223$ & none & $\operatorname{PSp}_6(2)$ & $1369$ & none\\
$A_{10}$ & $430$ & none & $\Omega^+_8(2)$ & $11171$ & none\\
$A_{11}$ & $788$ & none & & &\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

For each group listed with ``none'', every $i$ with $1<H_i<G$ has an index $j$ for which Lemma \ref{lem:subgroup-products} fails.
For $G\in\{A_5,A_6,\operatorname{PSp}_4(4)\}$, we consider only the classes $i$ with $1<H_i<G$.
Among these classes, only $H_2$ satisfies the condition for every $j$.
From TomLib, we obtain $|H_2|=2$.

For each of $G\in\{A_5,A_6,\operatorname{PSp}_4(4)\}$, let $n_j$ be the class index of $N_G(H_j)$.
We choose $y_j\in G$ with $N_G(H_j)^{y_j}=H_{n_j}$.
As $2\in S_{n_j}$ for every $j\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$, we choose $z_j\in G$ with $H_2^{z_j}\leq H_{n_j}$.
Then, $x_j=z_jy_j^{-1}$ satisfies $H_2^{x_j}\leq N_G(H_j)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:involution-normalizers}, we conclude that $H_2$ is ordinary $G$-permutable.

To identify $H_2$ in $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(4)$, we compare its $3$ involution classes.
The centralizer orders are $256,3840,3840$.
Since the involutions in class $2$ have centralizer order $256$, the ordinary $G$-permutable subgroups are precisely $\langle t\rangle$ with $|t|=2$ and $|C_G(t)|=256$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Firstly, we verify the $5$ possibilities.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] For $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$, we use the classification in \cite{GT25}.
\item[(2)] For the Suzuki groups, we use the classification in \cite{GT23}.
\item[(3)] For the sporadic groups, we use the classification in \cite{GT22}.
Only $J_1$ has proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroups, namely all subgroups of order $2$.
The Tits group has no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup by \cite{GT22}.
\item[(4)] By Corollary \ref{cor:symplectic-even}, we have precisely the involution class in (4).
Every other simple $\operatorname{Sp}_4(q)$ with even $q$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $\operatorname{Sp}_4(q)$-permutable subgroup.
\item[(5)] By Theorem \ref{thm:symplectic-four-odd-all}, we have precisely the subgroups in (5).
For every other odd prime power $q$, the group $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$ has no proper nontrivial ordinary $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$-permutable subgroup.
\end{itemize}

We now consider the other simple groups.
Let $A<G$ be ordinary $G$-permutable.
By Corollaries \ref{cor:all-linear} and \ref{cor:all-unitary}, we have $A=1$ for simple $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ or $\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ with $n\geq3$.
In addition, by Theorem \ref{thm:alternating-all}, we have $A=1$ for $G=A_n$ with $n\geq7$.
For the other simple alternating groups, we use
$A_5\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)$ and $A_6\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(9)$, which belong to (1).
By Corollary \ref{cor:symplectic-all-higher-rank}, we also have $A=1$ for simple $G=\operatorname{PSp}_{2m}(q)$ with $m\geq3$.

By Corollaries \ref{cor:orthogonal-minus-all} and \ref{cor:orthogonal-plus-all}, we have $A=1$ for simple $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega^\pm_{2m}(q)$ with $m\geq4$.
By Theorem \ref{thm:orthogonal-odd}, we also have $A=1$ for $G=\Omega_{2m+1}(q)$ with $m\geq3$ and odd $q$.
For the exceptional families, we first use Theorems \ref{thm:g2-all} and \ref{thm:triality} to obtain that $A=1$ for $G_2(q)$ and ${}^3D_4(q)$.
In addition, by Theorem \ref{thm:e6}, we have $A=1$ for $E_6(q)$ and ${}^2E_6(q)$.
By Theorem \ref{thm:f4}, we conclude that $A=1$ for $F_4(q)$.
By Theorems \ref{thm:e7} and \ref{thm:e8}, we also have $A=1$ for $E_7(q)$ and $E_8(q)$.
Finally, by Theorems \ref{thm:large-ree} and \ref{thm:ree}, we have $A=1$ for the Ree groups.
In small dimensions, we use
$$
\begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{PSU}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{PSp}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q),\ 
 \mathrm P\Omega_3(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q),\\
 \mathrm P\Omega_4^-(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q^2),\ 
 \mathrm P\Omega_5(q)\cong\operatorname{PSp}_4(q),\\
 \mathrm P\Omega_6^+(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_4(q).
\end{gathered}
$$
The isomorphism $\mathrm P\Omega_6^-(q)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(q)$ is included in Corollary \ref{cor:orthogonal-minus-all}.
In even characteristic, $\Omega_{2m+1}(q)\cong\operatorname{Sp}_{2m}(q)$.
For the small derived groups, we use $\operatorname{Sp}_4(2)'\cong A_6$ and $G_2(2)'\cong\operatorname{PSU}_3(3)$.
Since ${}^2G_2(3)'\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(8)$, we have included ${}^2G_2(3)'$ in (1).
For the Tits group ${}^2F_4(2)'$, we use (3).
By the classification of finite simple groups, we have proved Theorem \ref{thm:main} for every nonabelian finite simple group $G$.

title: Remark
body_md:
The cyclic groups of prime order have no proper nontrivial subgroups.
Every normal subgroup $N\lhd G$ satisfies $NH=HN$ for every $H\leq G$.
Hence, a finite group $G\ne1$ with no proper nontrivial ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup is simple.
However, $A_5$ is simple and has ordinary $A_5$-permutable subgroups of order $2$.
